explanation: Rotation of plan/elevation until parallel to the other plane reveals TL and true inclinations θ and Φ.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: The TRUE INCLINATION θ of a line with the HP is seen in:
options: the ELEVATION-based construction only when the line is parallel to VP (or rotated to that position)
explanation: θ appears in the elevation of the line rotated parallel to VP; Φ similarly in the plan.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: The HORIZONTAL TRACE (HT) of a line is the point where:
explanation: HT is the piercing point on HP; VT is on VP. Traces help describe the line's location fully.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: For a line in the FIRST quadrant inclined to both planes with ends at different heights, the distance from xy of any point's:
options: front view = distance in front of VP
top view = height of the point
front view = distance of the point ABOVE HP
explanation: Elevation abscissa from xy measures height; plan distance from xy measures the in-front-of-VP depth.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem:
Assertion (A): A line parallel to both HP and VP is seen foreshortened in NEITHER view.
Reason (R): Projection on a plane PARALLEL to the line preserves its true length; parallelism to both planes keeps TL in both views.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Parallel-plane projection preserves TL (R) exactly as claimed in (A).

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: When a line is inclined to both planes, its plan is always SHORTER than the line's true length.
explanation: True: plan \(=TL\cos\theta\) and FV \(=TL\cos\phi\); both foreshorten with nonzero inclinations.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: Which hold for a line INCLINED to both principal planes? (Select all that apply.)
options: True length exceeds both projected lengths
explanation: Both views are foreshortened (cosine factors), so TL is greater than either view — the fourth is false.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: In projecting points and lines, the PROJECTOR (link) between front view and top view of a point is:
options: a line PERPENDICULAR to xy through the point's projections
explanation: Projection projectors meet at right angles to xy, keeping elevation and plan of one point vertically aligned.

stem: A plane SURFACE parallel to the VP appears in the front view in:
explanation: Parallel-to-plane surfaces project true shape; perpendicular ones collapse to an edge line.

stem: A plane PERPENDICULAR to the HP projects on the HP as:
explanation: A vertical plane is edge-on to the HP, so its plan collapses into a single line.

stem: A circular lamina INCLINED to the HP appears in plan as:
explanation: Inclination partially foreshortens the diameter across the incline; a circle's oblique view is an ellipse.

stem: When a plane figure is inclined to BOTH principal planes, the usual solution strategy is:
options: split into TWO stages: first inclined to one plane (resting on an edge/diagonal — apparent shape with true inclination), then tilted to the second
explanation: Two-stage working (one inclination at a time) converts compound inclination problems into simple ones.

stem: A lamina perpendicular to one plane and INCLINED to the other gives, on the second plane:
explanation: Edge view falls on the plane it is perpendicular to; the other plane sees the apparent shape.

stem: A HEXAGONAL lamina resting on VP parallel to it will show the hexagon's TRUE shape in the:
explanation: Parallel-to-VP surfaces present their true outline in the front view.

stem:
Assertion (A): A plane's apparent shape on an inclined projection is always smaller in extent than its true shape.
Reason (R): Foreshortening applies cosine factors for the inclination angle to the dimensions across the tilt.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Cosine foreshortening across the tilt (R) is precisely the cause of shrinkage noted in (A).

stem: The edge view of any plane is always a straight LINE.
explanation: True: any plane surface seen edge-on collapses to a straight line in that projection.

stem: An AUXILIARY PLANE is needed because ordinary VP/HP views:
options: may NOT show the TRUE shape of a face inclined to both principal planes; an auxiliary plane parallel to that face will
explanation: Auxiliary planes parallel to inclined edges/faces reveal true size/shape (or edge view) unobtainable directly.

stem: An AUXILIARY VERTICAL PLANE (AVP) is:
options: perpendicular to HP and INCLINED to VP
explanation: AVP stands normal to HP at an angle to VP, giving an auxiliary front view (of slanted-face structures).

stem: An AUXILIARY INCLINED PLANE (AIP) is perpendicular to:
options: VP and INCLINED to the HP
explanation: AIP normal to VP but inclined to HP shows the true shape of a surface tilted from horizontal.

stem: Projection ONTO an auxiliary plane from standard views requires carrying over, perpendicular to the new reference line:
options: the SAME heights (from FV) or depths (from TV) measured perpendicular to xy, transferred to the auxiliary view
explanation: Distances measured perpendicular to the original reference line are re-measured from the new reference line.

stem: An auxiliary view that shows a sloping roof surface IN TRUE SHAPE is typically drawn looking:
options: shapes parallel NORMAL to that surface (auxiliary plane parallel to it)
explanation: Looking normal (auxiliary plane parallel) to the incline gives true shape — used for roof plates, machine bases.

stem:
Assertion (A): With an auxiliary plane parallel to an inclined surface, the projected view of that surface is identical in shape to its true shape.
Reason (R): Lines parallel to a plane of projection project true length and angles, so a plane figure parallel to the projection plane projects true shape.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: True-length projection on parallel planes (R) yields exactly the claim in (A).

stem: An auxiliary TOP view projected on an AIP shows the true inclination of the surface with the VP.
explanation: False: AIP (perpendicular to VP, inclined to HP) shows true inclination with the HP, not the VP.

stem: The xy (reference) line represents:
options: the INTERSECTION of HP and VP on the drawing sheet
explanation: After rotating HP coplanar with VP, their common hinge is xy — heights plotted above, depths below.

stem: In INDIA/ISO convention, engineering offices generally use which projection system as standard?
explanation: BIS/ISO practice adopts first-angle (the projection symbol in the title block states whichever is used).

stem: Which DIMENSIONING rules follow drawing conventions? (Select all that apply.)
options: Dimension figures above and along the dimension line
explanation: Repetition breeds conflict; one clear placement per feature is the rule — the rest are standard conventions.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: A line parallel to HP and inclined to VP shows true length in the:
explanation: Horizontal lines show TL in the plan; their apparent lengths project into the elevation.

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: If plan length = 60 mm and true length = 75 mm for a line parallel to VP, its inclination to HP is about:
explanation: \(\text{plan}=TL\cos\theta \Rightarrow \theta=\cos^{-1}(60/75)\approx 36.9°\).

stem:
Assertion (A): A centre line should be drawn through every circular feature (hole, shaft) in its end view.
Reason (R): Centre lines locate axes of revolution and make alignment/dimensioning of circular features unambiguous.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Axis location for clarity/dimensioning (R) is exactly why centre lines are always drawn (A).

stem: A SQUARE lamina perpendicular to HP and inclined at 45° to VP shows its true shape in:
options: NEITHER standard view — apparent shapes in both, since it is inclined to both
explanation: Inclined to both planes → foreshortened views in both; true shape needs an auxiliary view.

stem: Which statements about auxiliary projections are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Auxiliary views show true shapes of inclined surfaces
Transfers take distances perpendicular to new reference line
explanation: AIP is parallel to VP (and inclined to HP), not parallel to HP; the rest are correct definitions.

stem: An object placed in the THIRD quadrant lies:
options: above HP, in front of VP
explanation: Quadrant III is below HP and behind VP; top view projects above xy in first-angle convention layouts.

stem: A LEADER line on a drawing ends, when pointing inside a circular feature or solid face, with:
options: a dot (if ending on a surface) or arrowhead (if on an outline)
explanation: Leader arrowheads touch outlines; a dot (~3 mm) terminates leaders ending on faces/surfaces.

stem: CUTTING-PLANE lines indicating where a section is taken are drawn:
options: CHAIN thin with THICK ENDS (arrows marking the direction of sight)
explanation: Chain thin body with thickened ends carries direction arrows and section letters (A-A etc.).

topic: Projections of Points and Lines Inclined to Both Planes
stem: When BOTH ends of a line have the same height above HP, its:
explanation: Equal end heights project the elevation as a line PARALLEL to xy (constant height); equal depths would do likewise in the plan.

stem: A triangular lamina has its true shape only when parallel to a projection plane; its EDGE view appears as a:
explanation: Any plane — curved edges included — collapses to a straight-line edge view when seen exactly edge-on.

stem: Primary purpose of an auxiliary FRONT view on an AVP is to display the:
options: true length/shape of features parallel to that AVP (e.g. slanted faces perpendicular to HP)
explanation: AVP parallel to an inclined-but-vertical face shows that face's true shape in an auxiliary front view.

stem: SOLIDS used in engineering-graphics projection problems are broadly divided into:
options: polyhedra (bounded by planes: prisms, pyramids) and solids of REVOLUTION (cylinder, cone, sphere)
explanation: Plane-faced polyhedra and rotatable curved-surface solids make up the two great families projected.

stem: A PRISM is a polyhedron with two equal parallel ends (bases) joined by:
options: PARALLELOGRAM (rectangular for a right prism) side faces
explanation: Bases are congruent polygons; lateral faces are rectangles (right prism) or parallelograms (oblique prism).

stem: A PYRAMID has a polygonal base and triangular side faces meeting at a point called the:
explanation: The apex; the line joining base centre to apex is the axis; base defines pyramid name (square, hexagonal...).

stem: A solid is called a RIGHT solid when its AXIS is:
options: PERPENDICULAR to its base plane (e.g. right circular cone/cylinder)
explanation: Right solids stand upright on bases; oblique solids have axes slanting to the base.

stem: A cylinder is generated by revolving:
options: a rectangle about one of its sides (as axis)
explanation: Rectangle rotated about a side sweeps a right circular cylinder; triangle about a leg sweeps a cone.

stem: A right circular CONE is generated by revolving:
options: a RIGHT TRIANGLE about one of its PERPENDICULAR sides
explanation: The leg is the cone height, the other leg sweeps the base circle, the hypotenuse trace: the slant height.

stem: The FIVE regular (Platonic) polyhedra each have all faces equal regular polygons; the set is:
explanation: Faces/edges/vertices: 4, 6, 8, 12, 20 regular polygonal faces respectively — the five Platonic solids.

stem: A FRUSTUM of a pyramid/cone is the part:
options: left after cutting off the TOP by a plane PARALLEL to the base
explanation: A cut parallel to the base leaves a frustum with two similar bases; oblique cuts give truncated solids.

stem: Every lateral (side) face of a RIGHT PRISM is a rectangle.
explanation: True: right prisms have edges perpendicular to the base, forcing rectangular lateral faces.

stem: Which are SOLIDS OF REVOLUTION? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Square prism is a polyhedron made of planes; cylinder, cone and sphere rotate profiles into being.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: When the axis of a solid is PERPENDICULAR to the HP, the solid's TOP VIEW shows:
options: its BASE in true shape (hexagon for hexagonal prism, circle for cylinder)
explanation: Vertical-axis solids rest on their base, which lies on HP, so its plan is the base's true outline.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A square PRISM with axis vertical (perpendicular to HP) shows its FRONT VIEW as a:
options: RECTANGLE of width base edge and height = axis length
explanation: Prism elevations with vertical axis are rectangles; width = base edge dimension as seen.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A cone resting on HP with axis vertical has its FRONT VIEW as:
options: an ISOSCELES TRIANGLE (base = circle diameter, height = axis)
explanation: Elevation of a cone = isoceles triangle; plan = circle with centre point (apex projection).

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: With a solid's axis INCLINED to one plane (say HP) and parallel to VP, its projection is solved:
options: in TWO STAGES: first simple position (axis perpendicular to HP), then tilted to the given angle keeping the VP condition
explanation: Simple-position first, then incline and re-transfer: the universal two-stage method for solids.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: In the FIRST STAGE of projecting a solid inclined to planes, the axis is drawn:
options: PARALLEL to both planes at once
PERPENDICULAR to that plane with respect to which the inclination is stated (simple position)
explanation: Simple position orients the axis perpendicular to the plane of stated inclination — plan/elevation are simple.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A solid resting 'on one of its BASE EDGES on HP with axis inclined' changes from stage I by:
options: TILTING the previously vertical simple-position view about that edge so the axis makes the given angle with HP
explanation: The edge is the hinge of tilt; after tilting the outline is re-projected point-by-consistent-point.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: After the second stage (tilting), EVERY point of the final view is fixed by:
options: combining distances: vertically from the reference height line of stage II and horizontally from the plan transferred from stage I
explanation: Projectors from the tilted view intersect depth transfers from the unchanged original plan to place each point.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A cone lying on a GENERATOR (slant element) on HP has, in plan, its:
options: the base seen as an APPARENT ELLIPSE with the apex shifted toward its rim (axis now parallel to HP)
explanation: With the axis//HP, plan shows ellipse-like base and apex projection on the base circumference end.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem:
Assertion (A): For solids inclined to both planes, projection needs THREE successive stages.
Reason (R): One stage handles the axis-perpendicular simple position, the second imposes one inclination, and the THIRD imposes the other inclination via auxiliary thinking/plan rotation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Doubly-inclined solids are worked stage by stage: simple position, first inclination, second inclination (R) — hence the multi-stage routine (A).

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: When a cone's axis is inclined at θ to HP with its APEX in HP, the':' no — the cone's:
options: frustum conical base LOzeNGE removed: the front view shows only a triangle lying wholly above xy touching at apex
explanation: Tilting about the apex lying at HP boundary pivots the base ellipse wholly above xy in elevation.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: The APPARENT shape of a circular base of an inclined cylinder/cone in plan is obtained by:
options: dividing the base circle into parts, transferring equal divisions through projectors and joining the loci smoothly (ellipse)
explanation: Twelve-division transfer from true circle through inclined-view projectors gives the pointwise ellipse.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A hexagonal pyramid standing on its base on HP with two base edges perpendicular to VP shows all its slant edges in true length in the front view.
explanation: False: only slant edges parallel to VP show true length; others appear foreshortened in the elevation.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: The shortest line showing a cone's GENERATOR in TRUE LENGTH is seen:
options: in the view where the generator is PARALLEL to the projection plane
explanation: Generators parallel to VP appear TL in elevation, e.g., the extreme outline generators.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A square prism tilted so that its AXIS makes 45° with HP will have the front-view outline:
options: still rectangle with same height as stage-I rectangle height × cos45° approximately
explanation: Tilting foreshortens the apparent height by cosθ; the laterally-projected widths adjust per rotation loci.

stem: For a solid whose best (true) face shape is inclined to both principal planes, the draftsperson uses:
options: an AUXILIARY VIEW taken looking NORMAL to that inclined face
explanation: Auxiliary views on planes parallel to inclined faces give the true shape lost in principal views.

stem: An auxiliary FRONT view of a solid is projected:
options: PERPENDICULARLY from the original ELEVATION (heights are common to both)
explanation: Auxiliary front views share heights with the original elevation; projectors run perpendicular to new reference line.

stem: An AUXILIARY TOP view of an object projected on an AIP is analogous to a top view except the reference line is now:
options: the intersection line of the AIP with the VP (drawn inclined to xy)
explanation: Auxiliary reference line = trace of the auxiliary plane with the principal plane it is perpendicular to.

stem: Auxiliary views of solids solve the practical drawing problem of:
options: SHOWING true profiles of sloping webs, lugs and inclined flanges that no principal view reveals
explanation: True-shape layout of inclined features for manufacturing is the industrial birthright of auxiliary views.

stem:
Assertion (A): In auxiliary views, projectors from the original view are drawn perpendicular to the NEW reference line.
Reason (R): Projectors are always perpendicular to the plane (hence to its reference trace) onto which the projection is made.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Orthographic projectors stay normal to the target plane (R), hence perpendicular to its reference line (A).

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: Dimensioning of drawings uses which UNITS by default (if unstated)?
explanation: Engineering drawings take all dimensions in mm unless otherwise specified in the title block.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: A dimension line carries its value written:
options: ABOVE the dimension line, in line with it (aligned/one-direction system as standard)
explanation: Figure placed above/along the dimension line between arrowheads touching extension lines.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: EXTENSION lines in dimensioning:
options: BEGIN just clear of the outline and EXTEND slightly beyond the dimension line
explanation: Small gap (~1-2 mm) separate outline from extension start; extension overruns the dimension line ~2 mm.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: The SCALE of a drawing is recorded in the TITLE BLOCK in ratio form, e.g.:
options: SCALE 1:10 (object 10 times bigger than drawing — reducing scale)
explanation: Ratio format drawing:object; 1:10 means drawing is one-tenth of real size.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: In the UNIDIRECTIONAL system of dimensioning, all dimension figures are lettered:
options: so they read from the BOTTOM of the sheet only, whatever the dimension-line direction
explanation: Unidirectional figures are read from the sheet bottom; the aligned system reads along/above each line instead.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: If a 10 mm measured line on a drawing represents an actual 200 mm member, the SCALE used is:
explanation: RF = 10/200 = 1/20 — a reducing scale denoted 1:20.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: ARAM annotation '4 HOLES Ø10 EQUI-SPACED' on a bolt circle means:
options: four holes each larger than 10 mm
four holes each of 10 mm diameter, equally ANGULARLY spaced on the pitch circle
explanation: Compact annotation conveys count, size and uniform angular distribution around the PCD.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: A NOTE in a drawing pointing to a specific feature uses a:
options: LEADER line with arrowhead touching the feature, the note written at the free end
explanation: Leaders connect feature to notes (e.g. DRILL Ø5 THRU) with arrow or dot termination.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem:
Assertion (A): Dimensions should, whenever possible, be placed OUTSIDE the outline of the view.
Reason (R): Outside placement avoids crossing object lines, keeping both the geometry and the figures free of clash and easy to read.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Clash avoidance for legibility (R) is exactly why outside placement is preferred (A).

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: Chain dimensioning (a series of consecutive dimensions along one direction) is generally preferred to a common-datum system for tight-tolerance work.
explanation: False: chain dimensioning ACCUMULATES tolerances; datum/baseline dimensioning accumulates none.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: Which are VALID dimensioning conventions? (Select all that apply.)
options: Dimensions placed crossing thick hatching always
explanation: Crossing dense hatching at will is bad practice; an unwalled clear space is preferred — the rest are valid.

stem: A TETRAHEDRON is bounded by:
explanation: 4 faces, 4 vertices, 6 edges — the simplest regular solid.

stem: A solid with 8 equilateral-triangular regular faces is the:
explanation: Octahedron = 8 triangular faces; dodecahedron has 12 pentagons, icosahedron 20 triangles.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A cylinder standing on HP (axis vertical) presents its FRONT view as a:
explanation: Cylinder elevation is a rectangle; its plan is a circle.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: The VERTEX (apex) of a cone resting on its base projects in the PLAN at:
options: the centre of the circle (axis foot)
explanation: Vertical-axis cone: apex is directly above base centre, so both coincide at the plan's centre point.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: While SECOND-stage tilting of a solid on HP, the points of the ORIGINAL top-view do NOT change their:
options: distances from the previously tilted edge (the plan rotates bodily, preserving point-to-edge relationships)
explanation: Rigid rotation preserves geometry of the tilted figure about the hinge edge — transfers stay consistent.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: Which SOLIDS have TRIANGULAR front views when standing upright on their bases? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Pyramids and cones converge to an apex — triangular elevation; cylinder and prism give rectangles.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: In true projection of a SOLID inclined to the HP, the HEIGHTS of all vertices measured in the elevation are taken:
options: PERPENDICULAR to xy up to the actual vertical position (stage-II transfer)
explanation: Heights are always measured normal to xy (or to the auxiliary reference line), never diagonally.

stem: For a MACHINE BRACKET with an inclined lug face, drawing the lug's true profile needs:
options: an AUXILIARY view (partial is admissible) parallel to the lug face
explanation: Partial auxiliary views limited to the feature cut clutter while conveying true inclined-face shape.

stem: The PYRAMID named after a HEXAGONAL base has, counting base and apex, a total of:
explanation: Hexagonal pyramid: 6 base vertices + apex = 7 vertices; 6 triangular side faces + base = 7 faces.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: An over-dimensioned drawing (same length dimensioned in two places with TOLERANCE conflict) leads to:
options: installer/inspection CONFLICTS — parts must satisfy contradictory limits, causing rejection
explanation: Double dimensioning with independent tolerances is contradictory; dimension once, leave derived.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: A drawing made FULL-SIZE is recorded in the title block as scale:
explanation: 1:1 denotes full size; 2:1 enlargement; 1:2 reduction.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem:
Assertion (A): Datum (baseline) dimensioning locates every hole from ONE reference edge instead of the previous hole.
Reason (R): Cumulative tolerance error is avoided when each distance is measured from a common datum rather than chained from the last feature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Common datum kills tolerance accumulation (R) — precisely the claim in (A).

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: Given a cone with axis inclined to HP AND a SPECIFIED base-edge contact, the pivotal element during stage-II is the:
options: the BASE contact edge/generator/corner actually specified to rest on the plane
the exact centre of the axis
explanation: The stated contact element is the hinge for the second-stage tilt in the elevation.

stem: Distances for an auxiliary FRONT view (AVP) are transferred FROM:
options: the original PLAN (depths measured from its xy)
explanation: AVP shares HP; depths come from the plan perpendicular to the new reference line.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem:
Assertion (A): The front-view outline of an upright hexagonal prism shows only SOME base corners at their true horizontal spacings.
Reason (R): Base edges parallel to VP appear in true length in elevation; edges inclined to VP are foreshortened when the prism is viewed from the front.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: VP-parallel length preservation (R) explains why only some widths are true in elevation (A).

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: The functional dimensions (deciding the part's WORKING, e.g. mating fits) are distinguished on drawings because:
options: THEY carry direct tight tolerances because they govern function; nonfunctional dimensions take general tolerance
explanation: Functional dimensions relate to performance and take specific tolerances; others follow general tolerance notes.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: A solid SUSPENDED from a point (hanging) behaves in projection like one resting on:
options: the DIAMETRICALLY OPPOSITE element from which it hangs (vertically below the suspension point)
explanation: Hanging inverts the support: the point opposite the suspension contact hangs vertically beneath it.

stem: A SPHERE projects, in EVERY orthographic view, as:
options: always a CIRCLE of true diameter
explanation: Spherical symmetry guarantees circular outlines with true diameter in all views.

topic: Projects of Solids (Prism, pyramids, cone, and cylinder): Inclined to Both the Planes
stem: When a pentagonal pyramid rests on a BASE CORNER on HP with its axis given incline, the FIRST point to locate exactly is:
options: the RESTING CORNER (the fixed tilt point); the plan is then rotated about it to meet the stated inclination
explanation: Fix the conditional contact point; rotate/tilt around it to satisfy the axis inclination.

topic: Draw Simple Annotation, Dimensioning and Scale
stem: Which are recommended practices of ANNOTATION on drawings? (Select all that apply.)
options: Each hole count/size annotated compactly (e.g. '4 HOLES Ø10')
explanation: Random scattering destroys readability; orientation, brevity and compact notation are standards.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A SOLID cut imaginary by a SECTION (cutting) PLANE is drawn so as to reveal:
options: the INTERNAL SHAPE/details that hidden lines would show confusingly
explanation: The portion between observer and cutting plane is considered removed, exposing interior construction.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: The surface revealed by cutting a solid and shown hatched is called the:
explanation: The cut face, bounded by intersection of the cutting plane with the solid, is hatched thin at 45°.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A HORIZONTAL cutting plane through an upright hexagonal PRISM (axis vertical) gives a TRUE SHAPE of section in the:
options: PLAN (a hexagon identical to the base)
explanation: Horizontal cut in a vertical prism is parallel to the base, so the plan shows the base-shape true section.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A cutting plane PERPENDICULAR TO VP and INCLINED to HP across an upright solid shows the TRUE SHAPE of the section only on:
options: an AUXILIARY plane parallel to the cutting plane
explanation: True section shape appears when projected normal to the cutting plane — the auxiliary view.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: Cutting a CONE by a plane PARALLEL TO ITS BASE yields a section that is a:
explanation: Plane parallel to base slices the cone in a smaller concentric circle — the frustum top.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A cylinder cut by a plane PARALLEL TO ITS AXIS (and off-centre) yields a section:
options: RECTANGLE (width = chord of cut, height = cylinder length)
explanation: Axial sections of cylinders are rectangles; on the centre plane the width equals the diameter.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A cylinder cut by a plane INCLINED to its axis reveals a section of TRUE SHAPE:
explanation: Oblique axial cuts give ellipses — seen true only in the auxiliary view normal to the plane.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A pyramid section by a plane parallel to the base produces a figure:
options: SIMILAR to the base (same angles, proportionately smaller)
explanation: Parallel sections of pyramids are SIMILAR polygons scaling linearly with height from the apex.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: To locate the SECTION outlined points when a prism is cut by an inclined plane (perpendicular VP), the basic working idea is:
options: each cutting-point is first identified where the plane crosses the solid's EDGES in the ELEVATION (edge view of plane), then projected to the plan/other views
explanation: The plane's edge view in elevation finds edge-intersection points; projectors carry them to other views.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: The trace of the cutting plane (edge-view line) chosen for an inclined section is drawn:
options: anywhere INCLINED in the view in which the plane shows its EDGE (perpendicular-to-plane view)
explanation: The cutting plane edge view (e.g. VT in the elevation for a plane ⊥VP) establishes the cut locations.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: A cone may be cut to give which TRUE section shapes? (Select all that apply.)
options: Ellipse (plane inclined to axis, cutting all generators)
explanation: Rectangles are prism/cylinder sections; conic sections from cones are circle/ellipse/parabola/hyperbola.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem:
Assertion (A): The true shape of a section by a plane perpendicular to VP and inclined to HP is NOT seen in the ordinary front or top view.
Reason (R): The sectioned surface itself is inclined to both principal planes (tilted), so it foreshortens in both views and needs an auxiliary projection.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Double inclination foreshortens both standard views (R) — exactly why true shape is missing there (A).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: The cone FRUSTUM produced after slicing off the top (plane ∥ base) projects in plan as:
options: two CONCENTRIC CIRCLES (base rim and cut rim)
explanation: Two concentric circles: true base circle and the smaller true cut circle of the frustum.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: When a cutting plane passes PARALLEL to a generator of a cone, the section's true shape is a:
explanation: Plane parallel to a generator → parabola; steeper planes giving both nappes → hyperbola; shallow → ellipse.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Section of Solids (Prism, Cylinder, Pyramid, Cone)
stem: In locating the section on the PLAN from elevation intersections for a prism cut inclined to HP:
options: project section points down the projectors onto the corresponding plan edges (transferring edge by edge)
explanation: Each elevation intersection projects onto its matching plan edge; joined points make the apparent section.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
stem: Auxiliary views in SECTION work are used mainly to:
options: display the TRUE SHAPE of the sectioned surface (AIP parallel to cutting plane)
explanation: Sections cut inclined to principal planes appear true only on auxiliary planes parallel to the cut.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
stem: When drawing the auxiliary true shape of a section, points are measured:
options: perpendicular to the auxiliary reference line from the cutting trace (taking the true widths from the original adjacent principal view)
explanation: Widths normal to the cutting trace from the adjacent principal view are stepped off on the auxiliary projection.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
stem: The DIFFERENCE between an ORDINARY auxiliary view (unit 3 sol) and an auxiliary SECTIONAL view is:
options: the auxiliary SECTIONAL view additionally shows the cut material HATCHED, looked at along the cutting plane's normal
explanation: Auxiliary sections combine true-shape display with hatching of the cut material in that auxiliary direction.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
stem:
Assertion (A): Ribs/webs, when the cutting plane passes ALONG their length, are NOT hatched in sectional views.
Reason (R): Hatching a rib along its length would give a FALSE impression of solid thickness; convention therefore leaves longitudinally-sectioned ribs unhatched.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The false-thickness concern (R) exactly motivates the non-hatching convention (A).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: The DEVELOPMENT (net) of a solid is:
options: the unfolded LATERAL surface LAID FLAT on a plane, to true size
explanation: Unfolding lateral surfaces flat shows true panel layout, vital in sheet-metal fabrication.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: The development of a square PRISM (without ends) is a:
options: single RECTANGLE of width = base PERIMETER and height = prism length, subdivided into face strips
explanation: Width equals perimeter (4×edge) — the four side rectangles unroll into one divided rectangle.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: A CYLINDER of diameter D and height H develops as:
options: a RECTANGLE of length \(\pi D\) and height H
explanation: Rolling the cylinder flat gives a πD × H rectangle — the standard duct/pipe blank layout.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: The development of a right circular CONE (base radius r, slant l) is a:
options: a full circle of radius l
SECTOR of a circle of radius l whose arc length equals the base circumference \(2\pi r\)
explanation: Unrolled cone = sector radius = slant height, arc length = base circumference \(2\pi r\).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: The sector ANGLE of a cone's development equals:
explanation: Equating arc lengths: \(\frac{\theta}{360}2\pi l=2\pi r\Rightarrow \theta=\frac{r}{l}\times360°\).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: The development of a square PYRAMID (without base) is:
options: FOUR ISOSCELES TRIANGLES of base = base edge and equal side = TRUE slant-edge length, joined at the apex
explanation: Each lateral face unrolls as a true-size isosceles triangle using the true slant-edge length.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: To develop the lateral surface of a TRUNCATED/sectioned pyramid (cut inclined), slant edges are first:
options: brought to TRUE LENGTH by ROTATING each edge parallel to VP (or AIP) then stepping onto the development
explanation: Slant edges are foreshortened in ordinary views; rotation to true length precedes stepping in the net.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: Applications of developments include making:
options: sheet-metal DUCTS, hoppers, transition pieces, funnels and tarpaulins
explanation: Sheet/fabrication industries cut blanks directly from true-size lateral developments.
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Regular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: A cone of base diameter 100 mm and height 180 mm has slant height \(l\) and development sector angle about:
explanation: \(l=\sqrt{h^2+r^2}=\sqrt{180^2+50^2}\approx186.8\) mm; sector angle \(=\frac{r}{l}\times360°=\frac{50}{186.8}\times360°\approx96°\).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: Which surfaces CAN be developed exactly? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Developable surfaces are ruled/prismatic; the doubly-curved sphere develops only approximately (gores).
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem:
Assertion (A): The development of a cone is always drawn from the SLANT (lateral) edge lengths, not the vertical height.
Reason (R): When rolled flat, every generator keeps its slant length; the sector radius equals the slant height, while the vertical height has no flat-plane role.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Generator slant lengths are preserved in flattening (R), so they set the sector radius (A).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: On a cylinder's development rectangle, the points of a SECTION edge (cut inclined) become:
options: the END-POINTS of generators stepped from true arc divisions, yielding a SMOOTH CURVE across the rectangle
explanation: Section endpoints sit at stepped generator heights across the πD length, drawing the cut's sine-like curve.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: In developments, hidden fold lines (base subdivision marks) are drawn thin; outside cut edges are drawn thick.
explanation: True: line-weight convention separates fold/construction marks from the blank's cut outline.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: A FULL SECTIONAL VIEW is obtained when the cutting plane:
options: passes COMPLETELY across the object, the front half considered REMOVED and the rest viewed in the cutting direction
explanation: Full section sweeps the whole object with the near half removed, giving a fully hatched interior view.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: A HALF SECTIONAL view of a SYMMETRICAL object shows:
options: ONE QUARTER removed: half of the view hatched in section, the other half as exterior with a centre line dividing them
explanation: For symmetric parts, half-exterior/half-interior in one view conveys both faces compactly.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: An OFFSET SECTION is chosen when:
options: important features (holes, webs) lie in DIFFERENT parallel/offset planes, the cutting plane being stepped to pass through them all
explanation: The stepped cutting plane bends to capture off-axis features into one inclusive sectional view.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: In SECTIONAL views of machine parts, hidden lines are usually:
options: OMITTED because the section now shows interiors directly
explanation: Sectioned interiors are visible; superfluous hidden lines purposely suppressed for clarity.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: In a building SECTION (vertical cut through a dwelling from FOUNDATION to roof slab), the drawn order of parts from BOTTOM to TOP is:
options: FOUNDATION footing → plinth masonry → DPC → wall → lintel → roof slab
explanation: Building sections stack footing, plinth, damp-proof course, wall body, lintels above openings, ending at the slab.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: The PLINTH level of a building, shown in sections, is the:
options: the level at which the SUPERSTRUCTURE starts above ground (top of the plinth masonry/substructure)
explanation: Plinth is the built-up base raising the ground floor above outside ground level, ending the foundation zone.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: The DPC (damp-proof course) shown in wall sections is placed at plinth level to:
options: STOP moisture RISING from the ground into walls/floors (capillary barrier)
explanation: DPC (bitumen/rich concrete layer ~25-40 mm) interrupts capillary rise of ground moisture into masonry.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: A stepped strip FOOTING shown in section widens downward because:
options: its steps spread the WALL LOAD onto the soil at a reduced bearing pressure within the soil's safe limit
explanation: Successive widened footing courses transfer load to a larger soil area at a steeper lean spread.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: In sectional PLANS/elevations of dwellings, a LINTEL is:
options: the HORIZONTAL structural member (RCC etc.) spanning across door/window OPENINGS to carry masonry loads above
explanation: Lintels bear wall weight over openings; their section and bearing show in building sections.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem:
Assertion (A): Building sections are dimensioned with LEVELS (foundation depth, plinth height, lintel/sill heights, slab top).
Reason (R): Level dimensions vertically locate every construction element, enabling accurate setting-out and quantity estimation at site.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Vertical location of elements for site work (R) is precisely why level dimensioning is mandatory (A).

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: Which items are usually marked in a building foundation-to-slab SECTION? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Structural vertical locations are marked; recipe belongs to the kitchen, not the construction drawing.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: The arrows at a cutting-plane line in an industrial drawing indicate:
options: the DIRECTION in which the remaining part is VIEWED after cutting (with section letters)
explanation: Arrows on thickened ends of the cutting-plane line point the sight direction for the lettered section view.

options: slender members (ribs, bars, spokes, rail sections) ON/NEAR the object itself without a separate full view
explanation: Cross profiles of elongated features are revolved in place or removed nearby for compact clarity.

options: NOT sectioned (left unhatched) since hatching standard machine elements hides their identity
explanation: Standard elements are conventionally exempted from sectioning so their outlines stay readable.

explanation: Intersections found on edge views are projected into each view, their convex join making that view's section.

explanation: True: frustum retains the base with a similar parallel top face of smaller size.

stem: A TRANSITION piece connecting a square duct to a round one is fabricated by:
options: its DEVELOPMENT (triangulation between the two openings)
explanation: Transition/offset pieces are laid out from triangulated true lengths — classic advanced development.

explanation: An axial 45° cut maps height linearly against developed arc, yielding a straight diagonal over the πD span.

stem: In an OFFSET section, the bends/offsets of the cutting plane are drawn as visible lines in the sectional view.
explanation: False: offsets/bends of the plane are NOT shown in the resulting section — it is drawn as one merged section.

stem:
Assertion (A): A section A-A taken through an industrial part is lettered and the view titled 'SECTION A-A'.
Reason (R): The cutting-plane trace with end arrows carries the same letters, uniquely linking the cut position to its resulting view.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Letter linking between trace and view (R) is exactly why sections are labelled (A).

stem: LOCAL (broken-out) sectioning is preferred when:
options: only a SMALL LOCAL region interior (e.g. a keyway or local recess) must be shown — outline broken irregularly
explanation: An irregular freehand break limits the section to the needed area, preserving the rest of the outside view.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids

stem: When the ESSENCE of a problem asks 'sectional top view' after an inclined cut of a prism perpendicular to VP, you draw the:
options: the section's TRUE shape in every case
the APPARENT section on the plan, projecting the cut points through their projectors onto matching plan edges
explanation: 'Sectional' views are apparent projections; 'true shape of section' specifically means the auxiliary view.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids

stem: Which are correct section-result statements? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: A cone cut parallel to its axis inclines to the base and is NOT a circle — the rest are correct as stated.

stem: For a pentagonal PYRAMID cut by a plane perpendicular to VP and inclined to HP, the SECTION TRUE SHAPE is located on an AIP:
options: parallel to the cutting plane, transferring TRUE slant-edge true lengths from rotated sections of the edges
explanation: Auxiliary distances along edges need true slant lengths from the rotation of edges parallel to VP.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Development of Surfaces Of Right Regular Solids: Prism, Pyramid, Cylinder And Cone
stem: The layout of a SQUARE pyramidal HOPPER (frustum) net requires, before fanning out:
options: the TRUE slant lengths of the truncated edges, found by rotating one edge parallel to the plane of projection
explanation: Frustum developments start by establishing true slant edge lengths of the cut (rotation method), then fanning the net.

stem: ALIGNED section convention (spokes/lugs rotated into the cutting plane) is applied to:
options: show symmetrical spokes of a wheel in ONE section as if they were rotated into the cutting plane (avoiding false asymmetry)
explanation: Aligning features into the section avoids misleading asymmetric presentations of rotational parts.

unit_title: Sections and Sectional Views of Right Angular Solids
topic: Draw The Sectional Orthographic Views of Geometrical Solids, Objects From Industry And Dwellings (Foundation To Slab Only)
stem: A building's SECTIONAL PLAN at plinth level fundamentally shows:
options: wall thicknesses, openings, and space layout as cut just above the floor level (plinth), with doors/windows marked
explanation: Horizontal cut just above plinth reveals walls/openings distribution — the basis of architectural plans.

stem: An ISOMETRIC view shows:
options: the object with its THREE principal axes mutually 120° apart, giving a pictorial (3D-looking) single-view representation
explanation: Isometric (iso = equal measure) places three axes 120° apart, so one view shows length, width and height together.

stem: In the standard isometric view orientation, the axes are drawn:
options: one VERTICAL, and the other two at 30° on either side of the horizontal
explanation: Vertical remains vertical; the two receding axes are set at 30° (set-square friendly) to the horizontal.

stem: Measurements in an isometric drawing are taken ONLY:
options: ALONG (parallel to) the isometric axes — true along the three axis directions but not along non-axis diagonals
explanation: Lengths may be scaled only along/parallel to the three isometric axes; diagonal distances distort.

stem: In an isometric view of a COMPOUND solid (e.g. cylinder on a square block, cone on a cylinder):
options: each component is located relative to a common origin along iso axes and TRUE shapes converted (circles → ellipses) where they lie in iso planes
explanation: Compound solid is built part by part from a chosen origin: the iso locations of each joining face are established first.

stem: A hemisphere placed flat-face down on a cube (in iso) appears as:
options: a half-ELLIPSE pair (semicircle → half-ellipse on the top face of the cube) forming the dome outline
explanation: The horizontal circular rim of the hemisphere projects as an iso ellipse on the cube top; dome tangent above.

stem: The PRINCIPLE behind isometric projection is the orientation of the object such that:
options: one face is parallel to plane
its three mutually perpendicular edges make EQUAL angles with the projection plane
explanation: Tilting the object equally to the projection plane makes the three mutually-perpendicular axes equally foreshortened.

stem: In a true ISOMETRIC PROJECTION, all three axes are foreshortened by the SAME ratio, namely:
explanation: Equal-tilt geometry yields the isometric ratio \(\sqrt{2/3}\approx0.816\) on every axis.

stem: The difference between an isometric DRAWING and an isometric PROJECTION is:
options: an isometric DRAWING uses TRUE (full) lengths along the axes for convenience; the projection uses 0.816× lengths from the true orthographic views
explanation: Practical drawings skip the 0.816 shrink and draw to full size along axes — so iso drawings are ~22% larger than projections.

stem: A CUBE's iso drawing has all its 12 edges:
options: of equal length and parallel in groups of four
explanation: Cube iso edges group into three parallel sets of equal iso length — the pictorial lattice used to box objects.

stem:
Assertion (A): Circles lying in the principal faces of an object appear as ELLIPSES in isometric views.
Reason (R): The iso axes of those faces are inclined to the line of sight, so equal diameters foreshorten unequally along the ellipse's two axes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Unequal foreshortening across an inclined circle (R) yields the iso ellipse noted in (A).

stem: Isometric drawings generally OMIT:
options: hidden (dashed) lines — they would clutter the pictorial view
explanation: Iso views show only the visible faces; hidden detail is read from orthographic views instead.

stem: An isometric scale is a specially-built scale that:
options: multiplies lengths by 0.816 (or provides correspondingly shortened units), allowing isometric PROJECTION lengths to be marked directly
explanation: The isometric scale applies the √(2/3) factor so the draftsman-steps true lengths to projection lengths directly.

stem: To CONSTRUCT an isometric scale graphically, one draws a 45° ray and a 30° ray from one origin, marks TRUE lengths along the 45° ray, and projects them:
options: ONTO the 30° ray, whose stepped marks then serve directly as the isometric scale
explanation: Projecting true lengths from the 45° line onto the 30° line automatically applies the 0.816-ish ratio geometrically.

stem: If a cube of 50 mm side is drawn as an isometric PROJECTION (true iso, not iso drawing), its axis direction edge measures:
explanation: True isometric projection applies √(2/3): 50 × 0.816 ≈ 40.8 mm.

stem: Conventions for ISO views dictate that the STARTING point (origin/corner) of an object is:
options: chosen so the most characteristic faces face TOWARD the viewer (typically front-top-right corner), revealing maximum features
explanation: Front/top/side visibility maximizes information; the corner facing the viewer is conventionally the main one.

stem: Letters and NUMBERS on iso views are positioned, conventionally:
options: in plain clear lettering readable from the bottom, NOT wrapped around the iso geometry
explanation: Notes stay legible rather than wrapped pictorially, though dimensions when used align with iso directions.

stem: Isometric views are suited perfectly to carry precise functional dimensions as the final working drawing.
explanation: False: iso views are pictorial — non-axis distances distort, so working dimensions belong to orthographic views.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple and Conversion of Isometric Views to Orthographic Views And Vice-Versa
stem: Converting an ISOMETRIC view to ORTHOGRAPHIC views requires reading the object's length, width and height along:
options: the THREE iso axis tracks and stacking them into front/top (and side) projections on proper planes
explanation: Iso axis lengths map to the orthographic length/depth/height set; shapes take their true proportions there.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple and Conversion of Isometric Views to Orthographic Views And Vice-Versa
stem: A LINE (edge) in an object that is NOT parallel to any iso axis appears in the iso view:
options: as a NON-ISOMETRIC line, located by finding its END POINTS along iso directions first
explanation: Non-iso lines are drawn by connecting endpoint coordinates found along the iso axes.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple and Conversion of Isometric Views to Orthographic Views And Vice-Versa
stem: A SQUARE LAMINA standing PARALLEL to an iso plane will appear in the iso view as a:
explanation: Iso faces map squares into parallelograms since the iso axes of that face are mutually inclined.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple and Conversion of Isometric Views to Orthographic Views And Vice-Versa
stem: To construct an iso view from given ORTHOGRAPHIC views, the sensible FIRST step is:
options: enclose the object in its smallest CONSTRUCTION BOX of L×B×H (the 'box method') and plot features inside along iso axes
explanation: Boxing fixes the overall iso envelope; features are then offset within it along iso directions.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple and Conversion of Isometric Views to Orthographic Views And Vice-Versa
stem: A circle drawn on the TOP iso face of a cube is drawn by the method of:
options: FOUR-CENTRE method (constructing the rhombus and joining arcs from the centres at obtuse corners and mid-side points)
explanation: The rhombus-plus-four-centres yields the iso ellipse approximating the circle on that face.
