stem: 'COMPUTER GRAPHICS' as covered in engineering drawing deals with:
options: GENERATING, storing and manipulating drawings with computers — CAD being the modern replacement/augmentation of board drafting
explanation: The unit surveys digital drafting: CAD tools, their screens, menus, commands and editing (zoom, erase, select).

topic: Listing the Computer Technologies that Impact on Graphical Communication
stem: Which tech changes strengthened GRAPHICAL COMMUNICATION with computers? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: T-square is a manual instrument; CAD, plotters and networked sharing digitized graphical communication.

topic: Listing the Computer Technologies that Impact on Graphical Communication
stem: A chief advantage of computer-based drawings over manual paper drawings is:
options: faster error-correction (modify/undo), easy perfect COPYING and revision management, and database storage/retrieval
explanation: Editability, duplication and digital archival fundamentally changed graphical communication speed and quality.

topic: Listing the Computer Technologies that Impact on Graphical Communication
stem: A PLOTTER in computer graphics is used to:
options: PRODUCE large-scale hard copy of CAD drawings on paper (substitute of the drawing board physically)
explanation: Plotters (pen/inkjet, large-format) output engineering sheets from computer files.

topic: Demonstrating Knowledge of the Theory of CAD Software
stem: CAD stands for:
explanation: Computer Aided Design/Drafting uses software to create, modify and document drawings.

topic: Demonstrating Knowledge of the Theory of CAD Software
stem: CAD drawings are stored internally as:
options: VECTOR data — geometric entities (points, lines, arcs with exact coordinates), not bitmaps
explanation: Vector entities keep drawings resolution-independent, infinitely zoomable and editable point-wise.

topic: Demonstrating Knowledge of the Theory of CAD Software
stem: The CAD concept of LAYERS corresponds on the drawing board to:
options: drawing each line-type group (outlines, centres, dims) on separate transparent overlays stacked for the final plot
explanation: Layers separate drawing components (dimensions, hatching, hidden) for control, visibility and plotting.

stem: The MENU (pull-down) system in CAD:
options: organizes commands under drop-down headings (File, Edit, View, Draw, Modify...) accessible by mouse clicks
explanation: Hierarchical pull-down menus expose the entire command set alongside quicker toolbar/command-line paths.

stem: The same CAD command is usually reachable through menu, toolbar, right-click menu AND typed command line at once.
explanation: True: menus, toolbars, shortcut menus and command typing are parallel entry points to the same commands.

stem: A menu item followed by three dots '...' (ellipsis) in Windows CAD typically means:
options: it OPENS a DIALOG BOX requesting more information before the command runs
explanation: Ellipsis flags dialog-box flows; '>' arrows flag cascading submenus.

topic: Toolbars (Standard, Object Properties, Draw, Modify And Dimension)
stem: Which are the CAD toolbars named in the syllabus set? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: T-square is not a CAD toolbar; the standard, properties and draw/modify/dimension bars are the named set.

topic: Toolbars (Standard, Object Properties, Draw, Modify And Dimension)
stem: The OBJECT PROPERTIES toolbar displays controls for:
options: current layer, colour, linetype and lineweight with which NEW objects are drawn/selected objects may change
explanation: Property controls set/read the active layer/colour/linetype of drawn geometry — the quick-by-layer panel.

topic: Toolbars (Standard, Object Properties, Draw, Modify And Dimension)
stem: Which toolbar pair correctly maps to their job: 'DRAW' bar buttons create entities; the 'MODIFY' bar buttons:
options: CHANGE existing objects: erase, copy, move, rotate, mirror, offset, trim, fillet, array etc.
explanation: Draw-vs-Modify partitions entity creation from entity editing in CAD interface design.

stem: The DRAWING AREA (graphics window) in CAD is the:
options: screen canvas (usually black/white background) where geometry is created and DISPLAYed, with crosshair cursor
explanation: The full drawing realm, bordered by toolbars/menus, where all construction happens.

stem: The CROSSHAIRS (cursor) in the drawing area serve to:
options: to SPECIFY points precisely, display the cursor's coordinate position and pick objects
explanation: Intersection readout of the crosshair locates points/selection precisely on the drafting canvas.

stem: CAD's COORDINATE SYSTEM: the fixed World Coordinate System (WCS) and the reorientable User Coordinate System (UCS) let the user:
options: to define a convenient LOCAL origin and axes for inclined-plane work while the WCS stays global
explanation: UCS re-anchors X-Y input to any chosen face/origin — key for angled constructions in 2D/3D.

stem: Entering a point as @30,40 at the prompt in many CAD packages means:
options: a RELATIVE point 30,40 from the LAST given point
explanation: '@' prefixes relative coordinates (cartesian or polar @dist<angle); bare numbers are absolute.

stem: A DIALOG BOX in CAD typically appears to:
options: COLLECT settings/choices (e.g. layer manager, text, dimension styles) before applying them, with OK/Cancel
explanation: Dialog windows gather rich parameter input (checkbox/dropdown/field) for the invoked command.

stem: The NEW/OPEN drawing dialogs let you begin from a TEMPLATE because:
options: templates save redrawing title blocks, layers and styles already set for the organization
explanation: Templates (.dwt) package units, limits, layers and title blocks so sheets start standardized.

stem: Multiple drawing files can be open simultaneously in separate WINDOWS, and entities copied between them.
explanation: True: multi-document interfaces allow tiled drawings and cross-drawing copy/paste.

stem: SHORTCUT (right-click) menus in CAD:
options: give CONTEXT-SENSITIVE commands (different by whatever is selected/mode: object snaps, grip edit, properties)
explanation: Right-button menus adapt to context, shortening the path to frequently-used actions.

stem: While a command like LINE asks for points, a right-click typically lets you:
options: choose an OBJECT SNAP mode (endpoint, midpoint...) or last options (undo/close)
explanation: In-command right-click menus offer snap overrides and running-command options.

stem: In AutoCAD-like systems, the COMMAND LINE at the bottom of the screen:
options: lets you TYPE commands and options while its prompts state what input is expected next
explanation: Command-line input with its prompts is the text interface: command names, options and values are exchanged here.

stem: The CAPITAL letters underlined in a command prompt (e.g. 'specify Next point or [Undo]') let you:
options: TYPE the option's capital letter shortcut (e.g. U for Undo) to invoke that option
explanation: Option letters permit keyboard-only driving — the seasoned-by-drafters fast path.

stem: Which modes are toggled/shown on the CAD STATUS BAR? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Spell-check is not a status-bar toggle; snap, grid, ortho and osnap/polar are the drafting-aid toggles.

stem: Turning ORTHO mode ON from the status bar restricts drawing to:
options: HORIZONTAL and VERTICAL directions only (90° constraint)
explanation: Ortho locks motion to axis directions; Polar Tracking generalizes this to chosen fixed angles.

topic: Different Methods of Zoom as Used in CAD
stem: ZOOM functions in CAD:
options: change only the DISPLAY magnification of the drawing (not the actual object size)
explanation: Zooming affects the view only — the stored geometry (always full size, 1:1) is untouched.

topic: Different Methods of Zoom as Used in CAD
stem:
Assertion (A): After ZOOM EXTENTS, the drawing's objects all fit the screen without any change to the objects themselves.
Reason (R): Zoom merely alters DISPLAY magnification/pan; the stored geometry stays full-size and untouched.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: View-only magnification (R) explains how extents fits everything without editing geometry (A).

topic: Different Methods of Zoom as Used in CAD
stem: ZOOM WINDOW works by:
options: drawing a RECTANGLE (two corners) around the area to be magnified to fill the screen
explanation: A two-pick window box defines the region enlarged to the graphics window.

topic: Different Methods of Zoom as Used in CAD
stem: REALTIME Zoom and PAN, typically wheel/mouse driven, let the drafter:
options: smoothly magnify/shrink (wheel or drag) and SHIFT the view around continuously without commands completed
explanation: Interactive pan/zoom navigates drawings fluently; commands continue uninterrupted.

stem: In ERASE/modify commands, SELECTING objects is done by picking individually OR by:
options: WINDOW selection (drag left-to-right: wholly inside window) and CROSSING window (drag right-to-left: touching/crossing also included)
explanation: Window = fully enclosed objects; Crossing = anything touched by the box — the two marquee selection modes.

stem:
Assertion (A): Objects erased by mistake can be brought back immediately after the ERASE command.
Reason (R): UNDO (or the OOPS command) restores the last-erased selection set, reversing the deletion step.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Undo/OOPS reversal of the deletion step (R) is exactly the recovery described in (A).

stem: Which are valid object-SELECTION methods in CAD? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Single-pick, window and crossing marquees are standard; selection is never by guessing.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple And Compound Solids
stem: For a CYLINDER lying with its axis PARALLEL to an iso axis, its base circles on the two iso faces appear:
options: as congruent ELLIPSES drawn in the two parallel iso planes and joined by tangent generators
explanation: Both end faces are iso planes → ellipses by four-centre construction, joined by the tangent outline generators.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple And Compound Solids
stem: A SQUARE FRUSTUM hopper (small square atop big square) is drawn in iso by:
options: drawing the bigger square's iso rhombus, offsetting the smaller one above at correct height, and joining corresponding corners
explanation: Both iso rhombi are built from axis-aligned box method at two levels, corners joined by the taper edges.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple And Compound Solids
stem:
Assertion (A): Construction boxes and offset measurements (box method) are the backbone of iso drawing of complex solids.
Reason (R): Since only iso-axis measurements are reliable, feature positions are located as offsets along those axes within the envelope instead of direct distances.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Axis-only measuring reliability (R) forces the envelope-plus-offset box method (A).

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple And Compound Solids
stem: An isometric view of a SOLID object inherently represents its:
options: the third dimension pictorially in ONE view, with the three axes drawn from a single viewpoint
explanation: Single-view 3-axis pictorial replaces multiple views for shape visualization, though not for precision.

topic: Isometric Views of Lines, Planes, Simple And Compound Solids
stem: Which are acceptable isometric-drawing conventions? (Select all that apply.)
options: Axes at 120° between them, 30° to horizontal
explanation: 120° inter-axis angle is fixed, not 80°; the other three statements are standard iso practice.

topic: Which includes dimensioning methods, different types of line, construction of different polygon, divide the line and angle in parts, use of stencil
stem: In the first drawing-lab exercise (lines and dimensioning), a CONTINUOUS THICK line is used for:
explanation: Line-type practice: thick continuous = visible, dashed = hidden, chain thin = centre, thin = hatch/dimension.

topic: Which includes dimensioning methods, different types of line, construction of different polygon, divide the line and angle in parts, use of stencil
stem: To DIVIDE a drawn straight line into n equal parts geometrically, the lab method is:
options: drawing a construction RAY at any angle from one end, stepping n equal arcs on it, joining the nth point to the line end and drawing parallels
explanation: The ray-and-parallel construction divides any segment exactly into equal parts without arithmetic.

topic: Which includes dimensioning methods, different types of line, construction of different polygon, divide the line and angle in parts, use of stencil
stem: To draw a regular PENTAGON/HEXAGON in the lab on a given circle, the compass is set to:
options: radius of the circle (hexagon) and a chord equal to golden-section based step (pentagon)
explanation: Hexagon sides equal the circle radius; pentagon chords from the golden-ratio construction using the compass.

topic: Which includes dimensioning methods, different types of line, construction of different polygon, divide the line and angle in parts, use of stencil
stem: STENCILS (lettering guides) are used in the lab to:
options: write uniform STANDARD LETTERS/digits quickly (guide edge plus pen/pencil through the grooves)
explanation: Stencils force consistent stroke thickness and letter proportions without lettering skill variance.

topic: Construction of Plane, Diagonal & Vernier Scales
stem: Given R.F. = 1/50 for a 3 m-long strip plan, the LENGTH OF SCALE drawn at full length is:
explanation: Length of scale = R.F. × max length to be measured = 3000 mm / 50 = 60 mm.

topic: Construction of Plane, Diagonal & Vernier Scales
stem: While constructing a DIAGONAL scale, the left-end smallest main division is subdivided by:
options: an inclined diagonal lattice of 10 strips so intersections read the third unit to 1/100 of the main unit
explanation: Ten horizontal strips with diagonal joins divide the last small division into ten further parts by intersection.

topic: Construction of Plane, Diagonal & Vernier Scales
stem: For a VERNIER scale to read 0.01 m against a plain scale of m/dm, the vernier is designed so that:
options: 10 vernier divisions equal 9 (direct) or 11 (retrograde) SMALL divisions of the plain scale, giving LC = small division/10
explanation: The n vs n-1 (direct) construction produces a least count of one small division/n.

topic: Construction of Ellipses, Parabolas, and Hyperbolas using the general method
stem: In the GENERAL METHOD of constructing an ellipse (major and minor axes given), the drafter:
options: motion described by concentric circles of radii = SEMI-AXES and rays through them locate circumferential points of the ellipse
explanation: Concentric-circle construction: semi-major/semi-minor circles and radial rays yield ellipse points quadrantwise.

topic: Construction of Ellipses, Parabolas, and Hyperbolas using the general method
stem: Constructing a PARABOLA (focus/directrix general method) begins by:
options: drawing the directrix, marking the FOCUS, and plotting points with FP = PM (perpendicular distance to the directrix)
explanation: Points equidistant from focus and directrix satisfy e = 1 — the parabola definition.

topic: Construction of Ellipses, Parabolas, and Hyperbolas using the general method
stem: For a HYPERBOLA by the focus-directrix method: take eccentricity e = 1.5, focus F, directrix D; the curve points P satisfy:
options: \(FP = 1.5\times\) (perp. distance of P from directrix D)
explanation: All conic constructions by this method stem from \(e=FP/PM\); e>1 gives the hyperbola arms.

topic: Construction of cycloid, epicycloid, hypocycloid, and involute of a circle
stem: In the LAB construction of a cycloid, the BASE line length for one arch equals:
options: the diameter of the generating circle
\(\pi D\) (one full circumference) of the generating circle
explanation: Roll the circle through one revolution: it advances one circumference, so base = πD stepped in equal divisions.

topic: Construction of cycloid, epicycloid, hypocycloid, and involute of a circle
stem: The epicycloid construction uses a BASE circle and a rolling circle whose arc lengths are divided:
options: into the same NUMBER of equal parts, the base arc amounting to the rolling circle's circumference
explanation: Equal divisions (usually 12) on both circles keep slip-free motion consistent through the plotted positions.

topic: Construction of cycloid, epicycloid, hypocycloid, and involute of a circle
stem: To construct the INVOLUTE of a circle in the lab, the circle is divided and tangents are drawn such that:
options: each tangent segment from its division point has length EQUAL TO THE ARC from the starting point to that division, the tangent ends tracing the involute
explanation: Unwound-string length equals the rolled-off arc — tangent lengths replicate that unwinding sequentially.

topic: Projection of Points and Lines inclined to both planes
stem: Projecting a POINT 30 mm above HP and 40 mm in front of VP in first-angle: the front view and top view are plotted:
options: front view 30 mm above xy; top view 40 mm below xy
explanation: Above HP height goes above xy; in-front depth goes below xy (after rotating HP down), distances perpendicular.

topic: Projection of Points and Lines inclined to both planes
stem: A line AB is inclined 30° to HP and parallel to VP; its projections set in the lab take the:
options: TL and true 30° angle in the FRONT view only
explanation: Line ∥VP with HP-inclination shows both TL and true θ in the elevation.

topic: Projection of Points and Lines inclined to both planes
stem: Finding TRUE LENGTH of a line inclined to both planes in the lab exercise, the plan (or elevation) is:
options: ROTATED until parallel to xy (keeping one end fixed) and the corresponding new elevation/plan found via projectors and unchanged heights/depths
explanation: Rotation to the parallel position converts the apparent view into a true length with its true angle.

topic: Projection of Points and Lines inclined to both planes
stem:
Assertion (A): When a line inclined to both planes is rotated in one view so a NEW view shows true length, the end distances from xy in the OTHER view remain what they were.
Reason (R): Rotating a view about a projector does not change the perpendicular distance of the points from the reference line (heights/depths are intrinsic coordinates).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Intrinsic coordinate preservation under rotation (R) is exactly the working principle stated in (A).

topic: Projections of Planes (e.g., rectangular, triangular) in inclined positions
stem: A rectangular lamina held PERPENDICULAR to HP and INCLINED to VP is projected in the lab so that:
options: the plan is one EDGE LINE inclined to xy, while the front view shows the APPARENT shape
explanation: Perpendicularity to HP makes the plan an edge line; the inclination to VP foreshortens the elevation's real shape.

topic: Projections of Planes (e.g., rectangular, triangular) in inclined positions
stem:
Assertion (A): Projections of a lamina inclined to BOTH planes take a TWO-STAGE construction.
Reason (R): One stage imposes the first inclination on an edge condition; the second stage imposes the remaining inclination by rotation with re-projection of all points.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Staged application of the two inclinations (R) directly explains the two-stage routine (A).

topic: Projections of Planes (e.g., rectangular, triangular) in inclined positions
stem: The TRUE SHAPE of a lamina appears only in the view projected on a plane parallel to that lamina.
explanation: True: parallel-plane projection preserves true lengths and angles of the lamina.

topic: Projection of Solids (prisms, pyramids, cones, and cylinders)
stem: For a hexagonal PRISM resting on HP with its axis vertical and two base edges parallel to VP, the lab draft shows:
options: plan = HEXAGON true shape; elevation = rectangle of projected base width × prism height
explanation: Vertical-axis, base-on-HP: plan reveals the true base polygon; elevation stacks the rectangular outline.

topic: Projection of Solids (prisms, pyramids, cones, and cylinders)
stem: A cone resting on a GENERATOR on HP is tackled in the lab by:
options: first drawing cone axis PERPENDICULAR to HP (base circle plan), then tilting the elevation so one generator lies on xy, and re-projecting the plan
explanation: Stage-I simple position, stage-II tilt about the resting element — the standard two-stage procedure.

topic: Projection of Solids (prisms, pyramids, cones, and cylinders)
stem: For a CYLINDER lying with its axis parallel to HP making an angle to VP, its plan at stage two will be:
options: an apparent ELLIPSE-faced figure with rectangular/envelope outline depending on axis direction
explanation: Angled horizontal cylinder gives ellipse-ended plan views when the axis tilts off VP-parallel directions.

topic: Projection of Solids (prisms, pyramids, cones, and cylinders)
stem: Which SOLIDS appear in the lab projection exercises? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Standard set from the syllabus; liquids are not solid-projection subjects.

topic: Drawing of Sections of Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, and Cones
stem: In a lab SECTION problem for a prism (cut by a plane ⊥VP, inclined to HP), the cutting plane is first drawn in the:
options: FRONT view as its EDGE TRACE (inclined line crossing the prism's elevation edges)
explanation: A plane perpendicular to VP shows its edge in the elevation — section points are read there and projected.

topic: Drawing of Sections of Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, and Cones
stem: The TRUE SHAPE of a section in lab work is finally produced:
options: in an AUXILIARY view taken parallel to the cutting plane, with the cut areas section-lined (hatched)
explanation: Auxiliary parallel-cut projection, hatched, presents the section truly.

topic: Drawing of Sections of Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, and Cones
stem: Section of a PYRAMID with a cutting plane crossing ALL its slant faces: the true section is:
options: a PENTAGON (if pentagonal pyramid) similar only when cut ∥ base — otherwise a DISTORTED polygon needing slant-edge true lengths
explanation: Inclined traverses are found per edge using true slant lengths; only ∥-base cuts yield similar polygons.

topic: Development of Surfaces for prisms, pyramids, cylinders, and cones
stem: The lab development exercise of a prism is drawn with its base as a:
options: STRAIGHT line marked with successive base-edge lengths (stretch-out/perimeter line) on which rectangle strips rise
explanation: The stretch-out line carries the base perimeter stepwise, and faces rise normally to it.

topic: Development of Surfaces for prisms, pyramids, cylinders, and cones
stem: A CONE's development exercise in the lab starts by:
options: drawing the SECTOR of radius = TRUE slant height; stepping base-circle division chords along its arc
explanation: Divisions of the base circle are chord-stepped onto the sector arc for generator rays, cut edges then joined.

topic: Development of Surfaces for prisms, pyramids, cylinders, and cones
stem: Developing a CUT pyramid (truncated inclined) requires slant edges first brought to TRUE LENGTH because:
options: edges inclined to the projection plane foreshorten, so nets built on apparent lengths would be WRONG shapes
explanation: Only true lengths belong in developments; edge rotation to true length precedes net layout.

topic: Development of Surfaces for prisms, pyramids, cylinders, and cones
stem: Adding flaps/edges for joining (tabs) on a development is a presentation choice, not part of the true surface geometry.
explanation: True: joining tabs are workshop additions; the development proper reproduces surface geometry only.

topic: Construction of Isometric views of lines, planes, and simple solids
stem: To draw the ISO of a simple solid in the lab, the drafter starts with:
options: a CONSTRUCTION BOX of L×B×H on the three iso axes and plots features INSIDE it along iso directions
explanation: The iso box (three axes at 120°, 30° to horizontal) envelopes the object; internal features offset along axes.

topic: Construction of Isometric views of lines, planes, and simple solids
stem: A circle on one iso face of a cube is LAB-constructed by:
options: the FOUR-CENTRE method on the enclosing iso rhombus (arcs from obtuse corners and from side-midpoint intersections)
explanation: Four-centre arcs within the face rhombus generate the iso ellipse accurately and quickly.

topic: Construction of Isometric views of lines, planes, and simple solids
stem: Non-isometric lines (slanted edges) in lab iso figures are drawn by:
options: first LOCATING THEIR END POINTS with iso-axis offsets, then joining them straight
explanation: Non-iso edges cannot be measured off directly — endpoints are established axis-wise before joining.

stem: CAD (in this lab module) introduces:
options: the drawing of geometry with software (AutoCAD-like), leveraging layers, snapping and commands instead of board tools
explanation: The CAD module introduces the screen elements (menu/toolbars, drawing area, command line) and basic draw/modify.

stem: Object SNAPS (osnap) in CAD work like:
options: magnets locking the cursor to precise geometric points (end, mid, centre, intersection) of EXISTING objects
explanation: Osnaps deliver the precision drafting hand cannot achieve freehand — picks snap to true geometrical points.

topic: Use of CAD software to draw basic geometric shapes, apply dimensions, and modify objects
stem: Which are basic DRAW entity commands in CAD? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: FORMAT DISK is an OS command; LINE, CIRCLE and RECTANGLE/POLYGON create drawing entities.

topic: Use of CAD software to draw basic geometric shapes, apply dimensions, and modify objects
stem: MODIFY commands such as MOVE, COPY, ROTATE, MIRROR and OFFSET in CAD serve to:
options: EDIT existing objects (relocate, duplicate, turn, reflect, make parallel copies)
explanation: Modify tools transform existing geometry — the editing counterpart of the draw set.

topic: Use of CAD software to draw basic geometric shapes, apply dimensions, and modify objects
stem: Which are CAD DIMENSION commands? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: DIM SPELLING does not exist; linear, radial, diameter and aligned dimensions cover basic dimensioning.

topic: Use of CAD software to draw basic geometric shapes, apply dimensions, and modify objects
stem:
Assertion (A): Drawings in CAD are created to the true 1:1 size of the object, and the sheet SCALE is decided only at plotting.
Reason (R): Since zoom is free and geometry is exact, full-size modelling in 'model space' lets a print-plot scale fit the drawing to the paper afterwards.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Full-size modelling with plot-time scaling (R) is exactly the CAD workflow stated in (A).

stem: A frame of reference in which Newton's first law holds without modification is called:
explanation: Inertial frames are unaccelerated; Newton's laws apply directly without pseudo-forces.

stem: To apply Newton's laws in a non-inertial frame, we must introduce:
explanation: Pseudo-forces like the centrifugal and Coriolis forces account for the frame's acceleration.

stem: In a frame rotating with angular velocity ω, the Coriolis acceleration of a particle moving with velocity v (relative to the frame) has magnitude:
explanation: a_cor = 2ω × v, giving magnitude 2ωv when v is perpendicular to ω.

stem: The centripetal acceleration of a point at distance r from the axis in a frame rotating at angular speed ω is:
explanation: a_c = ω²r, always directed toward the rotation axis.

topic: Centripetal and Coriolis acceleration and its application in weather system
stem: In the Northern hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects horizontally moving air:
options: To the left of its motion
To the right of its motion
explanation: Coriolis deflection is rightward in the Northern hemisphere, leftward in the Southern.

topic: Centripetal and Coriolis acceleration and its application in weather system
stem: The horizontal Coriolis effect on wind vanishes at:
explanation: The horizontal component varies as sin(latitude), which is zero at the equator.

stem: The differential equation of simple harmonic motion is:
explanation: SHM has restoring acceleration proportional to displacement: ẍ = −ω²x.

stem: The time period of a mass m attached to a spring of stiffness k is:
explanation: T = 2π√(m/k); stiffer springs give shorter periods.

stem: The total mechanical energy of a simple harmonic oscillator of amplitude A and spring constant k is:
explanation: E = ½kA², constant in time, exchanged between kinetic and potential forms.

stem: In SHM, the kinetic energy is maximum at:
explanation: Speed (hence KE) peaks at the mean position; PE peaks at the extremes.

stem: For SHM x = A sin ωt, the maximum velocity and maximum acceleration are respectively:
explanation: v_max = Aω at the mean position; a_max = Aω² at the extremes.

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem: The equation of a damped harmonic oscillator is:
explanation: Damping adds a velocity-proportional term bẋ to the SHM equation.

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem: A damped oscillator is critically damped when:
explanation: b² = 4mk is the boundary; larger b overdamps, smaller b gives damped oscillations.

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem: The system that returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating is:
explanation: Critical damping gives the fastest non-oscillatory return — used in vehicle shock absorbers.

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem: In a lightly (under) damped oscillator, the amplitude:
explanation: x(t) = A e^{−γt} cos(ω′t + φ): oscillation inside an exponentially decaying envelope.

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem: The angular frequency of a lightly damped oscillator (natural frequency ω₀, damping constant γ) is:
explanation: Damping lowers the oscillation frequency to ω′ = √(ω₀² − γ²).

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem: A high quality factor Q of an oscillator indicates:
options: Heavy damping and rapid energy loss
Light damping and slow energy loss
explanation: Q = ω₀/(2γ) is inversely related to damping; high Q means many oscillations before decay.

stem: Resonance in a forced oscillator occurs when the driving frequency is:
options: Much larger than the natural frequency
explanation: Near ω = ω₀ the amplitude response is maximum — the resonance condition.

stem: In the steady state, a forced oscillator vibrates at:
explanation: After transients die out, the system oscillates at the driver's frequency with constant amplitude.

stem: For a damped forced oscillator, the amplitude-resonance frequency is:
explanation: Maximum amplitude occurs slightly below ω₀ at √(ω₀² − 2γ²) due to damping.

stem: The sharpness of a resonance curve is controlled mainly by:
options: The amplitude of the driving force
explanation: Light damping (high Q) gives a tall, narrow resonance peak; heavy damping flattens it.

stem: According to Huygens's principle, every point on a wavefront acts as:
explanation: The new wavefront is the envelope of secondary wavelets from every point of the old one.

topic: Superposition of Waves and interference of Light by wave front-splitting and amplitude-splitting
stem: A sustained interference pattern requires the two sources to be:
explanation: Coherence — same frequency and constant phase relation — is essential for stable fringes.

topic: Superposition of Waves and interference of Light by wave front-splitting and amplitude-splitting
stem: Young's double slit is an example of ______ while the Michelson interferometer uses ______.
explanation: YDSE splits one wavefront at two slits; Michelson splits amplitude with a beam splitter.

topic: Superposition of Waves and interference of Light by wave front-splitting and amplitude-splitting
stem: For constructive interference, the path difference between two coherent waves must be:
explanation: Path difference nλ gives phase difference 2nπ — crests meet crests.

stem: In Young's double slit experiment, the fringe width β equals:
explanation: β = λD/d, where D is slit-to-screen distance and d the slit separation.

stem: In YDSE with λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m and d = 0.5 mm, the fringe width is:
If the entire YDSE apparatus is immersed in water (refractive index n), the fringe width:
explanation: Wavelength shrinks to λ/n in water, so β = λD/(nd) decreases by the factor n.

stem: In a Michelson interferometer, moving the mirror by a distance d shifts N fringes, where d equals:
explanation: Each λ/2 of mirror travel changes the round-trip path by λ, shifting one fringe: d = Nλ/2.

stem: If 200 fringes cross the field when the Michelson mirror moves 58.9 μm, the wavelength of light is:
explanation: λ = 2d/N = 2×58.9μm/200 = 589 nm (sodium light).

stem: The Michelson interferometer divides the incident beam using:
options: A partially silvered glass plate (beam splitter)
explanation: A half-silvered plate splits the amplitude into two perpendicular beams that later recombine.

topic: Fraunhofer diffraction from single slit and circular aperture
stem: In Fraunhofer diffraction from a single slit of width a, minima occur at angles satisfying:
explanation: Single-slit minima: a sinθ = mλ for m = ±1, ±2, … (m ≠ 0).

topic: Fraunhofer diffraction from single slit and circular aperture
stem: The angular width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction is ______ that of the other maxima.
explanation: The central maximum spans from −λ/a to +λ/a, twice the width of the secondary maxima.

topic: Fraunhofer diffraction from single slit and circular aperture
stem: For a circular aperture of diameter D, the first diffraction minimum occurs at sin θ equal to:
explanation: Airy pattern: sinθ = 1.22λ/D — the basis of the Rayleigh resolution criterion.

topic: Diffraction Grating and their resolving power
stem: The resolving power of a diffraction grating with N lines used in order m is:
explanation: R = λ/Δλ = mN — more lines and higher order give better resolution.

topic: Diffraction Grating and their resolving power
stem: The grating equation for principal maxima is (e = grating element):
explanation: (a+b) sinθ = mλ gives the directions of the principal maxima.

stem: LASER stands for:
options: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Absorption by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Rays
explanation: The acronym is Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.

stem: Einstein's A coefficient describes ______ and the B coefficients describe ______.
explanation: A gives the spontaneous decay rate; B gives stimulated absorption and emission rates.

stem: The ratio A/B of Einstein's coefficients is proportional to:
explanation: A/B = 8πhν³/c³, so spontaneous emission dominates at high frequencies — one reason X-ray lasers are hard.

stem: Population inversion means:
options: More atoms in the ground state than the excited state
More atoms in an excited state than in a lower state
explanation: Light amplification requires N₂ > N₁ so stimulated emission outweighs absorption.

stem: A metastable state is essential for laser action because:
options: It has a very short lifetime
Its long lifetime (~10⁻³ s) allows population inversion to build up
It emits photons spontaneously at once
explanation: Long-lived metastable levels store atoms, enabling inversion before spontaneous decay.

topic: Different types of lasers - Gas Laser, Helium-Neon Laser, Solid State Laser (Ruby, Neodymium), Semiconductor Laser
stem: The wavelength of the standard He-Ne laser output is:
explanation: He-Ne emits red light at 632.8 nm; lasing occurs in neon, helium assists pumping.

topic: Different types of lasers - Gas Laser, Helium-Neon Laser, Solid State Laser (Ruby, Neodymium), Semiconductor Laser
stem: The active material in a ruby laser is:
options: Cr³⁺ ions in an Al₂O₃ crystal
explanation: Ruby is chromium-doped alumina; Cr³⁺ ions provide the 694.3 nm three-level lasing transition.

topic: Different types of lasers - Gas Laser, Helium-Neon Laser, Solid State Laser (Ruby, Neodymium), Semiconductor Laser
stem: A semiconductor (diode) laser produces light by:
options: Electron-hole recombination at a forward-biased p-n junction
explanation: Forward-biased junctions (e.g. GaAs) emit photons on carrier recombination; feedback gives lasing.

topic: Different types of lasers - Gas Laser, Helium-Neon Laser, Solid State Laser (Ruby, Neodymium), Semiconductor Laser
stem: The ruby laser is a three-level laser. Compared with four-level lasers (e.g. He-Ne, Nd:YAG), it:
options: Needs more than half the atoms pumped out of the ground state
Cannot achieve population inversion at all
explanation: In three-level systems the lower laser level is the ground state, demanding very strong pumping.

stem: True or False: A photon produced by stimulated emission has the same frequency, phase and direction as the stimulating photon.
explanation: True — this coherence of stimulated photons is the origin of laser light's properties.

stem: True or False: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is maximum at the mean position.
explanation: False: acceleration ∝ displacement, so it is zero at the mean position and maximum at the extremes.

topic: Damped Harmonic motion: overdamped, critically Damped and lightly damped oscillators
stem:
Assertion (A): Critically damped systems are preferred in vehicle suspension design.
Reason (R): A critically damped system returns to equilibrium in minimum time without oscillating.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Fast, oscillation-free recovery is exactly why critical damping suits shock absorbers.

topic: Centripetal and Coriolis acceleration and its application in weather system
stem:
Assertion (A): Cyclones in the Northern hemisphere rotate anticlockwise.
Reason (R): The Coriolis force deflects moving air to the right in the Northern hemisphere.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Air rushing toward a low-pressure centre is deflected rightward, producing anticlockwise circulation.

stem: In Young's double slit experiment, the fringe width increases when: (Select all that apply.)
options: The slit separation d is increased
The screen distance D is increased
The apparatus is immersed in water
explanation: β = λD/d grows with λ and D; increasing d or immersing in water (λ→λ/n) shrinks the fringes.

stem: Which of the following are essential for laser action? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Inversion, a long-lived level and cavity feedback are required; thermal equilibrium actually forbids inversion.

stem: In the photoelectric effect, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons is:
explanation: Einstein's equation: KE_max = hν − φ, where φ is the work function.

stem: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm). KE_max of the photoelectrons is:
Increasing the intensity of incident light (frequency fixed, above threshold) increases:
options: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons
The number of photoelectrons emitted per second
explanation: Intensity sets the photon flux (hence current); KE_max depends only on frequency.

stem: The stopping potential V₀ is related to the maximum kinetic energy by:
explanation: The retarding potential that just stops the fastest electrons satisfies eV₀ = KE_max.

stem: The Compton shift in wavelength is given by Δλ =
explanation: Δλ = λ_C(1 − cosθ) with Compton wavelength λ_C = h/m₀c ≈ 0.0243 Å.

stem: The maximum Compton shift occurs at scattering angle:
explanation: At θ = 180°, (1 − cosθ) = 2, giving Δλ_max = 2h/mc ≈ 0.0485 Å.

stem: The Compton effect provides direct evidence for:
explanation: Photon-electron collisions conserving energy and momentum confirm light's particle behaviour.

stem: Wave-particle duality means that matter and radiation:
options: Exhibit both wave and particle behaviour depending on the experiment
explanation: Interference shows wave nature; photoelectric/Compton show particle nature — both apply to matter too.

stem: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum p is:
explanation: λ = h/p is de Broglie's relation linking momentum to wavelength.

stem: An electron accelerated through a potential difference V has de Broglie wavelength approximately:
explanation: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 12.27/√V Å with V in volts.

stem: An electron accelerated through 100 V has a de Broglie wavelength of about:
explanation: λ = 12.27/√100 = 1.227 Å — comparable to crystal spacings, hence electron diffraction.

stem: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle for position and momentum states:
explanation: Position and momentum cannot both be known more precisely than Δx·Δp ≥ ℏ/2.

stem: The uncertainty principle rules out the existence of electrons inside the nucleus because:
options: Confinement to ~10⁻¹⁴ m would demand electron energies far above those observed (~MeV scale ≫ β-decay energies)
explanation: Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁴ m forces Δp so large that the electron's energy would be ~20 MeV, contradicting experiment.

stem: The energy-time uncertainty relation is:
explanation: Short-lived states have broad energy widths: ΔE·Δt ≥ ℏ/2 explains natural linewidths.

stem: The physical significance of |ψ|² is that it represents:
options: The probability density of finding the particle
explanation: Born interpretation: |ψ|²dV is the probability of finding the particle in volume dV.

stem: The normalization condition on a wavefunction ψ is:
explanation: Total probability of finding the particle somewhere must be unity.

stem: An acceptable wavefunction must be:
explanation: Physical admissibility requires ψ to be single-valued, finite and continuous (with continuous ψ′).

stem: For a matter-wave packet, the group velocity equals:
explanation: v_g = dω/dk = p/m = particle velocity; the packet travels with the particle.

stem: For a de Broglie wave of a particle moving with speed v, the phase velocity is:
explanation: v_p = ω/k = E/p = mc²/mv = c²/v, which exceeds c but carries no information.

stem: The expectation value of position for a normalized wavefunction ψ(x) is:
explanation: ⟨x⟩ = ∫ψ*xψ dx — the probability-weighted average of measurements.

stem: If an operator  acting on ψ gives Âψ = aψ with a constant, then ψ is called:
options: An eigenfunction of  with eigenvalue a
explanation: Eigenfunctions return themselves scaled by the eigenvalue — measured values of the observable.

stem: The time-independent Schrödinger equation is:
explanation: Hψ = Eψ with H = −(ℏ²/2m)d²/dx² + V is the stationary-state equation.

topic: Application of Schrodinger Wave Equation for particle in one dimensional box: its wavefunction and eigenvalue of energy and moment
stem: The energy eigenvalues of a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L are:
explanation: Boundary conditions quantize energy as E_n = n²h²/8mL², n = 1, 2, 3…

topic: Application of Schrodinger Wave Equation for particle in one dimensional box: its wavefunction and eigenvalue of energy and moment
stem: The normalized wavefunction of a particle in a 1-D box (0 ≤ x ≤ L) is:
explanation: ψ_n = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L) vanishes at both walls and is normalized.

topic: Application of Schrodinger Wave Equation for particle in one dimensional box: its wavefunction and eigenvalue of energy and moment
stem: The ratio of the first excited state energy to the ground state energy for a particle in a box is:
explanation: E_n ∝ n², so E₂/E₁ = 4/1 = 4.

topic: Application of Schrodinger Wave Equation for particle in one dimensional box: its wavefunction and eigenvalue of energy and moment
stem: The minimum (zero-point) energy of a particle in a box is non-zero because:
options: n = 0 would make ψ vanish everywhere, violating the uncertainty principle
explanation: n = 0 gives ψ ≡ 0 (no particle); confinement forces Δp > 0, so E₁ = h²/8mL² > 0.

stem: Gauss's law states that the net electric flux through any closed surface equals:
explanation: ∮E·dA = q_enc/ε₀ — flux counts the enclosed charge.

stem: The electric field at distance r from an infinite line charge of density λ is:
explanation: A cylindrical Gaussian surface gives E = λ/(2πε₀r), falling off as 1/r.

topic: Divergence and Curl of Electrostatic fields
stem: The differential forms of electrostatics are:
explanation: Gauss's law in differential form plus the curl-free (conservative) nature of static E.

stem: The electrostatic field E is related to the potential V by:
explanation: E points from high to low potential: E = −∇V.

stem: In a charge-free region, the electrostatic potential satisfies:
explanation: With ρ = 0, Poisson's equation reduces to Laplace's equation ∇²V = 0.

stem: The electric displacement vector D is defined as:
explanation: D = ε₀E + P combines free-field and material polarization contributions.

stem: The bound surface and volume charge densities of a polarized dielectric are:
explanation: Polarization produces σ_b = P·n̂ on surfaces and ρ_b = −∇·P in the volume.

stem: At a charge-free boundary between two dielectrics:
options: E and D are both fully discontinuous
The normal E and tangential D are continuous
E and D are both fully continuous
The tangential E and the normal D are both continuous
explanation: ∇×E = 0 gives continuous E_tangential; ∇·D = ρ_free = 0 gives continuous D_normal.

stem: Inserting a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r between capacitor plates multiplies the capacitance by:
explanation: C = ε_r C₀ — polarization reduces the internal field, allowing more charge at the same voltage.

stem: The Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v in fields E and B is:
explanation: F = q(E + v×B) — the complete electromagnetic force law.

stem: A static magnetic field does no work on a moving charge because:
options: The magnetic force is always parallel to velocity
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity
explanation: F = qv×B ⊥ v, so the power F·v = 0; only speed direction changes, not kinetic energy.

topic: Biot-Savart and Ampere's circuital laws and their applications
stem: The magnetic field at perpendicular distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I is:
explanation: Ampère's law with a circular loop gives B = μ₀I/2πr.

topic: Biot-Savart and Ampere's circuital laws and their applications
stem: The magnetic field 10 cm from a long straight wire carrying 10 A is:

topic: Divergence and Curl of Magneto static fields
stem: The magnetostatic field equations are:
explanation: No magnetic monopoles (∇·B = 0); currents produce circulation (∇×B = μ₀J).

stem: The magnetic vector potential A is defined through:
explanation: Since ∇·B = 0, B can always be written as the curl of a vector potential A.

topic: Force and torque on a magnetic dipole
stem: The torque on a magnetic dipole of moment m in a uniform field B is:
explanation: τ = m×B, tending to align the dipole with the field; energy U = −m·B.

stem: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced emf equals:
options: The negative rate of change of magnetic flux
The rate of change of charge
explanation: emf = −dΦ_B/dt; the minus sign encodes Lenz's law.

stem: Lenz's law — the induced current opposes the change producing it — is a consequence of:
explanation: If induced currents aided the change, energy would be created from nothing.

stem: A rod of length l moving with velocity v perpendicular to a field B develops an emf of:
explanation: Motional emf = Blv from the magnetic force on the rod's free charges.

stem: The energy stored in an inductor L carrying current I, and the magnetic energy density, are respectively:
explanation: U = ½LI² and u = B²/2μ₀ are the standard magnetic energy expressions.

topic: Maxwell's equations in vacuum and nonconducting medium
stem: Maxwell's key modification of Ampère's law was the addition of:
explanation: ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t; the displacement current predicts electromagnetic waves.

stem: The continuity equation expressing conservation of charge is:
explanation: Charge leaving a volume (∇·J) must decrease the density inside: ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t.

stem: The Poynting vector S = E × H represents:
options: The direction and rate of electromagnetic energy flow per unit area
explanation: S gives power flow (W/m²) of the electromagnetic field — Poynting's theorem is energy bookkeeping.

topic: Wave Equations: plain electromagnetic wave in vacuum and their transverse nature and Polarization
stem: The speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum equals:
explanation: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s — Maxwell's triumphant identification of light.

topic: Wave Equations: plain electromagnetic wave in vacuum and their transverse nature and Polarization
stem: In a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum, the ratio E/B of field amplitudes equals:
explanation: E₀ = cB₀; both fields oscillate in phase, perpendicular to each other and to propagation.

stem: True or False: Photoelectric emission shows a measurable time lag when very dim light is used.
explanation: False: emission is essentially instantaneous (<10⁻⁹ s) — a photon is absorbed as a single quantum.

topic: Wave Equations: plain electromagnetic wave in vacuum and their transverse nature and Polarization
stem: True or False: Electromagnetic waves in vacuum are transverse, with E and B perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
explanation: True: E ⊥ B ⊥ k; the transverse nature permits polarization.

stem:
Assertion (A): No photoelectrons are emitted below the threshold frequency, however intense the light.
Reason (R): Each photon then carries energy hν less than the work function φ.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Emission is a one-photon process; if hν < φ no single photon can free an electron — R explains A.

topic: Divergence and Curl of Magneto static fields
stem:
Assertion (A): The divergence of the magnetic field is zero everywhere.
Reason (R): Isolated magnetic monopoles have never been observed; field lines always close on themselves.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: ∇·B = 0 encodes the absence of magnetic charge; R is the physical justification.

topic: Maxwell's equations in vacuum and nonconducting medium
stem: Which of the following are Maxwell's equations in vacuum (no charges or currents)? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: The first three are correct source-free forms; ∇·B = 0 (not μ₀J) is the fourth equation.

topic: Application of Schrodinger Wave Equation for particle in one dimensional box: its wavefunction and eigenvalue of energy and moment
stem: For a particle in a 1-D infinite box, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: The ground state energy is zero
explanation: Energies E_n ∝ n² are quantized and ψ(0) = ψ(L) = 0; zero-point energy E₁ > 0, so the second is false.

stem: In the classical free electron theory of metals, conduction electrons are treated as:
options: A gas of free particles moving through the lattice
explanation: Drude/Lorentz theory models valence electrons as a free 'electron gas' colliding with ions.

stem: Electrical conductivity in the free electron model is σ =
explanation: σ = ne²τ/m, with n the electron density and τ the mean collision (relaxation) time.

stem: A major failure of the classical free electron theory is its inability to explain:
options: The very small electronic contribution to specific heat
explanation: Classically electrons should add (3/2)R to specific heat; experiment shows far less — resolved by quantum statistics.

stem: In the quantum (Sommerfeld) free electron theory, electrons obey:
explanation: Electrons are fermions; Fermi-Dirac statistics with the Pauli principle fixes the theory's failures.

stem: At absolute zero, the Fermi level represents:
options: The band gap centre of any solid
explanation: At 0 K all states below E_F are filled and all above are empty.

stem: The probability that a state exactly at the Fermi energy is occupied at any temperature T > 0 is:
explanation: f(E_F) = 1/(e⁰+1) = 1/2 — the defining property of the Fermi level.

stem: In an intrinsic semiconductor, the Fermi level lies:
options: Approximately midway between the valence and conduction bands
explanation: Equal electron and hole densities place E_F near the middle of the gap.

stem: The Fermi-Dirac distribution function is f(E) =
explanation: f(E) = [1 + e^{(E−E_F)/kT}]⁻¹; the +1 distinguishes fermions from bosons.

topic: Bloch's theorem for particle in a periodic Potential
stem: Bloch's theorem states that the wavefunction of an electron in a periodic potential has the form:
options: ψ = u_k(x) e^{ikx} with u_k having the lattice periodicity
A delta function at each ion
explanation: Bloch functions are plane waves modulated by a lattice-periodic function u_k(x).

topic: Bloch's theorem for particle in a periodic Potential
stem: Bloch's theorem applies to electrons moving in:
explanation: The theorem is the foundation of band theory for perfectly periodic crystals.

topic: Kroning-Penney model and origin of energy band
stem: The Kronig-Penney model demonstrates that a periodic potential leads to:
options: A continuous spectrum of allowed energies
Allowed energy bands separated by forbidden gaps
explanation: Solving the periodic square-well problem yields alternating allowed and forbidden energy regions.

topic: Kroning-Penney model and origin of energy band
stem: In the Kronig-Penney model, as the potential barrier strength P → ∞, the energy bands:
options: Shrink to the discrete levels of an isolated well
explanation: Infinite barriers isolate the wells, recovering sharp atomic-like levels; P → 0 gives the free-electron continuum.

topic: Kroning-Penney model and origin of energy band
stem: Energy bands in solids fundamentally originate from:
options: The overlap and splitting of atomic energy levels of many interacting atoms
explanation: N interacting atoms split each atomic level into N closely spaced levels — a band.

stem: The band gap of a typical insulator is roughly:
explanation: Insulators have wide gaps (diamond ≈ 5.5 eV); semiconductors ≈ 1 eV; metals have none.

stem: In a metal, the valence and conduction bands:
options: Are separated by a large gap
Overlap or the conduction band is partially filled
explanation: Partially filled or overlapping bands provide free states for conduction at any temperature.

stem: The approximate band gaps of silicon and germanium at room temperature are respectively:
explanation: Si ≈ 1.12 eV and Ge ≈ 0.66-0.72 eV — standard values.

stem: As temperature increases, the resistance of a pure semiconductor:
explanation: More carriers are thermally excited across the gap, so conductivity rises (negative temperature coefficient).

stem: In an intrinsic semiconductor, the electron concentration n and hole concentration p satisfy:
explanation: Each thermal excitation creates one electron-hole pair, so n = p = n_i.

stem: Doping silicon with phosphorus (group V) produces:
explanation: The fifth valence electron of the donor is easily freed, adding electrons as majority carriers.

stem: In a p-type semiconductor, the majority carriers and dominant impurity type are:
explanation: Group III acceptors (e.g. boron) create holes as majority carriers.

stem: The mass-action law for semiconductors in thermal equilibrium states:
explanation: np = n_i² holds for doped and intrinsic material alike in equilibrium.

stem: Silicon is doped with 10¹⁶ donors/cm³ (n_i = 1.5×10¹⁰ cm⁻³). The equilibrium hole concentration is approximately:
In an n-type semiconductor, the Fermi level lies:
explanation: Donor doping raises E_F toward the conduction band; acceptors pull it toward the valence band.

stem: Drift current in a semiconductor is caused by:
explanation: Drift = field-driven motion; diffusion = gradient-driven motion.

stem: Diffusion current flows from:
options: Low carrier concentration to high concentration
Positive terminal to negative terminal only
High carrier concentration to low concentration
explanation: Carriers diffuse down their concentration gradient, producing a diffusion current.

stem: The drift velocity of carriers with mobility μ in field E is:
explanation: v_d = μE defines mobility (units cm²/V·s).

stem: The Einstein relation connecting diffusion coefficient D and mobility μ is:
explanation: D/μ = kT/q (≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K) links diffusion and drift — both stem from carrier scattering.

stem: In semiconductors, the total current is generally the sum of:
options: Drift and diffusion components of both electrons and holes
explanation: J = J_n(drift+diff) + J_p(drift+diff) — all four components in general.

stem: The depletion region of a p-n junction contains:
explanation: Mobile carriers recombine/diffuse away, leaving fixed ionized impurities that set up the built-in field.

stem: The built-in potential of a p-n junction is given by:
explanation: V_bi = (kT/q) ln(N_A N_D/n_i²), typically ≈ 0.6-0.7 V for silicon.

stem: Under forward bias, the width of the depletion region:
explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in field, narrowing the depletion layer and enabling current flow.

stem: The ideal diode equation for the junction current is:
explanation: Shockley equation: I = I₀(e^{qV/kT} − 1); reverse saturation current is −I₀.

stem: In an unbiased p-n junction at equilibrium, the net current is zero because:
options: Drift and diffusion currents exactly cancel for each carrier type
No carriers exist near the junction
The depletion region is a perfect insulator
The Fermi levels are different on the two sides
explanation: Equilibrium means E_F is flat: diffusion of majority carriers is balanced by drift of minorities.

stem: Under reverse bias, the small current that flows is mainly due to:
options: Thermally generated minority carriers drifting across the junction
explanation: Minority carriers generated near the junction are swept across by the field — nearly voltage-independent.

stem: True or False: At T = 0 K, the probability of occupation of a state just above the Fermi energy is exactly zero.
explanation: True: the Fermi-Dirac function is a step at 0 K — filled below E_F, empty above.

stem: True or False: The conductivity of a metal increases as its temperature rises.
explanation: False: increased lattice vibrations enhance scattering, so metallic conductivity falls with temperature.

stem:
Assertion (A): The Fermi level of an n-type semiconductor shifts toward the conduction band.
Reason (R): Donor impurities greatly increase the electron concentration in the conduction band.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Higher n pushes E_F upward by E_F = E_c − kT ln(N_c/n); R correctly explains A.

stem:
Assertion (A): A p-n junction conducts heavily in forward bias but only feebly in reverse bias.
Reason (R): Forward bias lowers the junction potential barrier, allowing majority carrier injection.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The barrier reduction under forward bias enables exponential majority-carrier injection; R explains A.

topic: Kroning-Penney model and origin of energy band
stem:
Assertion (A): Solids exhibit allowed and forbidden energy bands.
Reason (R): Electrons in a crystal move in a periodic potential of the ion cores.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Band structure follows directly from Bloch waves in the periodic potential (Kronig-Penney result).

stem: Which statements about semiconductors are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: np = n_i² holds in thermal equilibrium
Intrinsic carrier concentration increases with temperature
Adding acceptors makes holes the majority carriers
explanation: The first three are standard results; doping increases carrier density, so it raises conductivity.

stem: Which of the following contribute to current in a semiconductor? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Drift and diffusion of both carrier types constitute the current; core electrons remain bound.

topic: Determination of Planck's constant and Photoelectric Work Function using Photoelectric cell.
stem: In the photoelectric cell experiment, Planck's constant is obtained from the graph of:
explanation: eV₀ = hν − φ, so the V₀-ν graph is a straight line of slope h/e and intercept −φ/e.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

stem: In the e/m (Thomson-type) experiment, the electron beam is deflected using:
explanation: Balancing electric and magnetic deflections of the beam yields the charge-to-mass ratio e/m.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of Wavelength of (He-Ne) LASER using Diffraction Grating Method.
stem: Using a diffraction grating with the He-Ne laser, the wavelength is computed from:
explanation: Measuring the diffraction angle of order m with known grating element gives λ from the grating equation.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of Wavelength of Sodium light by measuring the diameter of the Newton's Ring.
stem: In Newton's rings, the wavelength is obtained from the ring diameters using:
explanation: For reflected light, D²ₙ₊ₚ − D²ₙ = 4pλR, giving λ from measured diameters and lens radius R.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of Wavelength of Sodium light by measuring the diameter of the Newton's Ring.
stem: The centre of Newton's rings (reflected light) is dark because:
options: The air film thickness is zero and reflection introduces a π phase change
explanation: At contact the path difference is only the λ/2 phase jump on reflection, giving destructive interference.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of curvature of convex surface of a lens by Newton's ring.
stem: Newton's rings can be used to find the radius of curvature R of a lens surface from:
explanation: Rearranging D²ₙ₊ₚ − D²ₙ = 4pλR with known λ yields R.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Calculation of Energy Band Gap of a semiconductor.
stem: The band gap of a semiconductor is found by plotting (four-probe/thermistor method):
options: Resistance vs T on linear axes
Current vs voltage at fixed T
explanation: ρ ∝ e^{E_g/2kT}, so the slope of ln ρ against 1/T equals E_g/2k.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Verification of inverse square law using photocell.
stem: The inverse square law verified with a photocell states that illumination varies as:
explanation: Photocurrent (∝ intensity) falls off as the inverse square of the source distance.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of Dielectric constant using resonance method.
stem: In the resonance method for dielectric constant, inserting the dielectric into the capacitor of an LC circuit:
explanation: C increases by factor ε_r, and f = 1/2π√(LC) therefore decreases; ε_r is found from the shift.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Verification of existence of Bohr's Energy level with Frank-Hertz apparatus.
stem: The Franck-Hertz experiment shows dips in collected current at equally spaced accelerating voltages because:
options: Electrons excite atoms only at discrete energy transfers, losing energy quantum-wise
explanation: Current drops each time electrons gain exactly the atomic excitation energy — proof of discrete levels.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of the Earth's horizontal magnetic field intensity and magnetic Moment of a magnet by employing magnetometer.
stem: A deflection magnetometer used with a vibration magnetometer determines:
options: Only the Earth's horizontal field B_H
Both M and B_H by combining M/B_H and M·B_H
explanation: Deflection gives M/B_H and vibration gives M·B_H; solving the pair yields both.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Verification of Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law of Electromagnetic Induction.
stem: When a magnet is pushed into a coil, the induced current direction is such that the coil face toward the magnet becomes:
explanation: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the approach, presenting a like pole to repel the magnet.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of the capacitance and permittivity of the given material.
stem: The permittivity of a material sandwiched in a parallel-plate capacitor is calculated from:
explanation: C = εA/d, so measuring C with known geometry gives ε = Cd/A.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of Planck's constant and Photoelectric Work Function using Photoelectric cell.
stem: In the stopping-potential graph of the photoelectric experiment, the intercept on the frequency axis gives:
explanation: V₀ = 0 where hν = φ, so the ν-intercept is the threshold frequency ν₀ = φ/h.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Determination of Wavelength of (He-Ne) LASER using Diffraction Grating Method.
stem: True or False: Laser light is preferred in the grating experiment because of its high monochromaticity and directionality.
explanation: True: sharp single-wavelength, well-collimated beams give clean, easily measured diffraction orders.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Verification of Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law of Electromagnetic Induction.
stem:
Assertion (A): Faster movement of a magnet into a coil produces a larger galvanometer deflection.
Reason (R): The induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: emf = −dΦ/dt: faster motion means larger dΦ/dt — R exactly explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

topic: Calculation of Energy Band Gap of a semiconductor.
stem:
Assertion (A): A semiconductor's resistance falls as it is heated.
Reason (R): Thermal energy excites more electron-hole pairs across the band gap.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Carrier generation dominates over mobility loss, so resistance drops — R explains A.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

stem: In the magnetron/bar-magnet e/m method, the accepted value of e/m of the electron is approximately:
explanation: e/m ≈ 1.76×10¹¹ C/kg; 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ is e alone and 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg is the mass.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Physics Lab, Unit 1

stem: A function f(z) of a complex variable z = x + iy can be written as:
explanation: Every complex function splits into real and imaginary parts: f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y).

stem: The modulus of the complex number z = 3 + 4i is:
If f(z) = z², then in terms of u and v (z = x + iy):
explanation: (x+iy)² = x² − y² + 2ixy, so u = x² − y² and v = 2xy.

stem: For a limit of f(z) to exist as z → z₀ in the complex plane, the value must be the same:
options: Along circles centred at z₀ only
explanation: z can approach z₀ from infinitely many directions; all paths must give the same limit.

stem: f(z) is continuous at z₀ if:
explanation: Continuity needs existence of the limit, of f(z₀), and their equality.

stem: The function f(z) = \(\bar{z}\) (complex conjugate) is:
explanation: The difference quotient depends on approach direction at every point, so f(z) = z̄ is nowhere differentiable.

stem: The derivative of an analytic function f(z) = u + iv can be written as:
explanation: f′(z) = u_x + iv_x (equivalently v_y + iu_x using C-R equations).

stem: A function f(z) is analytic at a point if it is:
options: Differentiable in some neighbourhood of the point
explanation: Analyticity requires differentiability throughout a neighbourhood, not just at the point itself.

stem: A function analytic at every point of the complex plane is called:
explanation: Entire functions (e.g. e^z, sin z, polynomials) are analytic everywhere in ℂ.

stem: Which of the following functions is analytic everywhere?
explanation: e^z satisfies the C-R equations everywhere; z̄, |z|² and Re z fail them (|z|² only at 0).

stem: f(z) = |z|² is differentiable:
explanation: u = x²+y², v = 0: C-R equations (2x = 0, 2y = 0) hold only at the origin.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: The Cauchy-Riemann equations in Cartesian form are:
explanation: C-R: ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = −∂v/∂x — necessary for differentiability.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: The Cauchy-Riemann equations in polar form are:
options: u_r = r v_θ and v_r = r u_θ
explanation: In polar coordinates: ∂u/∂r = (1/r)∂v/∂θ and ∂v/∂r = −(1/r)∂u/∂θ.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: Satisfaction of the Cauchy-Riemann equations at a point is ______ for differentiability there.
options: Necessary but not sufficient without continuity of the partials
explanation: C-R alone can hold without differentiability; adding continuity of the first partials makes it sufficient.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: For f(z) = z³ = u + iv, the value of u_x at the point (1, 0) is:
explanation: u = x³ − 3xy², so u_x = 3x² − 3y² = 3 at (1,0) — consistent with f′(z) = 3z² = 3.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: If f(z) = u + iv is analytic and u is constant throughout a domain, then f is:
explanation: u_x = u_y = 0 forces v_x = v_y = 0 by C-R, so v is constant too — f is constant.

stem: A function φ(x, y) is harmonic if it satisfies:
explanation: Harmonic functions are solutions of Laplace's equation with continuous second partials.

stem: If f(z) = u + iv is analytic, then u and v are both:
explanation: Differentiating the C-R equations gives u_xx + u_yy = 0 and v_xx + v_yy = 0.

stem: The harmonic conjugate of u = x² − y² is:
explanation: v_y = u_x = 2x and v_x = −u_y = 2y give v = 2xy + c (f = z²).

stem: Is u = x³ − 3xy² harmonic, and if so what analytic function has it as real part?
explanation: u_xx + u_yy = 6x − 6x = 0; u is Re(z³) since z³ = x³−3xy² + i(3x²y−y³).

stem: The function u = e^x cos y is harmonic. Its harmonic conjugate is:
explanation: v_y = u_x = e^x cos y ⇒ v = e^x sin y + c; together they form f(z) = e^z.

stem: The level curves of u and its harmonic conjugate v intersect:
explanation: ∇u·∇v = u_x v_x + u_y v_y = 0 by C-R — the two families are orthogonal trajectories.

stem: True or False: If f(z) is analytic in a domain, its derivative f′(z) is also analytic there.
explanation: True — analytic functions are infinitely differentiable; derivatives remain analytic.

stem: True or False: Differentiability of f(z) at a point implies its continuity at that point.
explanation: True — as in real analysis, complex differentiability implies continuity (not conversely).

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem:
Assertion (A): f(z) = \(\bar{z}\) is not analytic anywhere.
Reason (R): For f = x − iy, u_x = 1 while v_y = −1, so the Cauchy-Riemann equations fail everywhere.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: C-R equations never hold (1 ≠ −1), which is exactly why z̄ is nowhere analytic.

stem:
Assertion (A): The real part of any analytic function is harmonic.
Reason (R): Differentiating the Cauchy-Riemann equations and using equality of mixed partials yields Laplace's equation for u.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: u_xx = v_yx and u_yy = −v_xy sum to zero — R is the standard proof of A.

stem: Which of the following functions are entire (analytic in the whole plane)? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: e^z, sin z and polynomials are entire; 1/z has a singularity at the origin.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: If f = u + iv is analytic, which relations hold? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: The two C-R equations hold and force the gradients to be orthogonal; the last contradicts C-R.

stem: \(\lim_{z\to 0} \dfrac{\bar{z}}{z}\):
explanation: Along the real axis the ratio is 1; along the imaginary axis it is −1 — path dependent, so no limit.

stem: e^{iθ} in Cartesian form equals:
explanation: Euler's formula: e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ.

stem: If f(z) is analytic and f′(z) = 0 throughout a domain D, then f is:
explanation: Vanishing derivative over a connected domain forces f to be constant.

stem: The derivative of f(z) = z² is:
explanation: Power rule holds for complex differentiation: d(z²)/dz = 2z.

stem: If v is a harmonic conjugate of u, then a harmonic conjugate of v is:
explanation: If u + iv is analytic then v − iu = −i(u+iv) is analytic, so −u is the conjugate of v.

stem: The function f(z) = 1/z is continuous:
explanation: 1/z is defined and continuous for all z ≠ 0; the origin is a singular point.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: For f(z) = e^z = u + iv, u equals:
explanation: e^z = e^{x+iy} = e^x(cos y + i sin y), so u = e^x cos y.

stem: f(z) = x² − y² + i·k·xy is analytic when k equals:
explanation: u_x = 2x = v_y = kx forces k = 2; then u_y = −2y = −v_x = −ky ✓ — giving f = z².

stem: Which of the following is NOT a harmonic function?
explanation: For x² + y²: u_xx + u_yy = 2 + 2 = 4 ≠ 0; the others satisfy Laplace's equation.

stem: The argument (principal value) of the complex number z = 1 + i is:
explanation: tan θ = 1/1 with z in the first quadrant gives arg z = π/4.

stem: f′(z₀) is defined as:
options: The partial derivative of u with respect to x only
\(\lim_{\Delta z\to 0}\dfrac{f(z_0+\Delta z)-f(z_0)}{\Delta z}\) with the same value for every approach of Δz to 0
explanation: Complex differentiability demands one limit value over all directions of Δz — a strong condition.

stem: Points where a function fails to be analytic are called:
explanation: Singularities are the points of non-analyticity — studied further via Laurent series.

topic: Cauchy-Riemann Equations in Cartesian and polar form
stem: If f(z) = u + iv is analytic with u = x² − y², using C-R equations f′(z) equals:
explanation: f′ = u_x + iv_x = 2x + i·2y = 2z (since v = 2xy).

stem: The value of a line integral of a complex function generally depends on:
options: Only the length of the path
The path joining the endpoints (unless the integrand is analytic in a suitable domain)
explanation: In general the path matters; analyticity in a simply connected domain gives path independence.

stem: \(\oint_C \dfrac{dz}{z}\) where C is the unit circle traversed counter-clockwise equals:

finiteness — it must terminate after a finite number of steps

topic: Idea of Algorithm: steps to solve logical and numerical problems
stem: The algorithm to swap two numbers a and b using a temporary variable is:
options: a = t; t = b; b = a
t = a; a = b; b = t
a = b; t = a; b = t
explanation: Save a into t first, then a = b overwrites a, then b = t restores original a into b — any other order loses a value.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Idea of Algorithm: steps to solve logical and numerical problems
stem: For computing the sum 1+2+...+n, the correct algorithm initializes sum = 0 and then:
options: multiplies sum by i each time
adds each i from 1 to n into sum in a loop
divides sum by n each step
reads n values from user only
explanation: Repeatedly accumulating sum = sum + i for i = 1..n yields the required total; order 1 + ... + n with zero start.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Idea of Algorithm: steps to solve logical and numerical problems
stem: Tracing: with a = 5 and b = 7, after the correct 3-step swap (t = a; a = b; b = t) the values become:
explanation: t holds 5; a is overwritten with 7; b then receives t = 5, so a = 7 and b = 5.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1
