options: start or end (terminal) of the flowchart
explanation: Oval/rounded boxes hold START and STOP — the terminals of the flowchart.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: Reading data into a program (e.g. READ a, b) is shown in a flowchart by a:
explanation: Input/output operations use parallelograms; rectangles are used for processing (e.g. c = a + b).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: The RECTANGLE in a flowchart represents:
options: a processing/computation step like area = pi * r * r
explanation: Processing steps (assignments, calculations) are written inside rectangles; flow of control uses arrows.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: PSEUDO CODE is:
options: an informal, English-like, structured description of an algorithm between plain english and a programming language
explanation: Pseudocode expresses algorithm logic in readable structured text without strict language syntax, as a design aid.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: Compare: which statement is TRUE about flowchart vs pseudocode?
options: Flowcharts are easier to modify for large programs than pseudocode
Flowcharts give a pictorial view with standard symbols; pseudocode is textual and easier to edit for large programs
explanation: Flowcharts visualize logic with symbols but modifying large ones is tedious; pseudocode is textual, compact and editable.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: In an algorithm/flowchart to find the LARGEST of three numbers a, b, c, the first comparison typically performed is (e.g.):
options: compare a with the sum, b + c
compare max(a, b, c) with given answer
check if a > b, then compare the winner with c
explanation: Conditional branching: if a > b then (a vs c) else (b vs c) — a ladder of comparisons determines the largest.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: SOURCE CODE refers to:
options: the machine code inside the CPU
the program text written by a programmer in a high-level language
explanation: Source code is the human-readable high-level program text (e.g. a .c file) that is fed to the compiler.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: A C program file normally has the extension:
explanation: C source files use .c; compilation produces .obj (object) and linking produces the executable (.exe on Windows).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: Every C program must contain the function:
explanation: Execution always begins at the main() function, which every complete C program must define.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: The line #include <stdio.h> at the top of a C program:
options: is a preprocessor directive that inserts the standard input-output header file contents before compilation
explanation: #include is handled by the preprocessor: it textually substitutes the header declarations needed by printf, scanf etc.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: In the build process of a C program the LINKER is responsible for:
options: combining object files with library code to produce the executable
explanation: The linker resolves references between object modules and library functions (e.g. printf) to create the final executable.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

stem: OBJECT code (file) is the output of:
options: the compiler (machine code not yet linked into an executable)
explanation: Compilation yields object code (machine-level but with unresolved external references), which the linker makes an executable.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: The library function used to display formatted output in C is:
explanation: printf from stdio.h prints formatted output to standard output; scanf is for input.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: What does the format specifier %d mean in printf/scanf calls?
explanation: %d formats a signed int; %f float, %c char, %s string, %lf double (in scanf).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: In scanf("%d", &x); the ampersand & before x is essential because:
options: scanf needs the ADDRESS of x (&x) so it can store the read value at that memory location
explanation: scanf writes into the caller's variable; &x yields the address (pointer) of x where scanf places the input.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: Comments in a C program are written as:
explanation: C supports // for rest-of-line comments and /*...*/ for multi-line blocks; the compiler ignores comments entirely.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: A VARIABLE in a programming language is:
options: a named memory location whose stored value may change during program execution
explanation: A variable name refers to an allocated memory cell; assigning new values updates the stored content at that address.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: Which is NOT a valid C identifier?
explanation: Identifiers must begin with a letter or underscore — 2ndValue starts with a digit, violating the rule.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: C is said to be CASE-SENSITIVE, which means:
options: keywords can be written in any case
identifiers Marks, MARKS and marks refer to three DIFFERENT variables
variable names must use only capitals
explanation: In C, uppercase and lowercase letters are distinct in identifiers and keywords; int and Int differ.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: The basic data type used in C to store a single character like 'A' is:
explanation: char stores a one-byte character constant; strings need a char array.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: On typical modern C implementations, the size of an int, float and double are respectively:
explanation: Commonly int = 4 bytes, float = 4 bytes (single precision), double = 8 bytes (double precision); char = 1 byte.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: The C data type appropriate for storing the value 3.14159 with high precision is:
explanation: Floating values need float/double; double gives 8-byte double precision (about 15 significant digits).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: Every variable in C associates with a memory ADDRESS. The operator that yields the address of a variable v is:
explanation: The unary & is the address-of operator; * is the dereference (indirection) operator used with pointers.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: A keyword (reserved word) in C is:
options: a word usable as any identifier
a word with predefined language meaning that cannot be used as a variable name, e.g. int, if, while
explanation: C has 32 reserved keywords like int, do, break, for; using them as identifiers is a syntax error.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem: A SYNTAX error is:
options: a violation of the language grammar detected by the compiler (e.g. missing semicolon)
an error in the formula used
an error producing wrong output only
explanation: Syntax errors break language rules and are caught at compile time; the program will not build until corrected.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem: A LOGICAL error is dangerous because:
options: the program compiles and runs but produces WRONG results due to flawed logic
explanation: Logical errors (e.g. area = b + h instead of 0.5bh) pass compilation silently and only show as incorrect output.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem: The statement: printf(Sum is %d, s)  leads to a compile-time error because:
options: the format string is missing its enclosing double quotes
explanation: The format string needs double quotes: printf("Sum is %d", s); — without them the code violates syntax rules.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem: Division of an integer variable by zero at run time gives a:
explanation: Division by zero cannot always be spotted at compile time — it surfaces during execution as a runtime fault.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem: int a = 5, b = 2; float c = a / b; yields c = 2.0. This unexpected result stems from:
options: integer division: both operands are int, so fraction is truncated BEFORE assignment to float
explanation: 5/2 evaluated in integer arithmetic is 2, then converted to 2.0; use 5.0/2 or (float)a/b to get 2.5.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Idea of Algorithm: steps to solve logical and numerical problems
stem: An algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps.
explanation: True: finiteness is a defining property of an algorithm — an endless procedure is not an algorithm.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Introduction to components of a computer system (disks, memory, processor, where a program is stored and executed, operating system, compilers etc.)
stem: The CPU can execute a program directly from the hard disk without loading it into RAM.
explanation: False: the CPU fetches instructions from main memory only; programs must first be loaded into RAM.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem: A program with a logical error fails to compile.
explanation: False: logical errors slip through compilation because the code is grammatically correct; they appear as wrong output.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: In flowcharts, the circle symbol represents an on-page connector.
explanation: True: small circles serve as connectors joining flow sections of a large flowchart on the same page.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Idea of Algorithm: steps to solve logical and numerical problems
stem:
Assertion (A): An algorithm is written before writing the actual program code.
Reason (R): Developing logic in a language-independent form first avoids mixing design thinking with language syntax and detects design flaws early.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Separating logical design from coding (R) is the practical reason for algorithm-first development (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Introduction to components of a computer system (disks, memory, processor, where a program is stored and executed, operating system, compilers etc.)
stem:
Assertion (A): Compiled languages generally run faster than interpreted languages.
Reason (R): Compilation translates the whole program once into machine code, so no per-statement translation cost is paid at run time.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: One-time translation (R) removes the run-time interpretation overhead, explaining compiled-code speed (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem:
Assertion (A): 'int' cannot store the value 3.14 faithfully in C.
Reason (R): The int type stores only whole numbers; the fractional part is discarded (truncated).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: int has no fractional field (R), so assigning 3.14 stores 3 — exactly as A states.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Syntax and Logical Errors in compilation
stem:
Assertion (A): Testing is essential even for programs that compile without errors.
Reason (R): A program free of syntax errors may still contain logical or runtime errors that only execution with test data can reveal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Compilation certifies grammar only (R); logical/runtime faults need testing, which is why A holds.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

stem:
Assertion (A): Object files cannot be executed directly even though they contain machine code.
Reason (R): Object files need to be compiled again by the assembler.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true — object files have unresolved external references. R is false: they need LINKING (not re-assembling) with libraries.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Introduction to components of a computer system (disks, memory, processor, where a program is stored and executed, operating system, compilers etc.)
stem: Which of the following are primary (main) memory types? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: RAM, ROM and cache are directly accessible primary memory; the hard disk is secondary (auxiliary) storage.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Idea of Algorithm: steps to solve logical and numerical problems
stem: Which are essential properties of an algorithm? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Ambiguity is prohibited in algorithms; finiteness, definiteness and effectiveness (plus input/output specification) are essential.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Representation of Algorithm: Flowchart/Pseudo code with examples
stem: Which flowchart-symbol mappings are CORRECT? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: The parallelogram represents input/output, not loops; the other three mappings are standard ANSI flowchart symbols.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: Variables (with data types) variables and memory locations
stem: Which of the following are valid C identifiers? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: 'int' is a reserved keyword and cannot be an identifier; the others start with letter/underscore and use allowed characters.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

topic: From algorithms to programs; source code
stem: Which steps occur in the pipeline from C source code to running program? (Select all that apply.)
options: Linking object files with libraries to form the executable
explanation: Preprocess - compile - link - load is the standard pipeline; the OS does not generate flowcharts.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

stem: Regarding object and executable code, which statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Object code is the compiler's output
Executable code is produced by the linker
Executable is machine code ready to be loaded into RAM and run
Object code can always run without linking
explanation: Object code usually has unresolved external references and needs linking before it can load and execute; the rest hold.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 1

stem: In C, the modulus operator % gives:
explanation: a % b yields the remainder when integer a is divided by b; it cannot be applied to float operands.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The value of the C expression 17 % 5 is:
explanation: 17 = 5 x 3 + 2, hence 17 % 5 = 2 (remainder of integer division).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The value of the C expression 7 / 2 (both integers) is:
explanation: Integer division truncates the fractional part: 7/2 = 3 (not 3.5).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: To obtain 3.5 from dividing int a = 7 by b = 2, one should write:
explanation: Casting one operand to float (or using a floating literal) forces floating-point division: 7.0/2 = 3.5.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The statement x += 5; is equivalent to:
explanation: The compound assignment operators +=,-=,*=,/=,%= apply the operation and store back: x = x + 5.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Difference: x = ++i vs x = i++ (i initially 5) assigns to x respectively:
explanation: Pre-increment increments then yields 6; post-increment yields the old value 5 then increments i. So x = 6, then x = 5.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: With int i = 10; the expression i++ + ++i evaluates in a sequence where post- then pre-increment are observed; the final value of i is:
explanation: Each of ++ operations increments i once: 10 -> 11 -> 12 regardless of evaluation order arguments; i ends at 12.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Which of the following is the C 'EQUAL TO' comparison operator?
explanation: == compares for equality; a single = is the ASSIGNMENT operator — a classic confusion source of bugs.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: In C, a relational expression such as (a > b) evaluates to:
explanation: C has no boolean keyword in classic C; relational/logical expressions produce integer 1 (true) or 0 (false).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: if (x = 5) — this condition always behaves as 'true' because:
options: the assignment operator = assigns 5 to x and the assigned value 5, being non-zero, is treated as true
explanation: Assignment inside if yields the assigned value; any non-zero is true — a common bug; intended was if (x == 5).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The C logical operators are:
explanation: Logical AND (&&), OR (||) and NOT (!) combine conditions; single & | ^ ~ are BITWISE operators.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The expression (x >= 10 && x <= 99) is TRUE when:
options: x is any two-digit number 10 through 99 inclusive
explanation: Logical AND demands both bounds hold simultaneously: 10 <= x <= 99.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: SHORT-CIRCUIT evaluation in C means: in (a && b), if a evaluates to false, then:
options: b is NOT evaluated, since the whole AND is already false
explanation: For && a false first operand settles the result; for || a true first operand does — the second operand is skipped.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The expression !(a > b) is equivalent to:
explanation: Negation of 'greater than' among ordered numbers is 'less than or equal to' (De Morgan for comparison).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The C bitwise operators operate on:
options: the individual bits of integer operands
explanation: Bitwise & | ^ ~ << >> act on binary bit patterns of ints; they are not defined on floats.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: If a = 5 (0101) and b = 3 (0011), the result of a & b is:
explanation: 0101 AND 0011 = 0001 = 1; each output bit is 1 only where both input bits are 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: With the same a = 5 (0101), b = 3 (0011): a | b and a ^ b respectively give:
explanation: 0101 OR 0011 = 0111 = 7; XOR gives 0110 = 6 (bits set where operands differ).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Left-shifting an unsigned integer x by 1 bit (x << 1) is equivalent to:
explanation: Each left shift appends a zero bit, i.e. multiplies by 2; similarly x >> 1 performs integer divide by 2.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: In C operator precedence, which is CORRECT (highest to lower)?
explanation: Parentheses rank highest, * / % above + -, then shifts/relational/equality, logical ops, and assignment lowest.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The expression 2 + 3 * 4 evaluates to:
explanation: Multiplication binds tighter: 2 + (3 x 4) = 2 + 12 = 14.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: The simple if statement executes its statement block only when:
options: the tested condition evaluates to true (non-zero)
explanation: In C, any non-zero condition value is true; the if-block runs only then, else control skips it.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: In an if-else statement, if the test condition is FALSE, control passes to:
explanation: With else, exactly one of the two branches executes: if-block on true, else-block on false.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: Grading: if (m >= 60) print "First"; else if (m >= 45) print "Second"; else print "Fail". For m = 50 the output is:
explanation: m = 50 fails the first test but satisfies m >= 45, so the second branch prints Second.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: For multiple statements under one if, C requires:
options: each statement on a new line only
braces { } to group them into a single compound block
explanation: Without braces only the first statement is conditional; braces make the full block the if's body.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: The ternary (conditional) operator ?: is used as:
options: a compact if-else: condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false
explanation: max = (a > b) ? a : b; selects between two values like an if-else in expression form.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: The switch statement selects among alternatives based on the value of:
options: an integer (or char) expression, matched against case labels
explanation: switch takes an expression evaluating to int/char/enum and jumps to the matching case; floats/strings are not allowed.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: If the 'break' statement is omitted at the end of a switch case:
options: execution FALLS THROUGH into the next case's statements
explanation: Without break, control cascades into subsequent cases (fall-through) until a break or the switch end.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: The 'default' case of a switch statement executes when:
options: no case label matches the switch expression value
explanation: default handles non-matching values; it may be placed anywhere in the switch and is optional.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The three parts of a for statement header are:
explanation: for (init; condition; update): initialize once, then repeat body while condition holds, updating after each pass.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) printf("%d ", i); prints:
explanation: i takes 1,2,3,4,5; when i becomes 6 the test fails, so the loop stops after printing 5.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The total number of times for (i = 0; i < n; i++) executes its body is:
explanation: i runs 0,1,...,n-1: exactly n iterations; i = n fails the test.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The key difference between while and do-while loops is:
options: do-while executes its body AT LEAST ONCE, because its test is after the body
explanation: while tests BEFORE the first iteration (entry-controlled); do-while tests AFTER (exit-controlled) so body runs >= 1 time.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: A while (0) { ... } loop in C will:
explanation: The condition 0 is false, so the entry-controlled while body is skipped entirely.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: A do { ... } while (0); loop executes its body:
explanation: Exit-controlled: body runs, then the (false) condition stops repetition — exactly one execution.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Which loop construct is best termed an ENTRY-CONTROLLED loop?
explanation: while and for test before each iteration including the first; do-while is exit-controlled.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The break statement inside a loop:
options: immediately terminates the innermost enclosing loop or switch
explanation: break transfers control out of the closest enclosing loop/switch, abandoning its remaining iterations.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The continue statement inside a loop:
options: skips the REST of the current iteration and proceeds with the next iteration
explanation: continue abandons the remaining statements of the current pass only, re-testing/jumping to the update — unlike break.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i == 3) break; printf("%d ", i); } prints:
explanation: Loop prints 0,1,2; at i = 3 break triggers before printf, so output ends with 2.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i == 3) continue; printf("%d ", i); } prints:
explanation: Only i == 3 is skipped by continue; prints 0 1 2 and 4.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: for (;;) is:
options: an infinite loop (headers omitted, test defaults to true)
explanation: An omitted condition in a for header is always true; only break (or return/exit) can end the loop.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: A for loop with a misplaced semicolon: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++); { printf("Hi"); } prints 'Hi':
options: once (the semicolon makes the for an EMPTY loop; the block runs just once)
explanation: The lone ';' is the whole loop body (empty). The braced block then executes once, unconditionally.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Nested loop: for (i = 1; i <= 2; i++) for (j = 1; j <= 3; j++) printf("*"); prints stars:
explanation: Outer 2 x inner 3 = 6 total executions of printf.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Pattern logic: to print n rows of a triangle with i stars in row i, the inner loop bound j should run:
explanation: Row i prints j = 1..i stars as i grows from 1 to n — inner bound follows the row index.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Loop to sum first n natural numbers: sum = 0; for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) sum += i; For n = 10 the sum is:
explanation: 1+2+...+10 = 10 x 11/2 = 55, matching accumulation of i from 1 to 10.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The goto statement in C:
options: is the recommended modern control flow
performs an unconditional jump to a labeled statement, whose overuse harms readability (spaghetti code)
explanation: goto jumps to a label; structured programming discourages it since break/continue/loops cover clean flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: In C, the condition expression of an if statement may be any expression; a non-zero value counts as true.
explanation: True: C treats zero as false and any non-zero value (even negative) as true in conditionals.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: The operators & and && are interchangeable in C conditions.
explanation: False: && is logical (with short-circuit, yields 0/1), & is bitwise (evaluates both operands bit-by-bit) — totally different.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: A do-while loop always executes its body at least once.
explanation: True: its test follows the body, so at least one pass occurs even if the condition starts false.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Parentheses () have the highest precedence in C expressions.
explanation: True: parenthesized sub-expressions evaluate first, overriding default operator precedence.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem:
Assertion (A): Writing if (a = 10) compiles without error in C but is usually a bug.
Reason (R): Assignment = inside if is legal; it assigns 10 and the result 10 (non-zero) evaluates as true, unlike the intended comparison ==.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The assignment evaluates to a non-zero value (10) treated true (R), which is exactly why such code silently misbehaves (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem:
Assertion (A): A counter-controlled for loop can always be rewritten as an equivalent while loop.
Reason (R): Initialization, test and update of a for header map to separate statements around/inside an equivalent while loop.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: for and while differ only in placement of the loop parts (R), hence full mutual convertibility (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem:
Assertion (A): When many multiway branches depend on one integral variable, switch is preferable to long if-else ladders.
Reason (R): A switch organizes cases around a single expression, is more readable, and compilers can implement it with efficient jump tables.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Readability and jump-table efficiency (R) are precisely the advantages of switch over ladders of if-else-if (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem:
Assertion (A): In if (x != 0 && y/x > 2), a division-by-zero fault can never occur.
Reason (R): Short-circuit evaluation of && guarantees y/x is evaluated only when x != 0 is true.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: If x = 0 the first operand is false and the second (division) is skipped (R), so A holds — a classic use of short-circuiting.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem:
Assertion (A): The expression 1/2 x PI x r^2 in C computes zero when written as (1/2)*3.14*r*r with uncast ints 1 and 2.
Reason (R): Integer sub-expression 1/2 evaluates to 0, which zeroes the whole product regardless of r.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Integer truncation of 1/2 to 0 (R) then multiplies through and yields 0 — exactly the pitfall of A.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Which of the following are valid C arithmetic operators? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: C has no exponent operator ** (that is another language); +, % and the unary ++ are valid.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Which statements about loop control are CORRECT? (Select all that apply.)
options: break exits the current loop entirely
break inside a switch exits the switch
continue inside a switch exits the outer loop
explanation: continue has no effect on switch (it acts on loops); the remaining statements describe break/continue correctly.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Given a = 6 (0110) and b = 3 (0011), which evaluations are correct? (Select all that apply.)
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

topic: Writing and evaluation of conditionals and consequent branching
stem: Which are valid multiway selection tools in C? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: C has no repeat-until keyword (do-while serves that role); the other three implement multiway selection.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: ON nested loops, which statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Inner loop completes all its iterations for each outer iteration
break affects only the loop in which it appears
Both loops may use the same counter variable safely in all cases
Total iterations of printf multiply outer x inner counts
explanation: Statements 1,2,4 hold; sharing one counter between nested loops corrupts both counters — unsafe.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: Which are C relational operators? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: C has no <> operator (not-equal is !=); >=, == and <= are the valid relational forms.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 2

stem: In C, the first element of an array declared as int a[10]; is accessed as:
explanation: C arrays are zero-indexed: a[0] through a[9] are the ten elements of int a[10].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: For the declaration int a[10]; the LAST valid subscript is:
explanation: Valid indices run 0 to size-1, i.e. 0 through 9; a[10] is out of bounds.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The declaration int a[] = {1, 2, 3}; creates an array of size:
explanation: When size is omitted with an initializer, the compiler counts the elements: three ints here.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: int a[5] = {1, 2}; results in the array:
explanation: Partial initialization zero-fills the remaining elements of a static array in C.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: If int b[5]; and a program writes to b[7], C:
options: does NOT check bounds — the write may silently corrupt other memory (undefined behaviour)
explanation: C performs no array bound checking; out-of-range access compiles and leads to undefined behaviour.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: int a[3][4]; declares a 2-D array containing how many int elements?
explanation: 3 rows x 4 columns = 12 elements, indexed a[0][0] through a[2][3].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A two-dimensional C array is stored in memory in:
explanation: C stores a 2-D array row by row: all elements of row 0 first, then row 1, and so on.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

explanation: Row 1 is {4,5,6}; index 2 within it is 6.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: If int requires 4 bytes, sizeof(int a[10]) evaluated on typical machines equals:
explanation: 10 elements x 4 bytes each = 40 bytes; sizeof returns bytes occupied by the whole array.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Elements of int a = {1,2,3,4,5}. The count of elements in any int array arr (locally known) can be computed as:
explanation: Total bytes / bytes per element gives the element count; C has no length(arr) builtin.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: To traverse an integer array a of n elements and print them, the loop runs:
explanation: Indices span 0..n-1, hence for (i = 0; i < n; i++), avoiding the off-by-one a[n] access.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Algorithm to REVERSE an array a[0..n-1] in place swaps:
options: a[i] with a[n-1-i] for i = 0 to n/2 - 1 only
explanation: Swapping the symmetric pairs over the first half of the array reverses it without a second array.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Finding the MAXIMUM of n array elements by a simple scan requires how many comparisons?
explanation: Initialize max = a[0], then compare max with each of the remaining n-1 elements: n-1 comparisons.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: When an array is passed to a C function, what actually reaches the function?
options: a full copy of the array
the array name decays to a pointer/address of the first element (efficient: no copying)
explanation: Only the base address is passed; the function accesses the caller's array through a pointer — changes reflect back.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A function f(int a[], int n) modifies a[0] = 99; from inside. After the call, the caller's array shows a[0] as:
options: 99 (arrays are passed by address, so changes are visible to the caller)
explanation: Since the callee receives the array's base address, in-place modification persists in the caller's array.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Reading n numbers into int a[50] with scanf in a loop, the correct scanf call is:
explanation: scanf needs the address of the target variable, so &a[i]; the array-name shortcut only applies to whole-array reads like char strings.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Loop error analysis: for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = i; with int a[n]; is dangerous because:
options: a[n] gets written once — one location out of bounds
explanation: The <= n boundary includes i = n, writing a[n] which is past the last valid element a[n-1].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Matrix addition of two m x n matrices A and B typically uses:
options: two nested loops: c[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j]
explanation: A pair of loops (rows i, columns j) adds elementwise — the standard double-loop structure for 2-D arrays.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Matrix multiplication C = A x B (all n x n) requires the classic triple loop with inner statement:
explanation: c[i][j] accumulates dot product of row i of A and column j of B over k = 0..n-1.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The array name a in an expression (e.g. passing a to printf) behaves essentially as:
explanation: An array name 'decays' into a pointer to its first element in most expressions — the basis of array-pointer duality.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: In C, a string is:
options: an array of characters terminated by the null character '\0'
explanation: There is no built-in string type; strings are char arrays ending with the terminating byte '\0'.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: char s[] = "HELLO"; occupies how many bytes?
explanation: Five letters plus the terminating '\0' = 6 bytes stored.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: strlen("HELLO") returns:
explanation: strlen counts characters BEFORE the null terminator; it does not count '\0'.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: char s[5] = "HELLO"; is invalid because:
options: five letters plus the needed '\0' require SIX bytes, exceeding s[5]
explanation: Room for terminator is mandatory: char s[6] = "HELLO" is the minimal legal size.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The string library functions like strlen, strcpy, strcat, strcmp come from the header:
explanation: string.h declares the string-handling functions; stdio.h covers I/O, math.h math, stdlib.h general utilities.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: strcmp("apple", "apple") returns:
explanation: strcmp returns 0 for equal strings, negative if first is lexicographically smaller, positive otherwise.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: strcmp("apple", "apply") returns a value:
explanation: First mismatch at 'e' (101) vs 'y' (121): 101 - 121 < 0, so a negative value results.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The correct way to copy the string "Bihar" into char t[20]; is:
explanation: Array names are not assignable; strcpy copies characters including the terminator into the destination array.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: After char a[20] = "Ram"; strcat(a, "esh"); the string in a is:
explanation: strcat appends the second string at the end of the first WITHOUT inserting any space: "Ramesh".
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: scanf("%s", s); reads a string but STOPS at:
explanation: The %s conversion reads a whitespace-delimited token; a full line needs fgets/gets-style reading.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Why is & NOT used with char s[20]; in scanf("%s", s)?
options: s itself IS the address of the first character (array name)
explanation: A string's destination is an address, and the array name already IS that address; using &s would be wrong type.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Reversal logic: counting characters until s[i] == '\0' directly computes:
explanation: A loop scanning until the terminator counts characters, replicating strlen manually.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Given char s[] = "INDIA"; the element s[2] equals the character:
explanation: Zero-based indexing: s[0]='I', s[1]='N', s[2]='D', s[3]='I', s[4]='A'; so s[2] is 'D'.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A function in C is:
options: a self-contained named block of statements performing a task, callable from elsewhere
explanation: Functions encapsulate statements under a name, accept parameters and optionally return a value.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The three parts of using a user-defined function correctly are:
explanation: Prototype tells the compiler the signature; definition gives the body; the call invokes it.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A function declaration int add(int, int); is called the:
explanation: The prototype states return type, name and parameter types without a body, placed before use.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The 'return' statement inside a function:
options: transfers control back to the caller, optionally carrying one value
explanation: return expr; exits the function and hands expr back to the calling point; void functions may use plain return.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A function that returns no value is declared with return type:
explanation: The void type indicates absence of a returned value, e.g. void greet(void) { ... }.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: In x = add(2, 3); the arguments 2 and 3 are the ____ parameters, while int a, int b in the definition are the ____ parameters.
explanation: Call-site values are actual parameters (arguments); the names in the function header are formal parameters.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: C passes ordinary (non-array) arguments by VALUE, which means:
options: squawks are issued at link time
only a copy of the argument reaches the function; the caller's variable is UNCHANGED
explanation: The callee works on copies in its own stack frame; the originals in the caller stay as they were.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: void swap(int x, int y) { int t = x; x = y; y = t; } called as swap(a, b) with a=3, b=7 results in:
explanation: Only the copies are exchanged; to swap caller variables use pointers: swap(int *x, int *y) and swap(&a,&b).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: sqrt(), pow(), abs(), scanf() are examples of:
options: built-in (library) functions provided by C standard libraries
explanation: These come from standard headers/math.h, stdio.h etc., linked automatically — saving re-implementation.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: To use sqrt(25.0) in a program, the required header is:
explanation: sqrt, pow, sin etc. are declared in math.h (and linked with the math library).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A variable declared INSIDE a function body has ____ scope:
explanation: Local variables live on the stack frame of the function and are invisible outside it; globals are the opposite.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems
stem: Recursion means:
options: a function that calls ITSELF (directly or indirectly) to solve sub-problems
explanation: A recursive function reduces the problem to a smaller instance and solves until a base case is reached.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems
stem: Every valid recursive function MUST have:
options: one or more BASE CASES to stop the recursion, and a step moving toward it
explanation: Without a base case + convergence toward it, recursion never ends — a stack overflow follows.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Example programs, such as Finding Factorial, Fibonacci series, Ackerman function etc.
stem: The recursive factorial relation is:
options: fact(n) = n x fact(n - 1) with fact(0) = 1
explanation: n! = n x (n-1)! with base fact(0) = 1; e.g. fact(5) = 120.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Example programs, such as Finding Factorial, Fibonacci series, Ackerman function etc.
stem: With the standard recursive fact, fact(4) evaluates to:

topic: Example programs, such as Finding Factorial, Fibonacci series, Ackerman function etc.
stem: The Fibonacci recurrence used in the common recursive program is:
options: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), with fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1
explanation: Each term is the sum of the previous two; seeds 0 and 1 generate 0,1,1,2,3,5,8,...
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Example programs, such as Finding Factorial, Fibonacci series, Ackerman function etc.
stem: fib(6) under fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1 equals:
explanation: 0,1,1,2,3,5,8 — the 7th term (index 6) is 8.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Example programs, such as Finding Factorial, Fibonacci series, Ackerman function etc.
stem: The Ackermann function with A(0, n) = n + 1; A(m, 0) = A(m-1, 1); A(m, n) = A(m-1, A(m, n-1)) gives A(1, 2) =:
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems
stem: The data structure the system uses to keep track of active (called but unfinished) function invocations is the:
explanation: Each call pushes a stack frame (locals + return address); frames pop as calls return. Deep recursion may overflow the stack.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems
stem: Recursion that never reaches its base case results in:
options: stack overflow (the program crashes after exhausting stack space)
explanation: Endless frames accumulate until the process runs out of stack memory and is terminated.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems
stem: Iteration vs recursion: which is TRUE?
options: loops are generally faster and use less memory, while recursion often gives shorter, clearer code for recursive problems
explanation: Each call costs a stack frame, so iteration wins on speed/memory; recursion wins on elegance for naturally recursive problems.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A pointer in C is a variable that stores:
explanation: Pointers hold memory addresses; declared int *p, a pointer can store the address of an int.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: int *p; and then p = &x; makes p point to x. Accessing the VALUE of x through p uses:
explanation: The unary * is the dereference operator: *p denotes the value stored at the address held by p.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: If int x = 5; int *p = &x; then *p = 10; changes:
explanation: Writing through the dereferenced pointer writes into the pointed-to variable; x becomes 10.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Pointer arithmetic: int *p = a; (a an int array) — then p+1 points to:
options: a[1] — pointers advance by sizeof(int) bytes, i.e. 4 bytes
explanation: C scales pointer arithmetic by the pointed type's size: p+1 lands on the next int element.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: The array-pointer duality: for int a[10]; the expression *(a + 3) is exactly equal to:
explanation: a[i] is defined as *(a+i); hence *(a+3) = a[3].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: int **q; declares:
options: a pointer to a pointer to int
explanation: **q is a pointer whose value is the address of another int pointer — a chain of indirection.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Call by reference in C is SIMULATED by:
options: passing the value of the variable
passing addresses (pointers) of the variables so the function writes at the caller's locations
explanation: Pure C supports only call by value; pointer arguments let a function modify caller data in place.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A CORRECT pointer-based swap definition and call pair is:
options: void swap(int x, int y)... called swap(&a,&b)
void swap(int *x, int *y) { int t = *x; *x = *y; *y = t; } called as swap(&a, &b)
explanation: The function receives addresses via &a,&b and swaps the caller variables through dereferencing.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: A pointer that points to NOTHING valid should be assigned the constant:
explanation: NULL (0) marks an invalid/unassigned pointer; dereferencing NULL is an error.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Use of Pointers in self-referential structures
stem: A SELF-REFERENTIAL structure is one that:
options: contains a pointer member pointing to an object of its OWN structure type (basis of linked lists)
explanation: E.g. struct node { int data; struct node *next; } — nodes chain through next to form linked structures.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Use of Pointers in self-referential structures
stem: A singly linked list is a set of nodes where each node contains:
options: data plus a key field only
data and a pointer to the next node
explanation: Each node's next pointer links to the following node; the last node's next is NULL.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: A structure in C is used to:
options: group values of DIFFERENT data types under one user-defined record type
explanation: struct bundles heterogeneous members (roll no - int, name - char array, marks - float) into one composite type.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: struct student { int roll; float marks; }; struct student s; Accessing the roll member of s uses the operator:
explanation: The dot operator accesses members through a structure variable; -> is used through a structure POINTER.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: If p is a POINTER to struct student, the marks member is accessed as:
explanation: For pointers, use -> (equivalently dereference then dot: (*p).marks); dot needs a structure object, not pointer.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: Initialization: struct point { int x, y; }; struct point p = {10, 20}; assigns:
explanation: Brace initializers map members in declaration order: first value to x, second to y.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: An ARRAY OF STRUCTURES is declared as:
options: struct student s[50]; — valid, e.g. 50 student records
explanation: Declaring an array of a structure type is identical in syntax to any array: type name, variable, [size].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: 'Structures within structure' (nesting) means:
options: one structure type used as a MEMBER of another, e.g. an address struct inside an employee struct
explanation: A member may itself be a structure, e.g. struct date dob inside struct student for date-of-birth.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: The typedef keyword, as in typedef struct student STUD; is used to:
options: create an ALIAS (a simpler new name) for an existing type
explanation: typedef coins a synonym for a type so later declarations can use STUD s1 instead of struct student s1.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Structure: defining, declaring, initializing; accessing structure members, processing of structure, array of structures, structures within structure, structure and function, type definition
stem: Passing a structure TO a function by value copies:
options: ALL members (a complete copy is made; large structures are expensive to copy)
explanation: Whole-structure copying is the cost; passing struct pointers avoids it and allows in-place changes.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Union: definition, declaration, accessing union members, initializing union
stem: The fundamental difference between a UNION and a STRUCT is:
options: all members of a union SHARE THE SAME memory location (one valid at a time), whereas struct members occupy separate memory
explanation: Union overlays its members in one shared area, so only the last-written member holds a valid value.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Union: definition, declaration, accessing union members, initializing union
stem: sizeof of a union equals (ignoring padding):
options: the size of its LARGEST member
explanation: A union reserves space only for its largest member, since all members overlap at one address.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Union: definition, declaration, accessing union members, initializing union
stem: union data { int i; float f; char c; }; sizeof(union data) is (4-byte int/float):
explanation: Largest members int/float need 4 bytes; char needs 1 — the union takes 4 (largest).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Union: definition, declaration, accessing union members, initializing union
stem: After u.i = 65; u.f = 3.14; reading u.i gives:
options: undefined — writing f overwrote the shared storage, so i is no longer valid
explanation: Only the LAST-written member is meaningful in a union; earlier members are clobbered.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Introduction to file handling, file declaration, opening and closing a file, working with text and binary files, I/O operations on file, error handling, random access to files
stem: File handling in C uses the special pointer type:
explanation: FILE is a structure defined in stdio.h; a FILE * stream pointer is used for all file I/O.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Introduction to file handling, file declaration, opening and closing a file, working with text and binary files, I/O operations on file, error handling, random access to files
stem: The function used to OPEN a file is:
explanation: fp = fopen("data.txt", "r"); returns a stream pointer, or NULL if the open failed.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Introduction to file handling, file declaration, opening and closing a file, working with text and binary files, I/O operations on file, error handling, random access to files

stem:
Assertion (A): C programmers must keep array indices within declared limits themselves.
Reason (R): C performs no built-in array bound checking, so out-of-range access gives undefined behaviour rather than an exception.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The absence of runtime bounds checks (R) transfers responsibility for index safety to the programmer (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem:
Assertion (A): Changes made to an array inside a function are visible back in main().
Reason (R): Passing the array passes the base address, so the function accesses the caller's original elements.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Address passing (R) lets the callee reach the caller's cells directly, hence visible changes (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Recursion, as a different way of solving problems
stem:
Assertion (A): A recursive solution can always be converted into an iterative one.
Reason (R): Recursion internally relies on a stack, and a loop with an explicit stack can imitate the same computation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Since recursion is fundamentally stack-based (R), loop+stack rewrites exist for every recursive algorithm (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Union: definition, declaration, accessing union members, initializing union
stem:
Assertion (A): A union uses less memory than an equivalent struct holding the same members.
Reason (R): Union members overlap in shared memory, so total size equals only the largest member instead of the sum.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Member overlapping (R) is precisely why a union's footprint is the max member size rather than the sum (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

topic: Introduction to file handling, file declaration, opening and closing a file, working with text and binary files, I/O operations on file, error handling, random access to files

Assertion (A): A program should check the value returned by fopen before using the file.
Reason (R): fopen returns NULL when the file cannot be opened; using the pointer would otherwise cause errors.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: NULL on failure (R) is the standard fopen contract, making the NULL check (A) mandatory error handling.

struct int s; (a struct OF the primitive keyword as tag...)

strcpy copies a string into another array
Strings can be assigned with = between arrays

source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Units 3-5

stem: Linear (sequential) search finds an element by:
options: checking every element one by one from the start until found or list ends
explanation: Linear search inspects elements in order; it needs no precondition such as sortedness and stops on match or exhaustion.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: In the worst case, linear search on an array of n elements makes:
explanation: Worst case (element absent or last) requires testing every element: n comparisons — order O(n).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: The essential precondition for binary search is:
options: the array must be SORTED (ascending or descending)
explanation: Binary search halves the interval based on comparison with the middle element — valid only on sorted data.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: In binary search with low and high indices, the middle index is computed as:
explanation: mid = (low + high)/2 (integer division); the search then continues left or right of mid.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: If the search key is GREATER than a[mid] in a binary search on an ascending array, the next step is:
explanation: The key must lie to the RIGHT of mid, so the left half (including mid) is discarded via low = mid + 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Binary search for 23 in a = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91] (indices 0-9) finds it after how many probes?
explanation: mid=4(16, go right), mid=7(56, go left), mid=5(23, found) — 3 comparisons.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Binary search on the SAME array for 17 (absent): after probes mid=4 (16), mid=7 (56), mid=5 (23), what concludes the search?
options: low becomes 5 and high 4, low > high, so NOT FOUND
explanation: low crosses high (5 > 4) with no match: the interval is empty, so the key is absent.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Binary search on a sorted array of 1024 elements needs at most about:
explanation: Each probe halves the interval: log2(1024) = 10 probes worst case — the hallmark of O(log n).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: The failure (termination) condition for an iterative binary search loop while(low <= high) is:
explanation: When low exceeds high, the remaining interval is empty, so the loop exits with 'not found'.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Linear vs binary search on an UNSORTED array — which is applicable?
options: linear search only (binary needs sorted data)
explanation: Without sorted order the halving logic of binary search is invalid, so sequential scan is used.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Bubble sort orders an array by repeatedly:
options: comparing ADJACENT elements and swapping them if out of order, bubbling the largest to the end each pass
explanation: Adjacent compare-and-swap passes push the largest unsorted element to its final position, like a rising bubble.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)

explanation: Each pass fixes one element at the end, so n-1 passes place all elements.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: The number of comparisons in basic bubble sort (no early exit) for n elements is:
explanation: Pass lengths n-1, n-2, ..., 1 sum to n(n-1)/2 comparisons — O(n^2) behaviour.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: SELECTION sort places elements in order by:
options: inserting each element into a sublist
repeatedly FINDING THE MINIMUM of the unsorted part and swapping it to the front
explanation: Pass i finds the min of a[i..n-1] and swaps it into position i; the sorted prefix grows by one each pass.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Selection sort on [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]: after the FIRST pass (find min, swap to front), the array is:
explanation: Minimum 10 is at index 1; swapped with a[0]=29, giving [10, 29, 14, 37, 13].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: A distinctive property of selection sort (vs bubble sort) is:
options: it makes AT MOST n-1 swaps (one per pass), good when writing is expensive
explanation: Selection sort performs only one swap per pass even though comparisons remain O(n^2) — swap count is minimal.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: INSERTION sort builds the sorted array by:
options: taking the next element from the unsorted part and INSERTING it at its correct spot in the sorted prefix
explanation: Like arranging playing cards: the key element is compared backwards through the sorted prefix and inserted where it fits.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Insertion sort processing [8, 4, 3, 7]: with sorted prefix [8], inserting 4 gives prefix [4, 8]; inserting 3 gives:
explanation: 3 shifts past 8 and 4 to the head of the sorted prefix: [3, 4, 8].
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Insertion sort is particularly FAST (nearly linear) when the input array is:
explanation: With few inversions, almost no shifting is needed per element — best-case behaviour approaches O(n).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: The output after completely sorting [9, 7, 5, 3, 1] in ASCENDING order (any correct method) is:
explanation: Ascending sort yields the values in increasing order: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: To SORT DESCENDING instead of ascending in bubble sort you change:
options: the comparison in the swap test (swap when a[j] < a[j+1] instead of >)
explanation: Flipping the comparison condition makes larger elements bubble to the FRONT — descending order.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: As data size n grows, the 'order' (growth) of O(n^2) sorting algorithms means that doubling the input size makes the running time about:
options: QUAD (four times), since time grows with the square of n
explanation: For T ~ n^2, (2n)^2 = 4 n^2 — quadratic growth, an intuitive reading of order of complexity.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Rank the following growth orders from FASTEST (best for large n) to slowest:
options: O(log n) then O(n) then O(n^2)
explanation: Logarithmic grows slowest (fastest algorithm), then linear, then quadratic: log n < n < n^2 for large n.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: A single loop from i = 1 to n doing a fixed amount of work is an example of ____ complexity:
explanation: One pass, work per pass constant: time grows proportionally to n.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Two NESTED loops each running n times, with constant work inside, give a total order of:
explanation: n outer x n inner = n^2 constant-time executions — quadratic.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Which order describes an algorithm that HALVES the remaining data at each step (e.g. binary search)?
explanation: Halving per step means about log2(n) steps to finish — logarithmic growth.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Accessing a[i] directly by index in an array exhibits ____ behaviour:
options: O(1) — constant time, independent of n
explanation: Random access takes the same time no matter the array size — constant order.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: The BISECTION method for finding a root of f(x) = 0 requires, as its starting condition:
options: f(a) and f(b) must have the same sign
f(a) x f(b) < 0 (opposite signs, so a root lies between a and b)
explanation: A sign change between endpoints guarantees (for continuous f) at least one root in [a,b], per the intermediate value theorem.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Each bisection iteration computes c = (a + b)/2 and then:
options: replaces both a and b with c
replaces the endpoint whose f-value has the SAME sign as f(c), keeping the sign change within [a,b]
explanation: Keeping the interval across the sign change preserves the root bracket while halving its width every time.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: f(x) = x^2 - 4. Starting with a = 0, b = 4: f(0) = -4, f(4) = 12; midpoint c = 2 gives f(2) = 0. The bisection step:
options: stops (or reports) c = 2 as the root exactly
explanation: f(c) = 0 means c itself is a root (of x^2 - 4); the iteration terminates successfully at x = 2.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 with a = 1, b = 2: f(1) = -2, f(2) = 4. After first bisection c = 1.5 (f(1.5) negative, ~ -0.125), the new bracket is:
explanation: f(1.5) has the same sign as f(1), so a moves to 1.5; sign change remains between 1.5 and 2.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: The NEWTON-RAPHSON iteration formula for a root of f(x) = 0 is:
explanation: Tangent-line extrapolation: each new estimate subtracts f/f' (function over its derivative) at the current point.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: For finding square root of N via Newton-Raphson (f(x) = x^2 - N), the iteration simplifies to:
explanation: sqrt iteration (the Babylonian method): average of x(n) and N/x(n) converges quadratically to sqrt(N).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Newton-Raphson vs bisection: the trade-off is that Newton-Raphson:
options: converges much faster (nearly quadratic) BUT needs the derivative and a good starting guess, and may fail if f' is near zero
explanation: Derivative-guided steps converge fast; but f'(x)=0 or bad x0 breaks it, unlike the foolproof sign bracketing.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: The stopping criterion common to root-finding loops (bisection/Newton) is:
options: when |f(c)| or the change between successive approximations falls below a chosen TOLERANCE
explanation: Exact zeros are rarely hit numerically; loops stop once the approximation is accurate enough (e.g. error < 0.0001).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Bisection's convergence is described as:
options: linear and guaranteed (interval halves each time, but many steps are needed)
explanation: Halving per step gives steady but slow linear convergence: after n steps the interval is (b-a)/2^n.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: To solve the equation x^3 - x - 11 = 0 by bisection, valid initial guesses require:
options: f(a), f(b) must have OPPOSITE signs, so the interval brackets a root
explanation: Bisection brackets only intervals known to straddle a root — hence the sign-change requirement.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: An early-exit (flag) improvement to bubble sort detects sortedness when:
options: a complete pass makes NO swap at all
explanation: A swap-free pass means the array is already ordered, so the remaining passes can be skipped.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Typical implementation of bubble sort uses this loop skeleton:
options: two nested loops: outer over passes i, inner j = 0..n-2-i comparing a[j] with a[j+1]
explanation: The inner bound n-2-i shrinks with every pass since the largest elements are already in place at the end.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: A sentinel (or linear search with early break) loop usually looks like:
explanation: Scan elements; upon match, record the position and break out immediately (or continue if duplicates matter).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Binary search is most elegant in recursive form: search(a, low, high). Its recursive call after key > a[mid] is:
explanation: The right half begins just after mid, so recursion descends with low = mid + 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: A STABLE sorting algorithm is one that:
options: preserves the original order of EQUAL keys
explanation: Equal-valued elements appear in the same relative order after sorting; bubble and insertion are stable by nature.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Sorting names of students for an alphabetical merit list, one would sort an array of:
options: strings using strcmp comparisons in the sort logic
explanation: String sorting compares names with strcmp and swaps whole strings (or pointers) — same skeleton as numeric sorts.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Which task shows O(log n) behaviour through halving patterns?
explanation: Binary search halves the candidate interval every step; the others are linear/quadratic.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Which of the following is TRUE about algorithm choice for very LARGE n?
options: complexity (growth rate) dominates: an O(n log n) or O(n) method crushes an O(n^2) method regardless of constant factors
machine speed matters more than algorithm
explanation: Constants matter for small n; as n grows the asymptotic order decides which algorithm scales.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Binary search can be used on ANY unsorted array directly.
explanation: False: binary search relies on sorted order; without it, half-discard logic fails.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Bubble, selection and insertion sorts are all quadratic (O(n^2)) in the average case.
explanation: True: all three make O(n^2) comparisons in the average/worst case; they suit only modest n.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: The bisection method can proceed even when f(a) and f(b) have the same sign.
