explanation: False: same sign at both ends gives no guaranteed root in the interval — bisection cannot start.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: For large inputs, O(n log n) algorithms grow more slowly than O(n^2) algorithms.
explanation: True: n log n < n^2 for large n, so O(n log n) methods (e.g. advanced sorts) scale better.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem:
Assertion (A): On a large SORTED array, binary search is dramatically faster than linear search.
Reason (R): Binary search halves the search interval each step (O(log n)) compared with linear search's sequential O(n) scan.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Logarithmic halving versus linear scanning (R) is exactly the source of binary search's speed advantage (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem:
Assertion (A): Bubble sort owes its name to the way large elements move to the end of the array.
Reason (R): Successive adjacent compare-and-swap operations push the largest remaining element upward one cell per comparison, like a bubble rising.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The bubbling mechanism (R) directly motivates the name given in A.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem:
Assertion (A): Newton-Raphson may fail to converge while bisection (started with a valid bracket) cannot fail to converge.
Reason (R): Newton relies on the tangent slope, and a nearly zero derivative or poor initial guess can send the iterate astray; bisection only needs a sign change.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Dependence on derivative geometry (R) is precisely the fragility that bisection's bracketing avoids (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem:
Assertion (A): Insertion sort is often used for small or nearly-sorted inputs.
Reason (R): Its best case approaches O(n) because almost no shifting happens when the array is already near-sorted.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Near-linear best case (R) is the reason insertion sort is chosen for small/nearly-sorted data (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem:
Assertion (A): An O(n^2) sort on a few dozen elements can be perfectly acceptable in practice.
Reason (R): For small n, asymptotic growth barely matters and simple quadratic sorts are easy to program correctly.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Small inputs neutralize asymptotic disadvantages (R), justifying simple quadratic sorts in practice (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Which statements about binary search are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Has O(log n) comparisons worst case
Works by comparing with the middle element
Works correctly on any unsorted list
explanation: Binary search on unsorted data is meaningless; the other three are its defining facts.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Which are characteristic facts of the three basic sorts? (Select all that apply.)
options: Selection: find-min and one swap per pass
Insertion: insert each key into sorted prefix
All three work only on strings
explanation: The three sorts operate on any orderable data (numbers, strings); the mechanism descriptions are the matchups.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

stem: Which are needed to apply the BISECTION method? (Select all that apply.)
options: The function must be continuous on [a, b]
An initial bracket [a, b] straddling a root
explanation: Bisection needs no derivative — only continuity plus an opposite-sign bracket.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Notion of order of complexity through example programs (no formal definition required)
stem: Which problems/orders pairings are correct? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Direct-index array access is O(1); the other three pairings are standard.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Basic Sorting Algorithms (Bubble, Insertion and Selection)
stem: Which swaps/traces are correct for ONE pass of bubble sort ascending? (Select all that apply.)
options: Input [1,2,3,4] makes zero swaps in pass 1 (flag exits early)
Each pass bubbles the SMALLEST to the front
Pass counts shrink the inner loop range each time
explanation: Bubble pass 1 moves the LARGEST to the end (not smallest to front); the other statements are correct.
source: BEU syllabus — Programming for Problem Solving, Unit 6

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: GI sheet, commonly used for sheet-metal products, is:
options: galvanized iron — steel sheet coated with a layer of zinc for rust resistance
explanation: Galvanizing (zinc coating) protects the underlying steel from corrosion, ideal for buckets and ducting.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: Tin plate is:
options: steel sheet coated with a thin layer of tin
an alloy of tin and zinc
explanation: Tin-coated thin steel combines steel strength with tin's corrosion resistance — used for containers and cans.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: Sheet-metal thickness is expressed by a GAUGE number such that:
options: higher gauge number means THICKER sheet
gauge equals the width of the sheet
higher gauge number means THINNER sheet
explanation: Wire/sheet gauges run inversely: 16 gauge is thicker than 22 gauge; increasingly, mm thickness is quoted.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: A sheet metal gauge instrument measures:
options: thickness (gauge number) of a sheet or wire
explanation: The slotted sheet-metal gauge gives thickness/gauge by trial insertion of the sheet into its slots.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: Why are aluminium sheets widely used for light cooking ware and aircraft sheet parts?
options: they are light (low density), corrosion-resistant and formable
explanation: Aluminium couples low density with good formability and natural oxide corrosion protection.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: The steel rule used in the sheet-metal shop is a:
options: linear MEASURING tool graduated in mm/inches for laying out dimensions
explanation: Steel rule measures and guides straight scribed lines; common shop rules are 150/300/600 mm long.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: A vernier calliper can measure:
options: external, internal AND depth dimensions, with least count typically 0.02 mm
explanation: Outside jaws, inside jaws and the depth rod make the vernier calliper a three-in-one precision instrument.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: The least count of a standard metric vernier calliper is:
explanation: Typical LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = 0.1 mm; engineering verniers give 0.02 mm.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: The least count of an outside MICROMETER (50-division thimble, 0.5 mm pitch) is:
explanation: LC = pitch/no. of thimble divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: A SCRIBER is used for:
options: marking fine lines on the metal surface prior to cutting and bending
explanation: The hardened pointed scriber scratches layout lines on sheet metal — like a pencil on paper, but permanent.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: DIVIDERS in the sheet-metal shop are employed to:
options: scribe arcs/circles and transfer or divide distances
explanation: Like a compass, dividers step off distances and describe circular arcs on the sheet layout.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: Difference between PRICK punch and CENTRE punch:
options: centre punch is used on glass
prick punch makes a small light mark at intersections of scribed lines; centre punch makes a larger deep mark for drill starting
explanation: Prick punch (small angle ~30-60 degrees) locates layout points; centre punch (~90 degrees) gives drill bits a seat.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: SNIPS used in sheet metal work are:
options: hand shears for cutting sheet metal along straight or curved lines
explanation: Snips are scissor-like hand shears; straight snips for straight cuts and curved snips for curved outlines.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: For cutting CURVED profiles on sheet metal one should select:
explanation: Bent/curve snips follow curved outlines since their blades are profiled for turning during the cut.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: A MALLET rather than a steel hammer is used for bending sheet on a stake because it:
options: spreads the blow and does NOT damage/mark the soft sheet surface
explanation: Wood/rubber mallets deliver blows without denting or scratching the formed sheet; steel hammers bruise it.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: STAKES in a sheet-metal shop function as:
options: small anvils/form blocks of various shapes over which the sheet is bent, rolled or formed
explanation: Stakes (hatchet, blowhorn, funnel, round-head etc.) give shaped supports for forming operations.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: PLIERS are used in the sheet metal shop mainly to:
options: hold, grip and bend thin sheets and wires
explanation: Flat-nose/round-nose pliers grip, twist and form small bends on light sheet and wire.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: The flat cold chisel in sheet metal work serves to:
options: cut/shear sheet metal held in a vice and remove heavy waste
explanation: A chisel-struck sheet clamped closely along the line shears off cleanly for rough cutting.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: SCRIBING in sheet metal work means:
options: marking the full-size layout (development) of the product on the sheet with scriber and rule/divider
explanation: The developed outline of the job (funnel, box etc.) is first scribed full-size on the sheet before cutting.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: In sheet-metal terminology, the difference between PUNCHING and BLANKING is:
options: in blanking the punched-out piece IS the product; in punching the pierced hole is wanted and the punched slug is scrap
punching is done cold, blanking hot
explanation: Both push a punch through the sheet; they differ in which side of the cut is the useful part.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: BENDING in the sheet-metal shop is performed:
options: over a stake, vice edge or folding bar along the scribed bend line, using mallet blows
explanation: The sheet is progressively hammered (mallet) over an edge/form to the required angle along Scriber's bend lines.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: SHEARING of sheet metal refers to:
options: cutting the sheet along a line by a shearing action between two edges (snips, bench shear or guillotine)
explanation: Shearing severs the sheet where upper and lower cutting edges pass each other, as with snips or a bench shear.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: HEMMING (edge folding) of sheet-metal edges is done to:
options: stiffen and strengthen the raw edge, remove sharpness and improve appearance
explanation: A single or double folded hem makes the cut edge safe, rigid and neat — e.g. tray and box rims.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: In a LAP seam joint of two sheet-metal edges, the edges:
options: overlap and are folded/hammered flat (often soldered for leak-proofing)
explanation: Lapped folded seams (grooved seam) interlock sheets mechanically; solder makes them air/water tight.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: A WIRED edge on a sheet-metal rim involves:
options: rolling the sheet edge around a metal wire ring for extra stiffness and safety
explanation: The hem curls around an embedded wire, making a round, safe, rigid rim — used on buckets and funnels.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: Before making a sheet-metal funnel, the shape marked on the flat sheet is its:
options: DEVELOPMENT (flat pattern of the frustum surface unrolled, plus seam allowances)
explanation: Sheet products start from the surface development of the solid (here a conical frustum), laid out full-size.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: The cylindrical neck of a funnel, from sheet, is developed as:
options: a circle of diameter D only
a rectangle of width pi x D (circumference) and height equal to the neck length
explanation: A cylinder unrolls to a rectangle whose width is its circumference pi D and whose other side is its length.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: A funnel of bottom (neck) diameter 100 mm has a neck circumference in its development of approximately:
explanation: Circumference = pi x D = 3.14 x 100 = 314 mm (plus seam allowance).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: For making the hexagonal box with cap, the sides are developed as:
options: six rectangles joined in a strip, of width equal to the box side and height equal to the box depth
explanation: The lateral surface of a hexagonal prism develops into a strip of six equal rectangles (plus base and flaps).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: While developing a folded/seamed box, extra material called ALLOWANCE is left beyond the net dimensions for:
options: the overlaps of seams, hems and wired edges consumed during forming
explanation: Folded joints and hems consume extra sheet; layouts must add hem/seam allowances to the true size.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: Wire-edge allowance when curling a sheet edge around a wire of diameter d is about:
explanation: The wrap around a wire consumes about 2.5 times the wire diameter of extra sheet metal.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: After cutting with snips, the cut edge usually has a BURR, which is removed by:
options: filing (deburring) the edge with a smooth file
explanation: Filing smooths razor-sharp burred edges for safe handling and a quality finish.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: The general sequence of operations for making a sheet-metal job is:
options: marking/development -> cutting -> edge/surface finishing -> bending/forming -> seaming/joining -> final finishing
explanation: Layout comes first, then cut to shape, then form/roll and finally seam/join and finish — the logical build order.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: For holding sheet metal firmly during marking and sawing operations, use a:
options: bench vice (with wood/soft jaws so the sheet is not dented)
explanation: The bench vice grips work rigidly; soft jaw covers prevent bruising finished sheet surfaces.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: A ball-peen hammer's rounded face (peen) is used mainly for:
options: riveting and peening (spreading rivet ends) rather than flat striking
explanation: The flat face does general striking; the rounded peen shapes rivet heads and spreads metal locally.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: Copper sheets are chosen over steel sheets when the job demands:
options: high thermal/electrical conductivity and excellent formability (boilers, kettles, decorative ware)
explanation: Copper's conductivity and malleability suit heat exchangers, electrical and household ware.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: Brass is an alloy of:
explanation: Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze, in contrast, is copper + tin.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: NOTCHING in sheet-metal layout means:
options: cutting out small V/rectangular pieces from edges before bending, e.g. at box corners
explanation: Notches remove conflicting material at corners so flanges can fold up cleanly to form the box.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: A single-fold HEM allowance equals roughly the hem width, while a DOUBLE (locked) hem allowance equals about:
explanation: A double fold wraps twice the hem width of metal; a single fold needs just one width.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: The zinc coating on GI sheets protects the sheet by:
options: acting as a sacrificial (galvanic) barrier corrosion layer over the steel
explanation: Zinc corrodes preferentially (cathodic protection) and also forms a physical barrier against rust.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: Prick-punching scribed layout intersections before bending/cutting REPEATEDLY prevents:
options: loss/guess of the exact reference points when scribed lines get rubbed off during handling
explanation: Light punch dents preserve layout references on metal where pencil-like scribe marks can vanish.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: Gloves and careful handling are advised in sheet-metal work primarily because:
options: cut sheet edges have extremely sharp burrs that can cause deep cuts
explanation: Fresh sheared sheet edges are razor-sharp; gloves and prompt deburring prevent lacerations.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: Forming a CYLINDRICAL body from flat sheet uses which kind of stake/operation?
options: curving/rolling the sheet over a round blowhorn stake or mandrel
explanation: Sheet is progressively rolled over a round-form stake/mandrel to bring the edges together for seaming.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: Soldering of sheet-metal seams commonly follows the mechanical seam because it:
options: seals the joint leak-proof against air/water in addition to light holding
explanation: Grooved seams give mechanical strength; soft solder fills gaps to make containers leak-tight.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: The higher the sheet-metal gauge number, the thicker the sheet.
explanation: False: gauge numbers run inverse to thickness — higher gauge, thinner sheet.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: A mallet is preferred to a steel hammer while bending thin sheets to avoid surface damage.
explanation: True: the soft mallet face forms metal without bruising or cracking the sheet surface.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: In blanking operation, the hole left behind in the sheet is the useful product.
explanation: False: in blanking the punched-out piece is the product; the sheet-with-hole is the scrap.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: The full-size flat pattern of a sheet-metal component is called its development.
explanation: True: development means unrolling/unbending the 3-D surface into a flat 2-D layout.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem:
Assertion (A): GI sheets resist rusting far better than plain steel sheets.
Reason (R): The zinc coating on GI sheets acts as a barrier and corrodes sacrificially, protecting the underlying steel.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Barrier + sacrificial protection by zinc (R) explains the superior rust resistance of GI sheet (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem:
Assertion (A): Hemmed and wired edges are common on bucket and funnel rims.
Reason (R): Such edges stiffen the rim, improve safety by hiding sharp cut edges, and give a finished look.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Stiffness, safety and finish (R) are precisely the motivations for hemming/wiring exposed rims (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem:
Assertion (A): Simply cutting a rectangle of exactly 'finished-box' width would produce a SHORT sheet for a seamed cylinder.
Reason (R): Folded seams and hems consume extra metal, so the development must add allowances to the true sizes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The metal consumed in joints (R) explains why net dimensions alone are insufficient in the layout (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem:
Assertion (A): A centre punch mark is required before drilling a hole in sheet metal.
Reason (R): The dimple guides the drill point to the exact centre, preventing the bit from wandering at starting.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Preventing drill wander (R) is exactly why centre punching precedes drilling (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: Which tools belong to the MARKING category in sheet-metal work? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Rule, scriber and divider lay out dimensions/lines; the vice is a holding, not marking, tool.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: Which are standard sheet-metal shop OPERATIONS? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Marking, shearing, bending, seaming/hemming are core sheet operations; heat treatment in a furnace is not one.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Sheet material: GI sheets, aluminium, tin plate, copper, brass etc.
stem: Which materials are commonly used as SHEET METALS? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Cast iron is brittle and NOT rolled into workable shop sheets; GI, tin plate and brass/copper sheets are staples.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: Which statements about punches are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Prick punch: light mark for layout reference
Centre punch: deeper mark for drill starting
Both are struck with a mallet never with a hammer
Centre punch point angle is larger than that of prick punch
explanation: Punches are struck with a (small) steel HAMMER, not a mallet; the point-angle comparison and uses are right.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Tools: steel rule, vernier callipers, micrometer, sheet metal gauge, scriber, divider, punches, chisels, hammers, snips, pliers, stakes etc.
stem: Diversity of stakes: a FUNNEL stake is shaped suitably for forming the:
explanation: The funnel (tapered) stake provides the conical support for rolling and seaming funnel bodies.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: The CUTTING allowance (kerf) considered while laying out with snips is:
options: small extra (roughly the snip width), to be cut on the WASTE side of the scribed line
explanation: Always cut just outside the layout line and finish to the line by filing — preserves true dimensions.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Product development: hexagonal box with cap, funnel etc.
stem: The CAP (lid) of a hexagonal box is made as a slightly larger hexagonal tray so that it:
options: fits OVER the box mouth (sliding fit with folded edges for a snug close)
explanation: The cap's sides fold down around the box opening; its size must exceed the body by two sheet thicknesses.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

topic: Operations: scribing, bending, shearing, punching etc.
stem: Which of the following finish/stiffen sheet-metal EDGES? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Centre punching is a marking operation, not an edge treatment; hem, wired edge and seams all treat edges.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Sheet Metal Working

stem: Joining processes are broadly classified into:
options: permanent joints (welding, brazing, riveting) and temporary/semi-permanent joints (nuts-bolts, screws, cotter joints)
explanation: Permanent joints cannot be separated without damage; temporary (mechanical) joints can be dismantled and reassembled.

stem: Which of the following is a TEMPORARY (detachable) joint?
explanation: Nut and bolt assemblies can be unscrewed repeatedly; welded/riveted/soldered joints are destroyed on opening.

stem: SOLDERING joins metals using a filler (solder) that melts at a relatively:
options: temperature higher than the base metals
low temperature BELOW 450 degrees C (typical soft solder ~200-300 C), without melting the parent metals
explanation: Solder melts below 450 C and wets the un-melted parts; the joint is comparatively weak — good for sheet seams.

stem: The common solder alloy for sheet-metal (tin-smithy) work is:
explanation: Tin-lead soft solders melt low and wet sheet metals well; Cu-Zn alloy is the BRAZING filler (spelter).

stem: The flux used in soldering sheet metal (non-electronic) jobs, such as zinc chloride ('killed spirit'), serves to:
options: clean the joint surface of oxides and improve wetting/flow of solder
explanation: Flux chemically cleans the surfaces and stops re-oxidation so molten solder spreads and bonds.

stem: BRAZING differs from soldering mainly in that brazing:
options: uses filler that melts above 450 degrees C (but below the parent metal), giving a STRONGER joint than soldering
explanation: Brazing uses Cu-Zn (spelter) or silver fillers above 450 C; capillary action draws it into the close-fitting joint.

stem: The filler material ('spelter') for brazing brass/steel jobs is generally:
explanation: Brass spelter melts around 850-950 C and flows by capillarity into the joint; borax is the usual flux.

stem: The flux commonly used in brazing is:
explanation: Borax withstands brazing temperatures and chemically cleans the hot joint faces.

stem: In a brazed LAP joint, the alloy spreads between the closely fitting surfaces by:
options: capillary action (small even gap ~0.05-0.12 mm is ideal)
explanation: A small uniform clearance lets molten filler wick through the joint for maximum strength.

stem: Strength ordering of joints from weakest to strongest is typically:
explanation: Fusion-welded (parent metal melted) strongest; then brazed (high temp filler); soft-soldered weakest.

stem: RIVETED joints (e.g. boilers, structural steel, older bridges) are:
options: permanent mechanical joints formed by upsetting the tail of a hot rivet into a head
explanation: A red-hot rivet inserted through aligned holes is hammered over; on cooling it clamps plates tightly.

stem: A LAP riveted joint and a BUTT riveted joint differ in that:
options: butt joint uses strap(s) cover plate(s) over abutting plate edges; lap joint overlaps the plates directly
explanation: In lap joints plates overlap; in butt joints, plate edges butt together with cover strap(s) riveted to both.

stem: A cotter joint is used to connect two rods in ALIGNMENT transmitting:
options: axial tensile or compressive loads (e.g. piston rod to crosshead)
explanation: The tapered cotter wedges through aligned slots of spigot and socket to lock rods against axial pull/push.

stem: In arc welding, the heat necessary to melt the joint is produced by:
options: an electric arc between the electrode and the workpiece
explanation: An arc struck between electrode and work develops intense heat (~3500-6000 C) that fuses the joint members.

stem: The FLUX COATING on a covered arc-welding electrode serves to:
options: form a protective gas shield and slag over the molten pool, stabilize the arc and stop oxidation/contamination
explanation: Flux decomposes to shield the molten metal from air; the slag covers and protects the solidifying bead.

stem: During arc welding the work is connected to the machine through the ______ and the electrode is held in the ______:
explanation: The work cable with earth clamp completes the circuit; the electrode holder grips the electrode in the welder's hand.

stem: The welding shield/helmet and dark filter glass are essential for the welder because the arc:
options: emits intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that can cause 'arc eye' and skin burns
explanation: Arc flash without filter glass leads to painful eye inflammation; shield, gloves and apron are mandatory PPE.

stem: Arc welding machines may supply:
options: AC or DC (rectified) current at low voltage and high current
explanation: Welding transformers (AC) or rectifier/dynamo sets (DC) deliver low open-circuit voltage (about 50-90 V) with high current.

stem: The visible bead deposited by an arc-welding electrode must have its SLAG chipped off afterwards because slag:
options: is the broken flux crust covering the metallic bead and must be removed before the next run or inspection
explanation: Slag floats on the molten pool and solidifies over the bead; chipping hammer and brush clean it off.

stem: Oxy-acetylene gas welding uses a flame formed by burning:
options: acetylene with oxygen, producing a very high temperature (~3200 degrees C) flame
explanation: The oxygen-acetylene flame reaches roughly 3200 C — enough to melt and fuse steel edges for welding.

stem: The NEUTRAL (balanced) oxy-acetylene flame is obtained when:
options: oxygen and acetylene flows are nearly EQUAL, and it is used for most steel welding
explanation: Neutral flame has a clean well-defined cone, no excess O2 or C2H2 — the standard welding flame; carburizing suits repair, oxidizing suits brass/cutting.

stem: A CARBURIZING flame (excess acetylene) is characterized by:
options: a long luminous inner cone with two/three zones, adding carbon to the weld — used for high-carbon steel, cast iron and hard-facing
explanation: Excess fuel gas enriches the flame with carbon — compensates carbon loss in certain steels and metals.

stem: In oxy-acetylene cylinder identification, the OXYGEN cylinder (Indian convention) is painted:
explanation: Oxygen is stored in a BLACK cylinder and acetylene in a MAROON cylinder under Indian colour practice.

stem: Gas welding adds filler metal as a separate rod, while arc welding (consumable electrode) supplies it:
explanation: In gas welding the welder feeds filler rod by hand; in shielded metal arc welding the electrode melts as filler AND electrode.

stem: LEFTWARD (forehand) gas welding technique angles the torch direction:
options: towards the completed weld (torch moves left, works best for thin sheets)
explanation: Forehand points the flame ahead onto un-welded metal — preheats the joint for thin material; rightward for heavy.

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: A PATTERN in foundry practice is:
options: a replica (model) of the object to be cast, from which the impression (mould cavity) is formed in sand
explanation: The pattern is withdrawn from rammed sand leaving a cavity into which molten metal is poured.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: Wood (e.g. white pine, teak) is the commonest pattern material because it is:
options: cheapest, light and easily worked, though it absorbs moisture and wears with reuse
explanation: Wood patterns are cheap/easy but dry/warp and suit small-batch castings; metals suit large production runs.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: For large-scale production with repeated mould reuse, the BEST pattern material is:
options: metal (cast iron, brass or aluminium) which resists wear and warping at high re-use
explanation: Metal patterns survive thousands of reuses with accurate dimensions — economical at volume despite cost.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Types of patterns: split, single piece, match plate etc.
stem: A SPLIT pattern is made in two halves along the parting line mainly to:
options: permit easy withdrawal of the pattern from the mould without damaging the cavity
explanation: The two halves meet with dowel pins; each half lifts vertically out of drag/cope without scraping the sand.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Types of patterns: split, single piece, match plate etc.
stem: In a MATCH PLATE pattern, the two halves of a split pattern and the gating system are:
options: mounted on opposite faces of the same plate, so cope and drag halves are moulded aligning through the plate
explanation: Match plates register both halves automatically and boost production speed/accuracy in repetitive jobs.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Types of patterns: split, single piece, match plate etc.
stem: A SINGLE PIECE (solid) pattern is typically the:
options: simplest pattern, made of one piece, with one flat face lying on the parting surface of the drag
explanation: Solid patterns suit simple shapes; they are moulded in the drag and rammed over from the cope side.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: Patterns are made SLIGHTLY LARGER than the required casting to provide the SHRINKAGE allowance because:
options: molten metal contracts on solidification and cooling, so the cavity must oversize the finished size
explanation: All cast metals shrink on cooling; the pattern dimensions add the metal's shrinkage percentage.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: Typical shrinkage allowances (rule-of-thumb) for cast iron and aluminium are respectively about:
explanation: Cast iron shrinks ~10 mm/m (1%); aluminium ~13 mm/m (steel highest ~20 mm/m) — served by different 'shrink rules'.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: DRAFT (taper) allowance on vertical faces of a pattern is provided to:
options: allow withdrawal of the pattern from the sand mould without tearing the cavity walls
explanation: A slight 1-3 degree taper lets the pattern pull straight up cleanly out of compacted sand.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: MACHINING (finish) allowance on a pattern means:
options: extra metal left on surfaces that must later be machined/ground to accurate dimensions
explanation: Castings are rough; faces needing machined finish get a few mm extra on the pattern.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: In a two-box moulding flask, the COPE and the DRAG are respectively the:
options: top and bottom boxes (halves) of the flask
explanation: The drag is the lower flask box; the cope is the upper flask box; they close at the parting line.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: A CORE in sand casting is used to:
options: form internal cavities/holes in the casting (it is a body of baked sand placed inside the mould cavity)
explanation: Cores are baked-sand inserts occupying where metal should NOT solidify — producing hollow parts.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: CORE PRINTS on a pattern are extra projections which:
options: create recesses (seats) in the mould where cores are placed and supported
explanation: Core prints leave seat impressions so the core aligns and doesn't float or shift during pouring.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: A RIDDLE in foundry work is a:
options: sieve used to sift fresh facing sand over the pattern for a fine, lump-free mould face
explanation: Riddling throws fine sand over the pattern, giving a smooth surface to the casting.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: The RAMMER is used in mould making for:
options: packing/compacting the moulding sand firmly around the pattern in the flask
explanation: Sand is rammed (peen then butt end) so the cavity holds its shape under molten metal pressure.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: The SPRUE PIN is used while moulding to:
options: form the VERTICAL passage (sprue) through which molten metal flows into the mould
explanation: Withdrawn after ramming, the sprue pin leaves the tapered down-gate channel for the metal stream.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: A VENT ROD is worked through the rammed cope sand to produce:
options: small VENT HOLES that let hot air and gases escape from the mould during pouring
explanation: Gas vents prevent blowholes and misrun by relieving air/gas pressure as metal fills the cavity.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: TROWEL and SLICK (finishing tools) in moulding are used respectively for:
options: smoothening mould surfaces and repairing/finishing corners and loose edges of the cavity
explanation: Trowels smooth flat mould surfaces; slicks/lifters touch up edges and clean up the cavity after pattern draw.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Moulding sands: green sand, dry sand, loam sand, facing sand etc.
stem: GREEN SAND moulding means using sand:
options: in the moist (tempered) state with ~5-8% moisture and clay binder, moulded at once without baking
explanation: Moist clay-sand mixture is used as-rammed ('green') for most iron castings; dry-sand moulds are baked first.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Moulding sands: green sand, dry sand, loam sand, facing sand etc.
stem: FACING SAND is that special fine sand:
options: placed at the bottom of the pit
sprinkled (riddled) directly against the pattern surface to give a smooth casting finish
explanation: Only the first fine layer (backing sand fills behind) needs quality — economizing on good sand.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Moulding sands: green sand, dry sand, loam sand, facing sand etc.
stem: The desirable properties of moulding sand include permeability, refractoriness and:
options: cohesiveness (strength to hold shape) together with collapsibility after pouring
explanation: Sand must allow gases through (permeability), survive high temperature (refractoriness), hold shape (strength) and break away after (collapsibility).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Moulding sands: green sand, dry sand, loam sand, facing sand etc.
stem: LOAM sand moulding (high clay content, used in large moulds on sweeps) is characterized by:
options: sand mixed with a large clay proportion, used for large castings shaped with sweep boards
explanation: Loam moulds are built up in courses and dried; sweep templates shape big symmetrical castings without full patterns.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: The correct ORDER of the main steps in sand casting is:
options: pattern making -> moulding -> melting -> pouring -> shakeout/cleaning
explanation: The pattern is made first, mould rammed around it, metal melted and poured, then the flask broken (shakeout) and casting cleaned (fettling).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: The CUPOLA furnace in a foundry is used for melting:
options: cast iron (with coke, flux and metal charge in a shaft furnace)
explanation: The shaft-type cupola melts cast iron continuously on a coke bed with limestone flux and air blast.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: The SPRUE, RUNNER and GATE in a mould's gating system are respectively:
options: vertical channel into which metal is poured, horizontal channel, and the actual entrance into the cavity
explanation: Gating path: pouring basin -> sprue (down) -> sprue well -> runner (horizontal) -> gate -> mould cavity; riser feeds shrinkage.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: A RISER mounted on a mould acts mainly to:
options: feed molten metal to the cavity to compensate for shrinkage as the casting solidifies
explanation: The riser stays molten longest and supplies liquid metal into the shrinking cavity, preventing shrinkage cavities.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: Blowholes/pinholes in a casting are defects chiefly caused by:
options: entrapped gases/steam because of poor venting or too-wet green sand
explanation: Gas bubbles formed as metal poured onto damp/poorly vented sand get trapped in the solidifying casting.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: MISRUN and COLD SHUT casting defects occur when:
options: the pouring temperature is too LOW or the section too thin for the metal's fluidity
explanation: Metal that loses fluidity partially fills (misrun) or two cold streams fail to fuse (cold shut).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: FETTLING of a casting refers to:
options: the cleaning stage: removing gates/risers, sand, fins and surface dressing of the solidified casting
explanation: After shakeout, gates/risers are cut off and the casting chipped/ground/wire-brushed clean for use.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem: The flux coating of a welding electrode protects the molten weld pool from atmospheric contamination.
explanation: True: flux gases shield and the slag covers the bead, blocking oxygen and nitrogen attack.

stem: Brazing melts the base (parent) metals to form the joint.
explanation: False: as with soldering, only the filler melts in brazing; fusion (melting parents) defines WELDING.

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: A pattern is always made exactly to the size of the finished casting.
explanation: False: patterns are oversized by shrinkage and machining allowances and carry draft tappers.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Moulding sands: green sand, dry sand, loam sand, facing sand etc.
stem: Green sand gets its name from its green colour.
explanation: False: 'green' means moisture-tempered sand used undried, not the colour.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: The core forms the EXTERNAL shape of the casting.
explanation: False: cores create INTERNAL cavities; the mould cavity itself forms the external shape.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem:
Assertion (A): Soldered joints are NOT suitable for load-bearing structural applications.
Reason (R): The soft solder filler melts below 450 degrees C and has low strength compared to a fused weld.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Low-strength, low-melting filler (R) explains the structural unsuitability of soldered joints (A).

stem:
Assertion (A): A welder must use a face shield or helmet even for very short arc-welding runs.
Reason (R): The welding arc radiates injurious ultraviolet and infrared rays which can damage eyes and skin in seconds.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Radiation from the arc (R) is precisely the hazard that the helmet and filter glass (A) guard against.

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem:
Assertion (A): A split pattern with dowel pins is favoured for casting shapes that cannot be withdrawn vertically in one piece.
Reason (R): Its two halves form the impression in drag and cope boxes separately and are removed without distorting the sand cavity.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Two-part withdrawal along the parting line (R) is the enabling logic of the split pattern (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem:
Assertion (A): Vent holes are pierced through the rammed cope before pouring.
Reason (R): Escaping air and steam from the hot mould would otherwise form blowholes or block metal filling.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Gas relief during pouring (R) is exactly what vent rodding accomplishes (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem:
Assertion (A): The neutral flame is the standard flame for welding mild steel.
Reason (R): With neither oxygen nor acetylene in excess, it neither oxidizes nor carburizes the molten metal, giving an uncontaminated weld.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Chemical neutrality of the flame (R) protects the weld pool, hence its standard use on steel (A).

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem:
Assertion (A): A riser (feeder head) on a mould keeps the casting free of shrinkage cavities.
Reason (R): Being large and staying molten longer, the riser feeds liquid metal into the cavity as the casting contracts during solidification.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Late-solidifying feed metal (R) is the working principle of risers for solidification-shrinkage control (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem: Which of the following produce PERMANENT joints? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Welding, riveting and soldering/brazing cannot be undone without damage; nut-bolt fasteners are detachable.

stem: Which are the functions of electrode flux coating in shielded metal-arc welding? (Select all that apply.)
options: Produce shielding gas around the arc
Increase the size of the electrode for grip
explanation: Grip/holding is mechanical, not flux's job; gas shielding, slag and arc stability are the flux functions.

stem: Which are typical oxy-acetylene flame types? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Neutral, carburizing and oxidizing are the three named oxygen/acetylene ratios; 'infrared' is not one.

topic: Tools: cope, drag, core, core prints, shovel, riddle, rammer, trowel, slick, lifter, sprue pin, bellow, mallet, vent rod, furnace etc.
stem: Which are FOUNDRY hand tools? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Electrode holder belongs to arc welding; rammer, riddle and moulder's trowels/slicks are foundry bench tools.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Pattern material: wood, cast iron, brass, aluminium, waxes etc.
stem: Which allowances are given on a PATTERN? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Patterns get shrinkage, machining and draft (taper) allowances; paint is only a surface coat, not an allowance.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: Which elements belong to the GATING system of a sand mould? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Sprue-runner-gate guide molten metal in; core prints are pattern projections to seat cores, not metal channels.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

topic: Moulding sands: green sand, dry sand, loam sand, facing sand etc.
stem: Which are desirable PROPERTIES of moulding sand? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Sand conductivity is irrelevant; permeability, refractoriness, strength and collapsibility matter.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem: Which are mechanical (detachable) fastening elements? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Bolts, screws, keys and cotters can be removed non-destructively; a weld bead is permanent.

topic: Types of patterns: split, single piece, match plate etc.
stem: Which are recognized PATTERN types? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Solid, split and match-plate are standard; 'hazard pattern' is not a foundry term.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem: The correct current setting for arc welding a particular electrode diameter depends chiefly on:
options: the electrode diameter (current rises with electrode size) and thickness of the job
explanation: Thicker electrodes/jobs need more current for adequate penetration; makers specify current ranges.

stem: Before opening an acetylene cylinder valve, standard safety practice includes:
options: cracking (briefly opening/closing) valves to clean the socket and standing to one side, keeping oil/grease off fittings
explanation: Valve cracking expels dust; oil on oxygen fittings can ignite explosively — both are classic safety rules.

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: The pouring basin's purpose above the sprue is to:
options: hold a smooth pool of metal that feeds the sprue steadily and reduces turbulence and slag entry
explanation: A basin lets metal enter the sprue quietly, reducing air entrainment and dross carry-over.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem: Compared to SOLDERED joints, BRAZED joints withstand HIGHER service temperatures because:
options: brazing fillers (brass/silver alloys) remain strong at temperatures that would melt soft solder
explanation: Brazing alloys melt far higher than soft solder, so the joint margin of hot service temperature is greater.

topic: Sand casting: Sand preparation, mould making, melting, pouring, and cleaning
stem: The process of removing the pattern from the mould is termed:
options: pattern withdrawal or drawing, often assisted by rapping the pattern
explanation: Gentle rapping (vibrating) loosens the pattern before vertical draw — the rap allowance covers the slight cavity growth.
source: BEU syllabus — Workshop, Pattern Making and Foundry

stem: Before welding two plates became cheap and common, boilers and steel bridges were overwhelmingly joined by:
explanation: Thickness and working pressures of boilers and the scale of bridge trusses made hot-riveting the classic permanent joint.

stem: FITTING shop work essentially involves:
options: shaping and finishing metal parts at the bench by hand operations (marking, sawing, chipping, filing) so they FIT together accurately
explanation: Fitting is precision bench work: parts are worked to size by hand to mate/assemble correctly, e.g. male-female joints.

stem: The usual sequence of operations in making a fitting job is:
options: marking -> clamping -> cutting (sawing/chipping) -> rough filing -> finishing/scraping -> checking
explanation: Define by marking, remove bulk by saw/chisel, refine by files, and verify against gauges/drawing at the end.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A FILE is classified by its GRADE (cut) into which of the following sequences from coarsest to smoothest?
options: ROUGH/BASTARD -> SECOND CUT -> SMOOTH -> DEAD SMOOTH
explanation: Bastard/rough removes stock fastest; dead smooth leaves the finest finish — the standard grade progression.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: Files are made of:
options: high carbon steel, HARDENED, so their teeth stay sharp while rubbing workpieces
explanation: High-carbon hardened steel (often with serrated teeth formed by chisel) gives files their cutting hardness.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A file with SINGLE-CUT teeth has:
options: one set of parallel grooves/serrations cut at an angle, suited to smooth finishing and soft metals
explanation: Single-cut (mill-type) files leave a fine finish, while double-cut files with crossed rows remove stock faster.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: Which file profile/shape should be picked to file the inside of a small round hole?
explanation: Round or half-round sections fit curved internal surfaces that flat squares cannot reach properly.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A TRIANGULAR (three-square) file is best suited for filing:
options: outside flat edges of a round bar
internal corners, square holes and sharpening saw teeth (acute V profiles)
explanation: The acute edges of the triangular section reach into V-shapes and corners flat files cannot touch.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: The TANG of a file is the:
options: pointed shank end that fits into the handle
explanation: The unhardened tang seats inside the wooden file handle; fitting the handle prevents hand injury.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: The SAFE EDGE of a file is:
options: an edge WITH NO TEETH so it can rest against a shoulder without cutting it
explanation: One edge is left uncut/untouched so filing flat surfaces next to a shoulder doesn't score the shoulder.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: The bench vice in a fitting shop is used to:
options: hold the workpiece firmly between hardened steel jaws during sawing/filing/chipping
explanation: Rigid clamping at correct height allows accurate bench operations; jaws are screwed/vice-clamped on the work.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: For gripping finished/precision surfaces WITHOUT damaging them in a vice, one should use:
options: soft jaw covers (copper/lead/wood fibre) over the vice jaws
explanation: Soft liners prevent jaw serrations from biting into the finished faces of the workpiece.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A V-block with clamp is used to hold:
options: any diameter of circular/rods work accurately horizontal for marking and drilling
explanation: Cylindrical jobs register truly in the V-groove for layout and drilling operations.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: The correct way to hold a hacksaw and apply pressure while cutting is:
options: forward stroke with pressure (teeth cut on the forward stroke), relaxed return stroke
explanation: Hacksaw teeth point forward, so the power is applied pushing forward; the return stroke only resets.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: While choosing a hacksaw blade, for THIN sections/tubes select a blade with MORE teeth per inch (e.g. 24-32 TPI) because:
options: at least 2-3 teeth must remain in contact to avoid teeth straddling and breaking on the thin wall
explanation: Too-coarse teeth on a thin wall span the section and snap; fine teeth keep multiple teeth engaged.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A FLAT (cold) chisel in a fitting shop is employed for:
options: chipping/removing excess metal, cutting sheet held in a vice and scrap removal
explanation: Struck with a hammer, the flat cold chisel shears surplus metal — roughing before the filing steps.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A TRY SQUARE is used at the bench to check/mark:
options: angles of 90 degrees (squareness of adjacent faces)
explanation: Blade and stock of the try square reference a true 90-degree check on edges and shoulders.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: SCRIBING BLOCK (scribing gauge/marking block) on a surface plate is for:
options: marking lines parallel to the datum edge at a set height on vertical faces
explanation: The adjustable scriber slides on a flat datum plate to scribe parallel layout lines.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: SURFACE PLATE provides a:
options: truly FLAT reference datum surface for marking out and checking flatness
explanation: Cast-iron/granite surface plates are precision-flattened bases for all accurate bench layout.

topic: Methods Of Filing: Cross Filling and Draw Filing
stem: CROSS filing refers to:
options: filing with the file held at an angle (across) the work for deliberate heavy material removal with long strokes
explanation: Angled long strokes remove stock quickly; final passes go straight and lighter.

topic: Methods Of Filing: Cross Filling and Draw Filing
stem: DRAW filing, used as the finishing method, means:
options: push-pull the file sideways along its LENGTH over the surface, producing a very fine flat finish
explanation: The file is grasped at both ends and drawn along its axis — a smoothing burnishing stroke.

topic: Other associated operations Marking, Sawing and Chipping
stem: CHIPPING is the operation of:
options: cutting away metal with cold chisel and hammer, roughly shaping before filing
explanation: Chipping strips excess metal (e.g. casting fins, weld crowns) in preparation for file finishing.

topic: Other associated operations Marking, Sawing and Chipping
stem: MARKING-out fluid often brushed on rough stock before scribing helps by:
options: coating it blue/white so scribed lines show up sharply
explanation: Layout blue/whiting gives contrast under the fine scriber lines for accurate reading.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: INTERNAL threads (nuts, holes) are cut with a:
explanation: Taps cut internal threads (taper, second/intermediate, plug in sequence); dies cut external threads.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: The usual ORDER of tap use for cutting an internal thread by hand is:
explanation: The tapered entry starts the thread easily; intermediate develops it; the plug/bottoming finishes full depth.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: EXTERNAL threads on a rod/bolt are produced by a:
options: split DIE rotated by a die-stock (die holder)
explanation: The round/split die mounted in a die-stock screws onto the rod end to cut its thread.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: Before hand-tapping an M6 x 1 hole, the TAPPING drill size should be approximately:
explanation: Tapping drill = D - P = 6 - 1 = 5 mm, so teeth of the tap cut only the thread depth.

topic: Safety and Precautions in Fitting Shop
stem: Using a file WITHOUT a fitted wooden handle is unsafe because the tang may:
options: pierce the palm if the file slips or digs in
explanation: The sharp exposed tang causes hand injuries — files must always have sound handles.

topic: Safety and Precautions in Fitting Shop
stem: While chipping metal with a cold chisel, the operator and bystanders should use:
options: goggles/safety glasses and a protective screen against flying chips
explanation: Flying chisel chips are a classic eye hazard; goggles plus a chip screen are standard shop safety.

topic: Safety and Precautions in Fitting Shop
stem: A mushroomed (spread) head of a cold chisel must be:
options: ground back to shape, since chips flying off the spread head during hammer blows are dangerous
explanation: Mushroom heads flake metal splinters on striking; grind them smooth at maintenance.

topic: Safety and Precautions in Fitting Shop
stem: Files should be cleaned of embedded chips (pinning) with a:
options: file card (short wire brush) used lengthwise along the teeth
explanation: A file card clears pinning; a clogged file loses cut and scratches the work.

stem: Carpentry in the workshop deals chiefly with:
options: cutting, shaping and joining WOOD into components (patterns, furniture, formwork)
explanation: The carpentry shop covers wood selection, seasoning, marking, sawing, planing, chiselling and jointing.

stem: SOFTWOOD (coniferous) trees primarily include:
options: pine, deodar (cedar) and spruce — needle-leaf, fast-growing, easier to work
explanation: Conifers produce softwoods used widely in carpentry; teak/sal/oak are hardwoods.

stem: HARDWOOD for durable furniture and structural work is exemplified by:
options: teak, sal (Shorea), oak and sheesham (Indian rosewood)
explanation: Broad-leaf deciduous timbers are dense, strong and long-wearing hardwoods.

topic: Seasoning of Wood: Types of Seasoning Methods
stem: SEASONING of timber means:
options: removing/reducing the moisture content of freshly cut wood to a safe level (~10-15%) for use
explanation: Controlled drying prevents warping, shrinkage and fungal attack, and raises strength/workability.

topic: Seasoning of Wood: Types of Seasoning Methods
stem: The two main seasoning methods are:
explanation: Air seasoning stacks planks outdoors for months; kiln seasoning dries quickly and uniformly in heated chambers.

stem: A KNOT in timber is a defect formed by:
options: the embedded bases of former branches left inside the trunk wood
explanation: Knots interrupt grain continuity, weakening the timber and hindering planing — large knots are serious defects.

stem: SHAKES in timber describe:
options: splits/cracks running along or across the grain due to unequal shrinkage or stress
explanation: Radial/ring/cup shakes are cracks that open grain along planes and seriously weaken the wood.

stem: WARPING of seasoned timber is:
options: the distortion (bow, cup, twist) of planks caused by uneven drying/shrinkage
explanation: Differential shrinkage among grain directions bows, cups or twists the board if seasoning is careless.

stem: The HEARTWOOD of a tree trunk is:
options: the central, darker, durable non-living core wood preferred for strong carpentry use
explanation: Heartwood is dense mature wood, usually darker and more rot-resistant than the outer living sapwood.

stem: ANNUAL RINGS seen on a cross-section of a trunk represent:
options: yearly growth: light spring (early) wood plus dense summer (late) wood of each year
explanation: Each ring pair (earlywood + latewood) corresponds to one year's growth and shows age.

stem: The GROWING layer of a tree trunk, where new wood cells form each season, is the:
explanation: The thin cambium between bark and wood generates the new annual layers of wood each season.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A MARKING GAUGE is used in carpentry to:
options: scribe lines parallel to an edge at a set distance for sawing/chiselling layout
explanation: The stock slides along the timber edge while the pin/roller marks a parallel line at the set offset.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A MORTISE gauge differs from a marking gauge in having:
options: TWO marking pins — one adjustable — to scribe BOTH sides of a mortise/tenon simultaneously
explanation: The twin pins mark both cheeks of mortise/tenon joints in one pass.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A RIP saw is designed for cutting:
options: along (with) the wood GRAIN, with big chisel-like teeth and few TPI
explanation: Rip teeth act like tiny chisels along grain; cross-cut saw teeth are knife-pointed to sever fibres across grain.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A TENON (back) saw has a stiffened back so it can:
options: cut accurately guided, straight, fine joints such as tenons and dovetails (non-wobbling thin blade)
explanation: The brass/steel back rigidifies the thin blade for controlled joinery cuts.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: For cutting CURVES and internal shapes (with blade passed through a starter hole), choose a:
options: coping/compass (keyhole) saw with thin narrow blade
explanation: The fine, narrow, replaceable blade of a coping/keyhole saw negotiates curves ordinary saws cannot.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: The BENCH PLANE that FLATTENS/SMOOTHS wood surfaces is the:
options: jack plane (all-purpose) followed by the smoother/finishing plane
explanation: The jack plane does general stock removal; smoothing planes finish; long trying planes true edges.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A FIRMER chisel is:
options: a general-purpose bench chisel for paring and light chopping of wood
explanation: Firmer chisels (square-section blades) are the everyday wood chisels; mortise chisels are thicker for heavy levering.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: The joinery removed when cutting a MORTISE (rectangular hole) is preferably chopped with a:
options: heavy mortise chisel of matching width
explanation: Thick rigid mortise chisels withstand levering waste out of deep rectangular sockets.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A BRACE with an AUGER bit is the carpentry equivalent of a:
options: hand-operated BORING tool that drills larger holes in wood
explanation: The ratchet brace turns auger bits for deep/large holes, while small holes use gimlet/hand drill.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A carpenter's MALLET is used in place of a hammer when:
options: striking CHISELS/gouges so their wooden handles are not split
explanation: The broad wooden mallet face drives chisels without damaging handles unlike a steel hammer head.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: A CLAW hammer doubles as a nail PULLER because of its:
options: the curved FORKED claw opposite the striking face, which levers out nails
explanation: The bent split claw slips under nail heads and levers them out of the timber.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: The strongest and most classic FRAME joint in carpentry is the:
options: mortise-and-tenon joint (a projecting tenon fitting into a rectangular mortise)
explanation: Interlocked tenon-in-mortise gives large glued bearing area and resists racking — used in doors and frames.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: DOVETAIL joints are preferred for DRAWER sides because their interlocking fan-shaped tails resist:
options: being pulled apart (tensile withdrawal along the drawer)
explanation: The wedge-shaped pins and tails lock mechanically along the pull direction even without glue.

topic: Carpentry Tools: Measuring Tools, Marking Tools, Cutting Tools, Planning Tools, Drilling and Boring Tools, Holding Tools, Striking Tools, Auxiliary tools
stem: Plane blades and chisels are sharpened/ground to correct angle and finished on a:
options: oilstone (sharpening stone) finished with honing on a leather strop
explanation: Water/oil stones and fine strops restore razor plane/chisel edges that sawing blunts.

topic: Safety and Precautions in Fitting Shop
stem: A chisel's mushroomed head should be ground off as soon as noticed.
explanation: True: mushroom heads throw dangerous metal splinters and must be ground square again.

topic: Fitting Tools: Files and their classification, Holding Tools, Cutting Tools, Measuring and Marking Tools, Thread Making Tools, Various Fitting Power Tools
stem: A double-cut file gives a SMOOTHER finish than a single-cut file of the same grade.
explanation: False: crossed double-cut teeth remove stock faster but leave a coarser surface; single-cut files finish smoother.

topic: Seasoning of Wood: Types of Seasoning Methods
stem: Kiln seasoning is faster than natural (air) seasoning of timber.
explanation: True: temperature/humidity-controlled kilns dry wood in weeks instead of months/years of air drying.

topic: Other associated operations Marking, Sawing and Chipping
stem: A hacksaw cuts during its return (backward pull) stroke.
