topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Load calculation: a residence has ten 100 W lamps, five 60 W fans and one 2000 W heater. Total connected load is:
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: For the above 3300 W load on 230 V single-phase, the supply current is about 14.3 A. The suitable main switch/MCB rating is:
explanation: I = 3300/230 = 14.3 A; choose the next standard rating above full-load current, i.e. a 16 A double-pole main switch/MCB.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: An MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker) is preferred over a rewirable fuse because it:
options: trips quickly and precisely on overload/short-circuit and is restored by a switch, needing no wire replacement
explanation: The MCB senses overload (thermal) and short circuits (magnetic), trips fast, and is reusable — unlike a fuse that must be re-wired.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The protective device that guards against EARTH-LEAKAGE (current leaking to ground, e.g. through a person) is:
options: the RCCB / ELCB (residual-current circuit breaker), typically 30 mA for homes
explanation: An RCCB compares line and neutral currents and trips within milliseconds on imbalance as small as 30 mA, saving lives from shock.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The MAIN purpose of earthing the metal body of an appliance is:
options: providing a low-resistance path for fault current, keeping the body near earth potential and blowing the protective device to safeguard users
explanation: If a live conductor touches the body, earthing conducts the fault current safely away, trips the protection and prevents shock.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: LIVE (phase) wires at every switch and every fuse must be used in the ______ conductor:
explanation: Switches and fuses are always placed in the live wire so the disconnected equipment becomes dead; a fused neutral leaves the device live.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The function of the DISTRIBUTION BOARD in a house installation is to:
options: split the incoming supply into several sub-circuits, each with its own protection (fuse/MCB)
explanation: After the main switch, the DB divides supply among lighting/power sub-circuits with individual protective devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Comparison: the ENERGY METER of a house is wired between:
options: the distribution board and the lamp
the service line and the main switch (first item in the installation)
explanation: The supply authority's meter is the first device on the consumer side to record ALL energy drawn, before the main switch.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The correct sequence of service-line equipment for a domestic connection is:
options: service line -> energy meter -> main switch (ICDP) -> distribution board
explanation: Incoming supply passes the meter first, then the iron-clad double-pole main switch, then the distribution board.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: A stair-case lamp that must be controlled from two different floors requires:
options: two two-way switches in a staircase wiring arrangement
explanation: Two-way switches at both locations allow the same lamp to be switched ON/OFF from either floor — standard staircase wiring.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: GODOWN wiring is an economy scheme for long corridors/godowns in which:
options: lamps are wired so that successive lamps are switched ON in series/parallel combination sequentially while passing through
explanation: In godown wiring one person walking through switches lamps on ahead and dims those behind, saving wiring switches at each lamp.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Copper is preferred to aluminium for house wiring conductors because copper:
options: conducts better (lower resistivity), is mechanically stronger and easier to joint reliably
explanation: Copper's lower resistivity gives smaller conductors for the same rating and its joints stay reliable; aluminium is used mainly for economy.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: PVC insulation is generally used on wiring cables rather than rubber because PVC is:
options: cheaper, tougher and resistant to moisture, chemicals and fire when suitably compounded
explanation: PVC-insulated (VIR-type replaced) cables dominate indoor wiring: durable, moisture-proof and flame-retardant grades are available.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem: Lead-free (RoHS-compliant) solders such as the tin-silver-copper (SAC) alloy were introduced mainly to:
options: exclude toxic lead from electronic products for health/environmental safety
lower the solder melting point drastically
explanation: Lead is toxic; RoHS restricts it, prompting SAC alloys which melt somewhat higher (~217 C) than 63/37 eutectic.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem: The recommended step order for making a good soldered PCB joint is:
options: melt solder first on the iron, then touch the joint
heat pad and lead together a second or two, feed solder to the heated joint (not the iron tip), let it flow, remove solder then iron
cool the joint with water immediately
explanation: The joint members must be hot enough to melt solder by themselves; proper order gives wetting, a shiny fillet and no dry joint.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: To limit voltage drop in a domestic installation the total drop from supply intake to farthest point is generally restricted to about:
options: 5 percent (about 2.5 percent up to the DB and 2.5 percent beyond, as a common rule)
explanation: Keeping the total drop near 5 percent of declared voltage ensures appliances get adequate voltage and stay efficient.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The rating of a fuse/MCB element is chosen as:
options: slightly above the full-load current of the circuit but below the cable's safe current-carrying capacity
explanation: Protection must carry normal load indefinitely yet blow/trip before the cable overheats on overcurrent — between load and cable limits.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The MAIN SWITCH (ICDP — iron-clad double pole) at the house intake switches:
explanation: A double-pole switch isolates live and neutral simultaneously, making the whole installation safely dead when opened.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The ideal value of earth-electrode resistance for a domestic installation should be approximately:
options: not exceeding about 5 ohm (as low as practicable)
explanation: Low earth resistance (a few ohms) ensures sufficient fault current to operate protective devices quickly and keeps touch voltages safe.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: The earth pit of a domestic installation is commonly made using a:
options: galvanized iron (GI) pipe or plate electrode buried in ground with charcoal-salt layers
explanation: GI pipe/plate earthing with alternate charcoal and common-salt beds provides a durable low-resistance connection to soil.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Socket outlets of 6 A and 16 A differ physically in that the 16 A socket:
options: has thicker pins/wider spacing, so a 16 A plug cannot be forced into a 6 A socket
explanation: Larger pin diameter and spacing of the 16 A pattern prevent heavy appliances being plugged into light 6 A circuits — a safety interlock.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem: Acid (zinc chloride) flux is recommended for soldering electronic circuit boards.
explanation: False: acid flux residues corrode fine tracks and joints; electronics soldering uses non-corrosive rosin flux.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: A switch must always be connected in the neutral wire of a lighting circuit.
explanation: False: switches must be in the live (phase) wire so the off-state completely de-energizes the fitting.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem: A solderless breadboard requires every connection to be soldered permanently.
explanation: False: breadboards use internal spring clips holding inserted leads — no soldering, fully reusable for prototyping.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Earthing is provided in an installation purely to save electricity.
explanation: False: earthing is a safety measure against electric shock; it carries fault current harmlessly to earth.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem:
Assertion (A): Flux is applied before/during soldering even on apparently clean copper surfaces.
Reason (R): Flux removes oxide layers and prevents their reformation at soldering temperature, enabling the solder to wet the metal.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Even bright copper carries invisible oxides; only flux action (R) lets solder bond, which is exactly why flux is always used (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem:
Assertion (A): A fuse is always placed in the LIVE wire and never in the neutral wire of a circuit.
Reason (R): If the fuse were in the neutral, the circuit would open on fault but the appliance would remain connected to the live supply, a shock hazard.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The hazard of a fused neutral (R) is precisely why protective gear is placed in the live conductor (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem:
Assertion (A): Conduit concealed wiring is costlier than casing-capping wiring.
Reason (R): Concealed conduit requires cutting wall chases, laying pipe, plastering back, and drawing wires, adding labour and material.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The concealed installation process and materials (R) directly account for the higher cost of conduit work (A).
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Which items should be considered while computing the CONNECTED LOAD of a house? (Select all that apply.)
options: Rating of every lamp and fan
Rating of power appliances (geyser, refrigerator, A.C.)
explanation: Connected load sums the wattage of all installed equipment and outlets; wall colour is irrelevant.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem: Which are good PCB soldering practices? (Select all that apply.)
options: Clean and tin the iron tip before use
Heat both pad and lead, and feed solder to the joint not the iron
Use excess solder so joints never fail
Inspect the joint for shine and a concave fillet
explanation: Excess solder risks bridging and dry blobs; correct amount with a heated joint and inspection are good practice.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Which are essential SAFETY rules for house wiring installations? (Select all that apply.)
options: Fuse/switch placed in the live conductor
Every appliance body earthed through the earth wire
Neutral and earth wires fused together
Correctly sized wires and an ELCB/RCCB at the intake
explanation: Fusing earth/neutral is dangerous and prohibited; the other three are standard installation safety requirements.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Which of the following are recognized types of internal wiring systems for buildings? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Cleat, casing-capping and conduit (surface/concealed) are the standard building wiring systems; there is no physical 'wireless wiring'.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soldering: Soldering and desoldering techniques, breadboard wiring, general-purpose PCB soldering/wiring
stem: Which are common desoldering tools/methods? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Wick and vacuum pump are the practical desoldering methods; mouth-blowing and ice are ineffective or unsafe.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: Why should the neutral and earth conductors NEVER have a fuse?
options: Fusing the neutral would leave the equipment live at phase potential after the fuse blows, and earthing must never be interrupted
explanation: Interrupting neutral leaves appliances at fault/phase potential; breaking earth removes shock protection — fusing either is prohibited.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Wiring: Types of residential and commercial wiring systems, general rules and guidelines for installation, load calculation and sizing of wire, rating of main switch, distribution board
stem: While selecting cable size for a sub-circuit, the chosen cross-section must satisfy BOTH:
options: current-carrying capacity (ampacity) AND permissible voltage drop limits
explanation: Ampacity prevents overheating of insulation; limiting voltage drop keeps terminal voltage acceptable at the farthest point.
source: BEU syllabus — Basic Electrical Engineering, Unit 6

stem: STRESS is defined as the:
options: internal RESISTING force developed per unit AREA (\(\sigma=P/A\), units N/mm² or MPa)
explanation: Stress quantifies internal force intensity; strain quantifies the resulting deformation per unit length.

stem: LINEAR STRAIN (\(\varepsilon\)) equals:
options: change in length divided by ORIGINAL length (dimensionless)
explanation: \(\varepsilon=\delta l/l\); being a ratio of lengths, strain has NO units.

stem: SHEAR strain differs from direct strain in that it measures:
options: the angular DISTORTION of an element (change in right angle, expressed in radians)
explanation: Shear strain is the small angle change suffered by initially perpendicular edges of an element.

stem: ST. VENANT'S PRINCIPLE states that:
options: stress distribution at sections NEAR the load point is irregular, but at sections far away (about a depth or more) the stress becomes nearly uniform
explanation: Local irregularities from how a load is applied fade with distance — remote sections feel uniform stress.

stem: St. Venant's principle justifies analyzing a bar's stress by formulas like \(P/A\) because:
options: near load-application points local effects dominate, while the SIMPLE uniform-stress formulas hold at distances greater than the largest cross-section dimension
explanation: The elementary formula applies away from load/attachment points by St. Venant equivalence of load systems.

stem: In a stress-strain DIAGRAM, the ordinate and abscissa are:
options: strain on y-axis, stress on x-axis
stress on y-axis, strain on x-axis
explanation: Convention: stress vertical, strain horizontal — the curve then gives E as the initial slope.

stem: The MODULUS OF ELASTICITY E is read from the stress-strain diagram as the:
options: SLOPE of the initial straight-line (proportionality) portion of the curve
explanation: \(E=\sigma/\varepsilon\) in the linear portion — geometrically the slope of the first straight segment.

stem: ELASTICITY of a material is the property by which:
options: it regains its ORIGINAL SIZE and shape completely on removal of the external load
explanation: Elastic recovery is complete on unloading; permanent set in plasticity remains after unloading.

stem: PLASTICITY manifests, after unloading, as a:
options: PERMANENT deformation (set) that does NOT recover
explanation: Beyond yield, glide/dislocation flow leaves a residual (plastic) deformation even at zero load.

stem: A rope pulling a load is under:
explanation: Forces stretching the member along its axis produce tensile (direct) stress.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a standard stress TYPE discussed in simple stress/strain theory?
explanation: Tensile, compressive and shear form the elementary set; 'indenting stress' isn't a standard category.

stem: HOOKE'S LAW states that within the ELASTIC LIMIT:
options: strain is proportional to stress squared
stress is directly proportional to strain (\(\sigma \propto \varepsilon\))
explanation: \(\sigma=E\varepsilon\) — the constant of proportionality is Young's modulus E only within elasticity.

stem: A wire of length 2 m and area 0.5 mm² stretches 0.8 mm under load. Strain is:
The key STAGES of the mild-steel tensile stress-strain curve in ORDER are:
options: proportional/elastic limit → YIELD points → STRAIN HARDENING → ULTIMATE stress → necking and FRACTURE
explanation: Elastic region, upper-lower yield plateau, strain hardening to UTS, then necking to fracture — the canonical curve.

stem: In the mild-steel curve, the YIELD POINT marks the stress at which:
options: the material starts deforming PERMANENTLY at almost constant load (elastic limit passed)
explanation: Lower yield stress defines the onset of plastic flow; civil design stress keeps members below yield.

stem: NECKING in a ductile tensile test appears AFTER the:
options: ULTIMATE (maximum) tensile stress point, after which the local section keeps reducing until fracture
explanation: Beyond UTS, local strain concentrates in one region — the section thins (necks) and load capacity falls.

stem: WORKING (allowable) stress for design is kept:
options: safely BELOW the elastic/yield strength by dividing by the factor of safety
explanation: Working stress \(=\text{yield or ultimate strength}/\text{FoS}\), keeping members in the elastic range.

stem: FACTOR OF SAFETY (FoS) is the ratio:
explanation: FoS covers uncertainties in loads, materials and workmanship; higher uncertainty → higher FoS.

stem: Why is FoS for CONCRETE typically kept higher (≈3) than for steel (≈1.5-1.67)?
options: concrete is HETEROGENEOUS and BRITTLE with large property scatter, whereas steel is ductile and predictable
explanation: Brittle, variable materials take higher FoS; ductile homogeneous steel tolerates lower FoS.

stem: Lateral strain is the strain measured in directions PERPENDICULAR to the applied axial load.
explanation: True: axial tension thins the cross-section laterally; that cross direction is the lateral strain.

stem: Which facts about POISSON'S RATIO are correct? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: \(\mu\) stays below 0.5 for stable isotropic materials; the first three facts hold.

stem: For a bar under UNIAXIAL tensile stress \(\sigma\) (Poisson's ratio \(\mu\)), the VOLUMETRIC strain equals:
explanation: Axial \(\varepsilon_x=\sigma/E\), laterals \(-\mu\sigma/E\) — sum: \(\varepsilon_v=\varepsilon_x+\varepsilon_y+\varepsilon_z=(\sigma/E)(1-2\mu)\).

stem: A material with \(\mu=0.5\) (e.g., rubber) is special because its:
options: VOLUME remains CONSTANT under uniaxial stress (incompressible)
explanation: \(\varepsilon_v=(1-2\mu)\sigma/E=0\) when \(\mu=0.5\) — lateral thinning exactly compensates elongation.

topic: Elastic moduli and the relationship between them
stem: Which are the principal ELASTIC MODULI? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: E, G and K handle direct, shear and volumetric response; there is no 'moment modulus'.

topic: Elastic moduli and the relationship between them
stem:
Assertion (A): The relation \(E=2G(1+\mu)\) holds between Young's modulus E and shear modulus G of an isotropic material.
Reason (R): The pure-shear state on a square element, expressed through principal stresses and strains, leads to \(G=E/[2(1+\mu)]\) and hence \(E=2G(1+\mu)\).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Principal-stress analysis of pure shear (R) is exactly the derivation behind the relation (A).

topic: Elastic moduli and the relationship between them
stem: The relation between E, K (bulk modulus) and \(\mu\) is:
explanation: Hydrostatic loading with volumetric strain \((1-2\mu)\) setups yields \(E=3K(1-2\mu)\).

stem: For a STEPPED bar (different areas A₁, A₂, ...) of the same material under axial load P, total elongation is:
explanation: Add the extensions of each prismatic segment: \(\delta=\sum\frac{Pl_i}{A_iE}\).

stem: For a uniformly TAPERING bar (d₁→d₂) of length l, axial deformation uses the mean section relation:
explanation: Integration over a linear taper yields \(\delta=\frac{4Pl}{\pi E d_1 d_2}\) — product of end diameters.

stem:
Assertion (A): In a bonded composite bar under axial load, individual materials carry load in proportion to their rigidity \(AE\).
Reason (R): Bonded members deform together (equal strain), so stress is proportional to E and load to AE.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Equal strain through bonding (R) makes stress proportional to E and load to AE — exactly the claim of (A).

stem: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa) and copper bar (E = 100 GPa) of equal area in parallel share a load; the STRESS ratio is:
explanation: Equal strain → stress follows E: 200/100 = 2:1, steel carrying the higher stress.

stem: A bar FREE to expand through temperature rise \(\Delta T\) develops:
options: temperature strain \(\alpha\,\Delta T\) but NO temperature STRESS
explanation: Free thermal expansion creates strain only; restraining the expansion induces stress \(E\alpha\Delta T\).

stem: A steel rail (\(\alpha=12\times10^{-6}/°C\), \(E=200\) GPa) fully RESTRAINED between abutments heated by 25°C develops thermal stress of:
explanation: \(\sigma=E\alpha\Delta T=200000\times12\times10^{-6}\times25=60\) N/mm², compressive (expansion prevented).

stem: STRAIN ENERGY U stored in an elastic bar (load P, extension \(\delta\), applied gradually) is:
explanation: Work done under the rising load equals the area under the load-deformation curve: (1/2)Pδ.

stem: Strain energy per unit volume can be read from the stress-strain curve as the AREA under the curve up to the given strain.
explanation: True: \(u=\int\sigma\,d\varepsilon\) — for a linear spring this is \((1/2)\sigma\varepsilon=\sigma^{2}/2E\).

stem: PROOF RESILIENCE is the:
options: MAXIMUM strain energy stored UPTO the elastic limit = \(\sigma_{e}^{2}/(2E)\) per unit volume
explanation: Upto elastic limit energy per volume; modulus of resilience is its measure, e.g. for steel ≈ higher E-work area.

topic: Gradual, sudden, impact and shock loadings
stem: A SUDDEN (instantaneously applied at once, not growing) load W on a springy bar produces a MAXIMUM stress:
options: TWICE the stress (2W/A) produced by the same load applied GRADUALLY
explanation: Equating Wδ = σ²V/2E work-energy gives peak stress double the static value — dynamic amplification ×2.

topic: Gradual, sudden, impact and shock loadings
stem: For an IMPACT load (weight W falling from height h) on a bar, the peak extension is found from:
options: W(h+\(\delta\)) = \(\dfrac{\sigma^{2}}{2E}\times\text{volume}\) — equating weight's potential energy to stored strain energy, with \(\delta\gg\)
explanation: Energy balance W(h+δ) = strain energy yields peak stress σ = (W/A)[1 + √(1+2hAE/WL)].

stem: Which members are sized using simple stress/strain (\(\sigma=P/A\), \(\delta=PL/AE\)) principles? (Select all that apply.)
options: Suspension cables and rails with thermal gaps
explanation: Paint film isn't a load member; ties, columns, cables and rails are axial-design members.

stem: A 20 mm diameter steel bar (E = 200 GPa) of length 1 m carries 40 kN tensile; extension is about:
explanation: \(\delta=PL/(AE)=40000\times1000/(\pi\times10^{2}\times200000)\approx0.64\) mm.

topic: Gradual, sudden, impact and shock loadings
stem:
Assertion (A): Springs and bumpers are given as cushioning between two colliding/impacting platforms.
Reason (R): Extending the stopping distance (larger δ) enlarges absorbed strain energy, sharply REDUCING the peak dynamic stress versus a rigid stop.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Energy absorption over greater deformation (R) is exactly why cushions tame impact (A).

stem: Which components specify the TWO-DIMENSIONAL state of stress at a point? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Temperature is not a stress component; σx, σy and τxy completely specify the 2-D stress.

stem: COMPLEMENTARY shear stresses arise because:
options: EQUILIBRIUM of an element carrying a shear stress on one pair of faces demands an EQUAL shear on the PERPENDICULAR pair (\|\tau_{xy}\|=\|\tau_{yx}\|)
explanation: Moment equilibrium of an infinitesimal element forces the two perpendicular-face shears to be equal and opposite in sense.

topic: Stress at a point on a plane
stem: The NORMAL stress on a plane inclined at angle \(\theta\) (with \(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\tau\) given) is found from:
explanation: Standard transformation equation: average normal stress plus deviatoric cosine and shear sine terms in 2θ.

topic: Stress at a point on a plane
stem: The SHEAR stress on that same inclined plane is:
explanation: Resolving element forces onto the oblique plane gives the shear transformation in 2θ.

topic: Stress at a point on a plane
stem: If an element carries only uniaxial stress \(\sigma_x=100\) MPa, the normal stress on a plane at 45° to the load is:
explanation: \(\sigma_{45}=\sigma_x\cos^2 45°=100\times0.5=50\) MPa (shear on it is also 50 MPa).

stem: PRINCIPAL PLANES are the planes on which:
options: the SHEAR STRESS IS ZERO, so the stress there is purely normal — the PRINCIPAL STRESSES
explanation: Principal planes carry no shear; the corresponding purely-normal stresses σ₁, σ₂ are the principal stresses.

stem: Principal stresses (major/minor) are computed as:
explanation: The mean normal stress plus/minus the Mohr-circle radius yields the two principal stresses.

stem: The two PRINCIPAL PLANES at a point are:
options: MUTUALLY PERPENDICULAR (90° apart in the material; 180° apart on Mohr's circle)
explanation: Directions of σ₁ and σ₂ are orthogonal; on the Mohr circle they plot 180° apart (θ vs 2θ).

stem: The MAXIMUM shear stress at a point equals:
options: \(\tau_{max}=\frac{\sigma_1-\sigma_2}{2}\) acting on planes at 45° to the principal planes
explanation: τmax is the Mohr-circle RADIUS = half the principal-stress difference, on planes bisecting principal directions.

stem: The orientation of a principal plane obeys:
explanation: Setting the transformed shear to zero yields \(\tan2\theta_p=2\tau/(\sigma_x-\sigma_y)\).

stem: On the plane of MAXIMUM shear stress, the NORMAL stress is generally nonzero, equal to \((\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/2\).
explanation: True: τmax-planes usually carry a normal stress equal to the circle centre value (the average of σx and σy).

stem: In MOHR'S circle of stress, the CENTRE lies on the σ-axis at:
explanation: Circle centre C = mean of the two face normal stresses; radius = √[((σx−σy)/2)²+τ²].

stem: An angle θ between two planes in the material appears as 2θ (doubled) on Mohr's circle.
explanation: True: Mohr circle coordinates use 2θ, so all material angles double at the circle's centre.

stem: For an element in PURE SHEAR (only \(\tau\), no normal stress), Mohr's circle gives principal stresses:
options: \(\sigma_1=+\tau\) and \(\sigma_2=-\tau\) acting at 45° to the shear faces
explanation: Circle centred at origin with radius τ — pure shear equals equal tension+compression at 45°.

topic: Ellipse of stress and their applications
stem: LAMÉ'S ELLIPSE of stress at a point is drawn with:
options: principal stresses σ₁ and σ₂ as its SEMI-AXES, showing resultant stress directions radiating from the point
explanation: The stress ellipse maps resultant-stress vectors on every oblique plane — axes equal the principal stresses.

topic: Ellipse of stress and their applications
stem: An application of the ellipse of stress is visualizing that the RESULTANT stress on an oblique plane:
options: is always normal to the plane
invariably makes an angle to the plane's normal unless the plane is principal — hence the obliquity found from the ellipse
explanation: Ellipse (and Mohr) methods decompose the resultant into normal and shear parts for any plane.

stem:
Assertion (A): Under biaxial stress, the strain in the x-direction equals \((\sigma_x-\mu\sigma_y)/E\).
Reason (R): The generalized Hooke's law superposes the direct strain of \(\sigma_x\) with the Poisson contraction due to \(\sigma_y\).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Superposition of direct and Poisson effects (R) is exactly what produces the stated strain (A).

stem: A plate stretched biaxially with EQUAL σx = σy = σ in its plane develops in-plane strains:
explanation: \(\varepsilon_x=\frac{\sigma}{E}-\mu\frac{\sigma}{E}=(1-\mu)\sigma/E\) — equal biaxial stretch shrinks the effective stiffness.

topic: Principal strains and principal axis of strain
stem: PRINCIPAL STRAINS \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\) are the:
options: largest and smallest NORMAL strains, occurring on axes where SHEAR strain vanishes (the principal axes of strain)
explanation: By analogy with stresses, strains possess orthogonal axes on which shear strain is zero and extremes occur.

topic: Principal strains and principal axis of strain
stem: For an ISOTROPIC elastic body, principal STRESS directions and principal STRAIN directions:
explanation: Isotropy makes the stress and strain tensors coaxial, so their principal axes align.

topic: Circle of strain and ellipse of strain
stem: MOHR'S CIRCLE OF STRAIN is drawn with axes:
options: \(\varepsilon\) on the horizontal and \(\gamma/2\) on the vertical axis
explanation: Using half the engineering shear strain mirrors the stress circle exactly — strains thus transform like stresses.

topic: Circle of strain and ellipse of strain
stem: The existence of a strain circle/ellipse of strain proves that strains at a point transform by the:
options: same conic/tensor law as stresses (same 2θ transformation)
explanation: Second-order tensors (stress/strain) share the Mohr-circle structure for inclined directions.

stem: Because E, G, K and \(\mu\) are interlinked for an isotropic material, the number of INDEPENDENT elastic constants is only:
options: TWO (e.g. E and \(\mu\)); the rest follow from \(E=2G(1+\mu)=3K(1-2\mu)\)
explanation: Any two constants determine all others for isotropic elasticity.

stem: Combining \(E=2G(1+\mu)\) and \(E=3K(1-2\mu)\) yields, in terms of K and G:
explanation: Eliminating μ from the two relations gives the harmonic-type combination \(E=9KG/(3K+G)\).

topic: Bending moment (BM) and shear force (SF) diagrams
stem: The SHEAR FORCE at a beam section equals the:
options: algebraic SUM of all vertical external forces acting on ONE SIDE (left or right) of the section
explanation: V = net transverse force to one side of the cut; the bending moment equals the net moment of those forces.

topic: Bending moment (BM) and shear force (SF) diagrams
stem: The fundamental DIFFERENTIAL relations between load, shear and moment are:
explanation: Shear is the slope of the BM diagram; load intensity is the slope of the SF diagram — the core diagram rules.

topic: Bending moment (BM) and shear force (SF) diagrams
stem: The usual SIGN conventions in SFD/BMD work are: sagging moment (concave-up, bottom fibres in tension) is taken as:
options: POSITIVE; hogging (top fibres tension) as NEGATIVE, upward left-face shear as positive
explanation: Sagging M positive, hogging negative; left-side upward forces positive — the standard convention.

topic: BM and SF diagrams for cantilevers simply supported and fixed beams with or without overhangs
stem: A CANTILEVER of length L with point load W at the FREE end has:
options: SF = −W constant along the length and BENDING MOMENT maximum at the FIXED END = −WL (hogging)
explanation: Constant SF of magnitude W; BM triangle from zero at free end to −WL at the fixed support.

topic: BM and SF diagrams for cantilevers simply supported and fixed beams with or without overhangs
stem: A SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam with a CENTRAL point load W has reactions and maximum BM of:
options: R = W each end, Mmax = WL/8
explanation: Symmetry halves the load to each support; the peak moment WL/4 occurs at the load point.

topic: BM and SF diagrams for cantilevers simply supported and fixed beams with or without overhangs
stem: Which features appear in the BMD/SFD of an OVERHANGING beam? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Overhangs introduce sign changes of moment; 'constant positive everywhere' is impossible there.

topic: Calculation of maximum BM and SF and the point of contra flexure under concentrated loads
stem: The POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE in a beam is the section where:
options: the BM changes SIGN (BM = 0 between hogging and sagging regions)
explanation: M = 0 with a sign change marks contraflexure; only at SF = 0 does M reach a local extremum.

topic: Calculation of maximum BM and SF and the point of contra flexure under concentrated loads
stem: BENDING MOMENT attains a LOCAL MAXIMUM or minimum where:
options: SF = 0 (since \(dM/dx=V\), the moment curve is stationary where shear vanishes)
explanation: Stationary M requires dM/dx = V = 0 — find max BM by locating the zero-shear section.

topic: Calculation of maximum BM and SF and the point of contra flexure under concentrated loads
stem:
Assertion (A): A sudden vertical JUMP in the shear-force diagram marks a concentrated point load at that section.
Reason (R): Since \(dV/dx=-w\), a concentrated force is a delta-like load intensity, so the shear value steps by the full load magnitude across an infinitesimal length.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The step equals the concentrated force (R), which is precisely the jump observed in the SFD (A).

topic: Uniformly distributed loads over the whole span or part of span
stem: For a SS beam with UDL w over the WHOLE span, which are correct? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: wL²/2 belongs to the cantilever case; all the other statements describe the SS beam.

topic: Uniformly distributed loads over the whole span or part of span
stem: Under a UDL portion of a beam, the SF diagram slopes linearly while the BM diagram is:
explanation: Constant w integrates V linearly and M quadratically — parabolic BMD under UDL stretches.

topic: Uniformly distributed loads over the whole span or part of span
stem: A CANTILEVER with UDL w over its entire length has the maximum BM at the fixed end of:
explanation: The whole UDL totals wL acting at L/2 from the wall: M = wL·L/2 = wL²/2.

topic: Combination of concentrated loads (two or three) and uniformly distributed loads
stem:
Assertion (A): For a beam under combined point loads and UDL, the SFD and BMD can be drawn by superposing the diagrams of each load case.
Reason (R): Equilibrium of beams under elastic, statically determinate conditions is LINEAR, so load effects add algebraically.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Linearity of the governing equations (R) is precisely what licenses superposition (A).

topic: Combination of concentrated loads (two or three) and uniformly distributed loads
stem: With several CONCENTRATED loads on a beam, the SF diagram between successive loads is:
options: a constant horizontal segment between consecutive point loads (no distributed load between)
explanation: Zero load intensity between point forces makes V constant there; jumps occur only at the forces.

stem: For a SS beam with a UNIFORMLY VARYING (triangular) load, 0 at one end to w at the other, the reactions are:
explanation: Total load wL/2 acting at 2L/3 from the zero end gives reactions wL/6 and wL/3 by moments.

stem: The APPLICATION OF MOMENTS principle (Varignon) used for support reactions states:
options: the MOMENT of the resultant of a distributed load about a point equals the SUM of moments of its elementary strips — so replace distributed load by its resultant at the centroid
explanation: Replacing a UDL/UVL by its total load at the centroid simplifies the moment equilibrium for reactions.

stem: SIMPLE (pure) BENDING of a beam refers to bending occurred under:
options: constant bending moment ALONE (with no shear force) so only BENDING stresses develop
explanation: In pure-bending stretches BM is constant and V=0; flexure theory is built on this clean case first.

stem: During sagging bending of a horizontal beam, the fibres:
options: between NA and OUTER SKIN: those ABOVE the neutral axis SHORTEN (compression) and those BELOW ELONGATE (tension)
explanation: Bending curves the beam; concave side compresses and convex side stretches, linearly from the neutral axis.

stem: BENDING STRESS at a fibre varies:
options: linearly with its distance y from the neutral axis (zero at NA, maximum at extreme fibre)
explanation: \(\sigma=(E/R)y\) — strain is linear in y, so by Hooke's law stress is linear too.

stem: A standard ASSUMPTION of simple bending theory is that:
options: PLANE cross-sections REMAIN PLANE and normal to the axis of the beam after bending
explanation: Bernoulli's hypothesis of plane sections is the geometric core of the linear strain distribution.

stem: Which set states the ASSUMPTIONS of pure-bending theory correctly?
options: material homogeneous/isotropic and elastic (Hooke), beam axis originally straight, loads in the plane of bending, plane sections remain plane
explanation: Straight prismatic member, elastic isotropic material, symmetric bending plane and plane-sections are the four pillars.

stem: Simple-bending theory assumes that stresses remain WITHIN the elastic limit and the beam's own weight is neglected.
explanation: True: elastic linearity (Hooke) and ignored self-weight keep the derivation \(\sigma/I=E/R\) exact internally.

topic: Derivation of bending equation: M/I = f/y = E/R
stem: The BENDING EQUATION is:
explanation: (f or σ) at distance y, M the moment, I second moment of area, R radius of curvature — the flexure formula.

topic: Derivation of bending equation: M/I = f/y = E/R
stem: Combining geometry \(\varepsilon=y/R\) with Hooke's law gives the fibre stress as:
explanation: Strain ratio from the sector geometry times Young's modulus gives stress linear in fibre position y.

topic: Derivation of bending equation: M/I = f/y = E/R
stem: From equilibrium \(\int\sigma\,dA=0\) with \(\sigma=Ey/R\), one derives that the NEUTRAL AXIS passes through the:
explanation: Zero net axial force forces the first moment of area about the NA to vanish — the centroid condition.

stem: The NEUTRAL AXIS of a beam cross-section is the line along which:
options: the BENDING STRESS is ZERO (fibres on it neither elongate nor shorten)
explanation: Fibres on the neutral axis (through the centroid) have zero strain and zero stress in pure bending.

stem: The CURVATURE of the neutral layer (elastic curve) is related to moment by:
options: \(\frac{1}{R}=\frac{M}{EI}\) — so EI, the FLEXURAL RIGIDITY, controls the bend
explanation: \(1/R = M/EI\); stiffer EI sections bend less — the quantity governing serviceability.

stem: For a beam bent double curvature (S-shape over supports), along the beam's length the neutral axis:
options: shifts repeatedly as curvature reverses sign at contraflexure points, with compressive and tensile sides exchanging top/bottom
explanation: Contraflexure = local curvature reversal; the same cross-sectional NA flips which side is in tension.

stem: To find the bending stress at a fibre, the working formula is:
options: \(\sigma=\frac{M\,y}{I}\) with y measured from the neutral axis
explanation: \(\sigma=My/I\): stress moment couple grows linearly with fibre distance from NA.

stem: A rectangular beam 100 mm × 200 mm (depth) carries M = 5 kN·m. Maximum bending stress is about:
explanation: \(I=100\times200^3/12=6.67\times10^{7}\) mm⁴; \(\sigma=5\times10^{6}\times100/I=7.5\) MPa at extreme fibre.

stem: Compression and TENSION zones of a sagging-loaded beam section are separated by:
options: the NEUTRAL AXIS — above it compression, below it tension (for sagging)
explanation: The NA divides the section into compression and tension zones whose forces form the resisting couple.

stem: The MOMENT OF RESISTANCE of a beam section equals:
options: the moment of the internal stress couple about the NA = \(\sigma_{max}\cdot Z = M\)
explanation: Internal stress resultant moment must equal external BM: M = (I/ymax)·σmax = σmax·Z.

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: SECTION MODULUS Z is defined as:
explanation: Z packs section strength into one measure; designers compare M with σallow×Z directly.

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: For a SOLID RECTANGLE b × d (depth in the bending plane), I and Z about the centroidal axis are:
explanation: With ymax = d/2 the section modulus is bd²/6 — note depth squared as the driver of strength.

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: For a SOLID CIRCLE of diameter d (\(I=\pi d^4/64\)), the section modulus is:

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: For the HOLLOW CIRCULAR section (outer D, inner d), the moment of inertia about the axis is:
explanation: Subtract the void: \(I=(\pi/64)(D^4-d^4)\); Z divides by D/2.

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: The general lesson comparing hollow vs solid sections is that a HOLLOW section with the same area:
options: can carry MORE moment for the same weight since material pushed far from the NA raises I steeply (radius-of-gyration effect)
explanation: I depends on distance^2 of area from NA — hence tubes, flanges and I-sections are bending-efficient.

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: A 50 mm × 100 mm wooden joist and a 100 mm × 50 mm flat plank of the same wood, bent about their respective strong axes: the UPRIGHT joist's Z is exactly:
options: exactly the SAME Z in both orientations
the UPRIGHT joist's \(Z=bd^2/6=50\times100^2/6\approx8333\) mm³, TWICE the plank's 4167 mm³
the plank is twice as strong
explanation: Z scales with depth² at fixed area: upright (100 mm deep) is twice as strong as the flat orientation.

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: I-SECTIONS dominate steel construction because:
options: their two flanges concentrate area FAR from the neutral axis, maximizing I and Z per unit weight
explanation: Flanges far from the NA carry bending, the web carries shear — the most weight-efficient flexural profile.

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: To find I of an I-section about its centroidal axis, the practical method used is:
options: SUMMING rectangle I's using the PARALLEL AXIS THEOREM \(I=\bar I + A h^2\) about a common axis
explanation: Add each flange/web's own centroidal I plus Ah² with h from its centroid to the section centroid axis.

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: For UNSYMMETRICAL sections like T, ANGLE or CHANNEL, the neutral axis location must be:
options: computed FIRST as the section CENTROID (first moment of areas), which is generally not at mid-depth
explanation: NA passes through centroid; lopsided sections have eccentric centroids needing first-moment calculation.

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: In an unsymmetric T-beam (flange at top) in sagging, the maximum tensile and compressive stresses:
options: differ because extreme distances y top y bottom to the NA are DIFFERENT — larger y sees the larger stress
explanation: With NA off mid-depth, \(\sigma=My/I\) with asymmetric y gives unequal peak stresses opposite NA sides.

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: The PARALLEL AXIS theorem can also compute an I-section's I about its own base edge, not only about the centroid.
explanation: True: \(I_{xx}=\bar I+A\bar y^2\) connects a centroidal I to any parallel reference axis.

stem: DESIGNING a beam section for flexure uses the condition:
options: \(M_{max}\le\sigma_{allowable}\times Z\) — pick a section whose Z satisfies
explanation: Required \(Z \ge M_{max}/\sigma_{allowable}\); economy then guides section family choice.

stem: A beam must carry M = 20 kN·m with allowable stress 150 MPa; MINIMUM required section modulus is:
explanation: \(Z=M/\sigma=20\times10^{6}/150\approx1.33\times10^{5}\) mm³ = 133 cm³.

stem: When comparing two sections for the same Z, the BETTER section for economy is the one with:
options: LESS AREA (lighter) for equal Z — a high strength-to-weight ratio, e.g. I over solid rectangle
explanation: Equal Z at lower weight = efficient section: flanges far from NA deliver that economy.

stem: FLEXURAL RIGIDITY (EI) expresses:
options: the STIFFNESS of the section against bending deformation (slopes/deflections depend on it)
explanation: Curvature = M/EI; larger EI → smaller curvatures and deflections under the same moment.

stem:
Assertion (A): Fibres ON the neutral axis carry no longitudinal stress during simple bending.
Reason (R): Since \(\sigma=E y/R\) with y measured from the NA, fibre stress at y = 0 is zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: y = 0 in \(\sigma=Ey/R\) (R) directly makes NA fibres stress-free (A).

stem:
Assertion (A): At a beam section, compressive bending stress sits on one side of the NA and tensile on the other.
Reason (R): Bending curvature shortens fibres on the concave side and lengthens those on the convex side, so the stress sign changes across the NA.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The curvature-induced shorten/lengthen geometry (R) directly produces the sign change across the NA (A).

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem:
Assertion (A): Strength (Z) of a rectangular beam grows much faster with DEPTH than with width.
Reason (R): For a rectangle, \(Z = b d^2/6\) — depth enters squared while width enters only linearly.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: d² vs b in the formula (R) is exactly why joists stand on edge (A).

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: Which sections are recognized as structural ROLLED sections for beams? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Ellipse plate is not a standard rolled profile; I, T, angle and channel are the classic families.

stem: Which are genuine ASSUMPTIONS of pure (simple) bending theory? (Select all that apply.)
options: Plane sections remain plane after bending
Material is homogeneous, isotropic and elastic
Beam is straight and loaded in its plane of symmetry
explanation: Warping violates the theory; the first three are the formal assumptions.

stem: Which statements about bending stress distribution are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Constancy contradicts the basis; the first three describe the linear elastic flexure distribution.

topic: I, T, Angle and Channel sections
stem: For an ANGLE (L) section the NEUTRAL axis for a principal-axis bending case is found as:
options: through the CENTROID of the L — found by splitting the L into two rectangles with first-moment calculation
explanation: Composite rectangle decomposition + first moment locates the centroid for asymmetric angle/channel parts.

stem: Design of a timber joist for a bathroom floor would check, beyond strength, the:
options: DEFLECTION limit (serviceability) using \(1/R=M/EI\) integration as well as stress
explanation: Serviceability (deflection) and bending strength are the twin checks in practical beam design.

topic: Section modulus of rectangular and circular sections (Solid and Hollow)
stem: RADIUS OF GYRATION k of a section, where \(I=A k^2\), indicates:
options: how far the area effectively spreads from the axis — larger k at same area means higher I share of a sq section
explanation: k = √(I/A) measures areal spread: thin tubes and flanged sections achieve high k per unit area.

stem: The SHEAR STRESS at a fibre in a beam cross-section is given by:
options: \(\tau=\frac{F\,A\bar{y}}{I\,b}\) — F = shear force, Aȳ = first moment of the area ABOVE the fibre about the NA, b = width there
explanation: Horizontal shear between layers balances bending-stress differences, giving τ = FAȳ/Ib across the width.

stem: In deriving \(\tau=FA\bar y/(Ib)\), the horizontal (longitudinal) shear between adjacent layers comes from:
options: the DIFFERENCE in bending stresses on the two sides of a cut element \(d(\sigma)=y\,dM/I\), resisted by shear along the layer
explanation: Bending-stress gradient along the span creates the shear flow — the core idea of the derivation.

topic: Shear stress distribution across various beam sections like rectangular, circular, triangular, I, T angle sections
stem: Across a RECTANGULAR beam section, the shear stress distribution is:
options: PARABOLIC — ZERO at top and bottom edges and MAXIMUM at the neutral axis
explanation: τ(y) varies parabolically; the NA fibre has the biggest first moment Aȳ — the largest τ there.

topic: Shear stress distribution across various beam sections like rectangular, circular, triangular, I, T angle sections
stem: For a rectangular section, the MAXIMUM shear stress equals:
options: \(\tau_{max}=1.5\times\) average shear stress (\(=\frac{3V}{2A}\)), at the neutral axis
explanation: Parabolic peak of 1.5 × mean; for solid circular sections the factor is 4/3 instead.

topic: Shear stress distribution across various beam sections like rectangular, circular, triangular, I, T angle sections
stem: For a SOLID CIRCULAR section of radius R, the maximum shear stress (at NA) is:
explanation: Circle gives 4/3 × average at the neutral axis (vs 3/2 for the rectangle).

topic: Shear stress distribution across various beam sections like rectangular, circular, triangular, I, T angle sections
stem: In an I-SECTION beam, almost the entire shear force is taken by the:
options: WEB — the shear diagram jumps nearly all the shear into the web, with small parabolic variation across it
explanation: Bending belongs to the flanges and shear to the web — the efficient division in rolled I-beams.

topic: Shear stress distribution across various beam sections like rectangular, circular, triangular, I, T angle sections
stem: At the FLANGE-WEB junction of an I-beam, the shear stress curve shows:
options: a sudden JUMP/change because τ inversely depends on the width b that changes abruptly from flange to web
explanation: Since τ ∝ 1/b, the width drop at the junction multiplies the stress stepwise.

topic: Shear stress distribution across various beam sections like rectangular, circular, triangular, I, T angle sections
stem: For a TRIANGULAR section, the maximum shear stress occurs:
options: at half the height (mid-depth) of the triangle, with value 1.5 × average
explanation: In a triangle, Aȳ/b peaks at mid-height rather than at the centroid — τmax = 1.5 τavg there.

topic: Slope and deflection: Relationship between moment, slope and deflection
stem: The fundamental differential relation connecting bending moment to deflection is:
explanation: Curvature 1/R ≈ d²y/dx² and M = EI/R give the basic beam equation for slope/deflection.

topic: Slope and deflection: Relationship between moment, slope and deflection
stem: SLOPE and DEFLECTION of a beam mean respectively:
options: the ANGLE the tangent to the elastic curve makes with the original axis (dy/dx) and the transverse DISPLACEMENT y
explanation: Slope = rotation dy/dx of the deflected axis; deflection = its lateral shift y(x) — both from integrating M/EI.

topic: Slope and deflection: Relationship between moment, slope and deflection
stem: For SMALL deflections of beams, the curvature 1/R is approximated by:
explanation: Since slope is small, (dy/dx)² ≈ 0 in the full curvature formula, simplifying to y''.

topic: Slope and deflection: Relationship between moment, slope and deflection
stem: Standard result — the maximum deflection of a SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam with UDL w over span L is:
explanation: 5wL⁴/384EI is the classic SS+UDL midspan deflection — worth memorizing.

topic: Slope and deflection: Relationship between moment, slope and deflection
stem: A CANTILEVER with a point load W at its free end has free-end deflection:
explanation: Integrating M = −Wx twice with fixed-end conditions gives WL³/3EI (and slope WL²/2EI).

topic: Slope and deflection: Relationship between moment, slope and deflection
stem: Deflection grows with the FOURTH power of span when the load is DISTRIBUTED (UDL), and with the THIRD power when it is POINT — hence:
options: doubling span multiplies UDL deflection by 16 and point-load deflection by 8
explanation: L⁴ vs L³: span is by far the dominant variable controlling beam deflection.

stem: The FIRST moment-area theorem states that the angle between tangents at two points of the elastic curve equals:
options: the AREA of the M/EI diagram between those two points
explanation: \(\theta_B-\theta_A=\int M/EI\,dx\) between A and B — the area-integral of the moment diagram.

stem: The SECOND moment-area theorem gives the deviation (deflection) of a point from the tangent drawn at another point as:
options: the MOMENT of the M/EI area between them about that point
explanation: Tangential deviation equals the first moment of the M/EI area between the two points.

stem:
Assertion (A): Moment-area theorems suit cantilever slope/deflection problems especially well.
Reason (R): The tangent at the FIXED end of a cantilever has zero slope, so all deviations read directly as M/EI area-moments from that reference.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The built-in zero-slope datum at the fixed end (R) is what makes moment-area readings immediate (A).

stem: MACAULAY'S method for slope and deflection works by:
options: writing ONE moment expression valid for the whole span (with Macaulay/bracket functions that vanish where negative), then INTEGRATING twice and fixing constants from boundary conditions
explanation: Bracket (singularity) functions let a single expression span load discontinuities; two integrations + b.c. yield y(x).

stem: In Macaulay's notation, the bracket term \([x-a]^2\) is treated as:
options: zero when x < a (bracket ignored) and \((x-a)^2\) when x ≥ a
explanation: The bracket-switches preserve validity across load points — the method's defining feature.

stem: While INTEGRATING Macaulay terms \([x-a]^n\), the correct handling is:
options: integrate as \(\frac{[x-a]^{n+1}}{n+1}\) WITHOUT expanding, and evaluate constants by b.c.
explanation: Brackets are integrated as indivisible units — this preserves the sectional validity of the result.

topic: Use of these methods to calculate slope and deflection for determinant beams
stem: Slope/deflection analysis of a determinate beam requires which steps? (Select all that apply.)
options: Apply boundary conditions (e.g., y = 0 at supports)
explanation: Classical methods need reactions, M(x) and boundary conditions — no FE mesh is involved.

topic: Use of these methods to calculate slope and deflection for determinant beams
stem: BOUNDARY CONDITIONS used (two per span) to evaluate integration constants for SS/mount-support beams are typically:
options: y = 0 at the two simple supports; θ = 0 and y = 0 at a fixed end
explanation: Zero deflection at supports (plus zero slope at fixed ends) supplies the needed conditions.

topic: Use of these methods to calculate slope and deflection for determinant beams
stem: For a symmetrically loaded SS beam, the point of maximum deflection coincides with the point of ZERO slope at midspan.
explanation: True: symmetry makes midspan slope zero — maximum deflection occurs where slope vanishes.

topic: Torsion: Derivation of torsion equation and its assumptions
stem: The TORSION EQUATION for circular shafts is:
explanation: T torque, J polar moment, τ at radius r, θ angle of twist over length l — core shaft formula.

topic: Torsion: Derivation of torsion equation and its assumptions
stem: Which are assumptions of the simple TORSION theory? (Select all that apply.)
options: Plane sections remain plane after twisting
explanation: Free warping invalidates the plane-sections assumption; the other three are formal assumptions.

topic: Torsion: Derivation of torsion equation and its assumptions
stem: Shear stress in a twisted shaft varies:
options: LINEARLY with radius — ZERO at the shaft centre and MAXIMUM at the OUTER surface (r = R)
explanation: Shear strain = rθ/l increases with radius, so τ = G·rθ/l peaks at the surface.

topic: Applications of the equation of the hollow and solid circular shafts
stem: The POLAR moment of inertia J equals, for solid and hollow circular shafts respectively:
explanation: Polar J is πd⁴/32 for solid; the hollow shaft subtracts the core: π(D⁴−d⁴)/32.

topic: Applications of the equation of the hollow and solid circular shafts
stem:
Assertion (A): A hollow circular shaft is materially more efficient in torsion than a solid one of equal weight.
Reason (R): Material near the axis carries little torque stress; removing it and pushing area outward raises J, and torque capacity \(T=\tau J/R\) rises with it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Higher J per unit material (R) is exactly why hollow shafts win (A).

topic: Applications of the equation of the hollow and solid circular shafts
stem: Power transmitted by a shaft is related to torque by:
options: \(P=\frac{2\pi N T}{60}\) with N in rpm
explanation: Work-per-revolution 2πT times N/60 → watts; used for shaft sizing from the driven power.

stem: TORSIONAL RIGIDITY of a shaft is the quantity:
options: \(GJ\) — torque per unit angle of twist per unit length (\(T=GJ\theta/l\))
explanation: GJ resists twist the way EI resists bending — the shaft's stiffness measure.

topic: Combined torsion and bending of circular shafts
stem:
Assertion (A): At the extreme fibre of a solid circular shaft under combined M and T, \(\sigma_b=32M/\pi d^3\) and \(\tau=16T/\pi d^3\).
Reason (R): Substituting \(I=\pi d^4/64\) into \(\sigma=My/I\) and \(J=\pi d^4/32\) into \(\tau=Tr/J\) with \(y=r=d/2\) yields these expressions.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The section constants of a circle fed into flexure and torsion formulas (R) produce exactly the quoted stresses (A).

topic: Principal stress and maximum shear stresses under combined loading of bending and torsion
stem: Under combined M and T on a shaft, the MAXIMUM SHEAR stress (for failure theories) is:
explanation: Mohr from σb and τ gives τmax = (16/πd³)√(M²+T²) — defines equivalent torque.

topic: Principal stress and maximum shear stresses under combined loading of bending and torsion
stem: The EQUIVALENT BENDING MOMENT (from the principal stress criterion) for M and T is:
explanation: Me = (M + √(M²+T²))/2 reproduces the same σ1 in pure bending — Rankine/Guest design.

stem: A CLOSE-COILED helical spring under an AXIAL load W deflects by:
options: \(\delta=\frac{64 W R^3 n}{G d^4}\) (n = turns, R = coil radius, d = wire dia)
explanation: Wire twisting through n coils produces this classic deflection formula.

stem: The STIFFNESS of a close-coiled spring is:
options: \(k=\frac{G d^4}{64 R^3 n}\) — force per unit deflection
explanation: Inverting the deflection formula: k = W/δ = Gd⁴/(64R³n).

stem: The wire of a close-coiled spring under axial load is stressed mainly in:
options: TORSION (plus small direct shear) — the coil converts axial force to wire torque
explanation: Close-coil geometry makes torque WR dominate; this is why spring wire is high-strength torsion-grade.

topic: Thin Cylinders and Spheres: Derivation of formulae and calculations of hoop stress
stem: For a thin closed cylinder under internal pressure p (diameter d, thickness t), which hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: Hoop stress = twice the longitudinal stress
explanation: pd/4t is the longitudinal, not hoop value; the other three statements are consistent.

topic: Longitudinal stress in a cylinder and sphere subjected to internal pressures
stem: LONGITUDINAL stress in a closed thin cylinder under internal pressure is:
explanation: End-cap load p·πd²/4 on the annular area πdt gives pd/4t — half of hoop.

topic: Longitudinal stress in a cylinder and sphere subjected to internal pressures
stem: In a thin SPHERE of diameter d under internal pressure p, the membrane stress equals:
options: \(\sigma=\frac{pd}{4t}\) uniformly in all directions — a SPHERE is therefore the most efficient pressure shape
explanation: A sphere shares pressure in two equal hoop directions: pd/4t — no weaker axis.

topic: Thin Cylinders and Spheres: Derivation of formulae and calculations of hoop stress
stem: A thin cylinder under internal pressure would fail first by splitting along a LONGITUDINAL seam, because hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress.
explanation: True: with σh = 2σl, circumferential tension bursts the shell along its length.

stem: The TENSION test on a mild-steel specimen is conducted on a:
options: UNIVERSAL TESTING MACHINE (UTM) with suitable grips
explanation: The UTM applies gradually increasing axial tension while load and extension are recorded.

stem: In a tension test, elongation of the specimen is measured accurately using an:
options: EXTENSOMETER clipped to the gauge length
explanation: Extensometers track gauge-length deformation precisely, especially in the elastic (small-strain) region.

stem: The standard GAUGE LENGTH for a circular tensile specimen (powder/rolled steel) is taken as:
explanation: \(l_0=5.65\sqrt{A_0}\) standardizes elongation so percent ductility is comparable across sizes.

stem: Which are DUCTILITY measures obtained from the tension test? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Both elongation% and reduction-of-area% gauge ductility; hardness/impact are different properties.

topic: Bending tests on simply supported beam and Cantilever beam
stem: BENDING TESTS in the lab use a beam model loaded at midspan with deflections read from:
options: DIAL GAUGES (or deflectometers) set beneath key sections
explanation: Dial gauges under the beam record its deflection history under point loads.

topic: Bending tests on simply supported beam and Cantilever beam
stem: A CANTILEVER bending test compares measured free-end deflection with:
explanation: Matching measured δ with WL³/3EI verifies flexure theory and lets E be back-computed.

topic: Bending tests on simply supported beam and Cantilever beam
stem: The SIMPLY SUPPORTED beam bending test on wood/steel also evaluates its strength as the:
options: MODULUS OF RUPTURE = \(6M/(bd^2)\) for a rectangular section (M at failure)
explanation: Transverse failure bending stress — the rupture modulus — rates wood/brittle beams practically.

stem: The standard specimen for the concrete COMPRESSION test in India (BIS/IS) is a:
options: 150 mm cube (standard) tested under a compression testing machine
explanation: 150 mm cubes cast in metal moulds are the national standard (100 mm accepted with correction).

stem: The compressive strength of the cube is calculated as:
explanation: Failure load divided by loaded face area gives nominal cube strength in MPa.

stem: A satisfactory concrete cube FAILURE pattern under a proper compression test is:
options: an approximately DOUBLE CONE (hourglass) with side spalling
explanation: Characteristic two-pyramid failure with face spalling indicates a correct well-supported test.

stem: Impact tests (Izod/Charpy) measure a material's:
options: TOUGHNESS — the energy (Joules) ABSORBED in fracture of a NOTCHED specimen by a single pendulum blow
explanation: The swing-through height difference gives absorbed fracture energy — the notch-toughness measure.

stem: In a Charpy impact test, the notched specimen is supported horizontally as a simply supported beam and struck on the face OPPOSITE to the notch.
explanation: True: Charpy = horizontal SS arrangement, struck behind the notch (Izod is the vertical cantilever).

stem: A material showing LOW impact (notched-bar) values at low temperature is said to undergo:
options: DUCTILE-BRITTLE TRANSITION — it shatters like a brittle solid under shock even though tough when warm
explanation: Structural steels can turn notch-brittle in the cold — the famous cause of Liberty-ship failures.

stem: The IZOD value reported from the impact machine is read as the:
options: ENERGY READ directly on the machine dial (difference of pendulum potential before/after breaking)
explanation: Scale reading of the residual swing height converts into Joules of absorbed fracture energy.

stem: In a SINGLE SHEAR test, the specimen fails across:
options: ONE plane only (shear strength = failure load/sheared area)
explanation: Single shear parted at one section (like one lap); double shear splits at two sections simultaneously.

stem: In DOUBLE shear (e.g. a rod in a double-cover fixture), the shear strength is computed as:
options: \(\tau=\frac{P}{2A}\) since TWO planes share the failure load
explanation: Two shear planes divide the load — double-shear jigs are standard for rivet/bolt coupons.

topic: Investigation of Hook's law that is the proportional relation between force and stretching in elastic deformation
stem: The lab investigation verifies Hooke's law by plotting:
options: FORCE (load) vs EXTENSION on a bar/spring within the elastic range and obtaining a STRAIGHT LINE through origin
explanation: A straight-through-origin load-extension graph confirms extension ∝ force — elastic behaviour.

topic: Investigation of Hook's law that is the proportional relation between force and stretching in elastic deformation
stem: In the Hooke's-law rig the load-extension graph is used to establish? (Select all that apply.)
options: The proportionality limit where the line departs from straightness
explanation: Slope → stiffness and the departure point → proportional limit; the other two are unrelated.

topic: Investigation of Hook's law that is the proportional relation between force and stretching in elastic deformation
stem: The Hooke's-law investigation confirms proportionality ONLY UP TO:
options: the ELASTIC/PROPORTIONALITY LIMIT — beyond it the load-extension line departs from straightness
explanation: Beyond the proportional limit permanent extension starts — the graph bends away from the line.

stem: In the torsion test on a shaft specimen, the angle of twist per applied torque (T/θ) evaluates:
options: the TORSIONAL RIGIDITY \(\frac{T}{\theta}=\frac{GJ}{l}\) from which the SHEAR MODULUS G is determined
explanation: Snugging θ against T over length l gives GJ/l → G = Tl/(Jθ).

stem: The angle of TWIST in the torsion test is read over a gauge length to apply:
options: \(\theta=\frac{T l}{G J}\) — twist grows linearly with length, so proportional gauges measures are used
explanation: Twist ∝ length × torque: linearity checked across gauge lengths validates the theory.

stem: A torsion test specimen twisted to FRACTURE shows a flat perpendicular fracture face (with spiral 45° faces for ductile materials in combined modes) — the CLEAN CUP-type snap across the section indicates failure by:
options: SHEAR across the plane of maximum shear stress (perpendicular to the shaft axis) for BRITTLE behaviour
explanation: Brittle shafts fail on the max-shear (transverse) plane; ductile shafts may show 45° helical facets.

topic: Measurement of forces on supports in statically determinate beam
stem: Support REACTIONS of a determinate beam are verified in the lab by hanging the beam on:
options: SPRING BALANCES (or load cells) at the supports and checking \(\sum F_y=0\) against applied loads
explanation: Spring-balance readings at supports should sum to the total applied vertical loads.

topic: Measurement of forces on supports in statically determinate beam
stem:
Assertion (A): The moment-equilibrium check (\(\sum M=0\)) verifies EACH support reaction individually in the beam rig.
Reason (R): A single vertical force equation alone cannot distinguish one wrong reaction from another.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Because ΣFy only fixes the sum (R), the moment balance is needed to validate each reaction (A).

topic: Measurement of forces on supports in statically determinate beam
stem: A beam model carries W₁ = 2 N at 0.2 m and W₂ = 3 N at 0.6 m from support A over span 0.8 m. The reaction at the FAR support B equals:
explanation: Moments about A: \(R_B\times0.8=2\times0.2+3\times0.6=2.2 \Rightarrow R_B=2.75\) N; then RA = 5−2.75 = 2.25 N.

topic: Determination of shear forces in beams
stem:
Assertion (A): In the SF rig, the external balancing force at the cut section EQUALS the shear force there.
Reason (R): Restoring the two halves to alignment cancels the internal shear, leaving the applied force alone to represent it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Cancelling the internal shear (R) makes the applied force equal the section's shear (A).

topic: Determination of shear forces in beams
stem: The verified rule in the SF experiment is that the shear force at a section equals:
options: the ALGEBRAIC SUM of all the external forces to ONE SIDE (left or right) of the section
explanation: SF = sum of left-side (or right-side) vertical forces — the definition validated by the rig.

topic: Determination of bending moments in beams
stem: The bending-moment rig verifies which statements? (Select all that apply.)
options: BM at a section = Σ(F x) of forces to one side
BM depends directly on Young's modulus
explanation: Equilibrium, one-sided sums and sagging/hogging signs are verified; E does not enter BM.

topic: Determination of bending moments in beams
stem: The BM beam rig compares experimental readings with the THEORETICAL maximum for a midspan point load:
options: \(M_{max}=\frac{WL}{4}\) for a simply supported span L
explanation: Central point load on an SS span gives WL/4 — the benchmark for the rig comparison.

topic: Measurement of deflections in statically determinate beam
stem: Beam deflection in the lab is typically read with a:
options: DIAL GAUGE / LVDT at midspan or other stations against the original level
explanation: Dial gauges or LVDTs measure the vertical displacement history at chosen sections.

topic: Measurement of deflections in statically determinate beam
stem: For the determinate beam deflection test, readings are checked against:
options: \(\delta=\frac{WL^3}{48EI}\) for a midspan point load on an SS beam (or 5wL⁴/384EI for UDL)
explanation: WL³/48EI is the classic closed-form the lab results are compared to.

topic: Measurement of deflections in statically determinate beam
stem: Open-ended deflection rigs substitute dial gauges with which modern sensor?
options: LVDT (linear variable differential transformer) with a data logger
explanation: LVDTs give an electrical output proportional to displacement suited to automatic recording.

topic: Measurement of strain in a bar
stem: Electrical-resistance strain gauges measure strain by converting the change of resistance of a bonded metal foil with deformation of the surface.
explanation: True: foil resistance changes with strain per \(\Delta R/R=G\varepsilon\), G ≈ 2.

topic: Measurement of strain in a bar
stem: An electrical resistance strain gauge works on the principle that:
options: resistor resistance CHANGES with its manufacturer dimensions: \(\Delta R/R=G\varepsilon\) where G ≈ 2 is the gauge factor
explanation: Stretching the foil lengthens/thins it, raising resistance in proportion to strain.

topic: Measurement of strain in a bar
stem: A DEMEC/flat contact gauge with 100 mm gauge length reading 0.04 mm extension indicates strain:
explanation: Strain = extension/gauge length = 0.04/100 = 0.0004.

stem: The BEND TEST on a steel bar (e.g. reinforcement) judges:
