explanation: Water's μ roughly halves from 20 to 40 °C — a strong exponential-like temperature sensitivity.

stem: The VELOCITY PROFILE between two parallel plates, one stationary and one moving at V, with Newton's law and no pressure gradient, is:
options: a straight LINE varying linearly from 0 at the fixed plate to V at the moving plate — PLANAR COUETTE flow
explanation: τ constant through the film: du/dy constant → linear velocity profile.

stem: The practical measure used to control pump cavitation is:
options: NPSH (NET POSITIVE SUCTION HEAD) margin — available suction head above the vapour-pressure head at the pump inlet
explanation: Engineers ensure NPSH_available > NPSH_required to suppress cavitation in pump suction.

stem: If 100 litres of water under 20 bar extra pressure reduce to about 99.9 litres, its apparent bulk modulus is roughly:
explanation: 20 bar / 0.1% strain ≈ 2 × 10⁹ Pa — the standard water K value.

stem: Pressure at a POINT in a fluid is defined as:
options: normal compressive force per unit area as that area shrinks to the point: \(p=dF/dA\) (in N/m²)
explanation: Limiting ratio of elemental force to elemental area — assessed at the point level.

stem: PASCAL'S LAW states that the pressure at a point in a fluid at rest is:
options: EQUAL in ALL directions (isotropic) — lateral and vertical components equal at the point
explanation: Isotropy of static pressure — pressure acts equally in every direction at a point.

topic: Pressure variation with temperature, density and altitude
stem: Hydrostatic pressure variation with DEPTH in a liquid is:
options: \(p=\rho g h\) — LINEAR increase with depth h from the free surface
explanation: dp = ρg dh integrates to the familiar linear hydrostatic variation p = ρgh.

stem: Which statements about power transmission through pipes/nozzles hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: Transmitted power at the pipe end = rho.g.Q.H with H = available head at outlet
Maximum power efficiency occurs at hf = H/3 for head transmission
A nozzle converts pressure head into velocity head at exit
Power flows indefinitely regardless of losses
explanation: Outlet power and the hf = H/3 transmission optimum; lossless flow assumption is false.

topic: Resistance to flow of fluid in smooth and rough pipes, Moody's diagram
stem: MOODY'S DIAGRAM plots which relationship used for pipe-flow computation?
options: friction factor f against REYNOLDS NUMBER for various RELATIVE ROUGHNESS (epsilon/D) — covering smooth, transition and rough regimes
explanation: The Moody chart supplies f for any Re and k/D — universal pipe-loss reference.

topic: Hydrostatic pressure and force: horizontal, vertical and inclined surfaces
stem: The TOTAL hydrostatic force on a submerged plane surface equals:
options: \(P=\rho g \bar h A\) = pressure at the CENTROID × AREA (\(\bar h\) = depth of centroid)
explanation: Integrated pressure over the surface collapses to centroid-pressure × area.

topic: Hydrostatic pressure and force: horizontal, vertical and inclined surfaces
stem: The CENTRE OF PRESSURE on a submerged surface lies BELOW the centroid at:
options: \(h^*=\bar h+\frac{I_G\sin^2\theta}{A\bar h}\) — with I_G the 2nd moment about the centroidal axis, θ inclination
explanation: Pressure grows with depth, shifting the resultant's point of action below the centroid.

topic: Hydrostatic pressure and force: horizontal, vertical and inclined surfaces
stem: On a CURVED surface the hydrostatic force is resolved into components:
options: vertical component = WEIGHT of the liquid column above the surface; horizontal component = force on the vertical PROJECTION of the surface
explanation: FH from vertical projection, FV from the actual liquid column weight — combined vectorially.

topic: Buoyancy and stability of floating bodies
stem: BUOYANCY on an immersed body equals (Archimedes):
options: the WEIGHT of the DISPLACED FLUID acting upward at the CENTRE OF BUOYANCY (centroid of displaced volume)
explanation: Upthrust = ρgV_displaced; floatation when buoyancy balances the body's weight.

topic: Buoyancy and stability of floating bodies
stem: A floating body is STABLE (returns to upright) if its META-CENTRE M lies:
options: ABOVE the centre of gravity G — with metacentric height \(GM=\frac{I}{\nabla}-BG > 0\)
explanation: GM = BM − BG with BM = I/V — the classic ship-stability criterion GM > 0.

topic: Classification of fluid flow: steady and unsteady flow; uniform and non-uniform flow; laminar and turbulent flow; rotational and irrotational flow; compressible and incompressible flow; ideal and real fluid flow; one, two and three dimensional flows
stem: Classify a flow where properties do NOT change with TIME at each point:
options: STEADY flow — all fluid properties remain time-invariant at every location (unsteady otherwise)
explanation: Temporal independence defines 'steady' — the flow field's snapshot stays put over time.

topic: Classification of fluid flow: steady and unsteady flow; uniform and non-uniform flow; laminar and turbulent flow; rotational and irrotational flow; compressible and incompressible flow; ideal and real fluid flow; one, two and three dimensional flows
stem: The distinction between LAMINAR and TURBULENT flow was established experimentally by:
options: OSBORNE REYNOLDS' dye filament experiments (smooth dye thread laminar then bursting into turbulent at higher Re)
explanation: The dye-thread transition in Reynolds' pipe rig exposed the two regimes.

topic: Stream line, path line, streak line and stream tube
stem:
Assertion (A): In steady flow, streamlines, path lines and streak lines coincide.
Reason (R): With the velocity field invariant in time, every particle passes through the same tangential curves at all instants.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Time-invariant velocity (R) makes all three curves lie on one another (A).

topic: Stream line, path line, streak line and stream tube
stem: Pathline vs streakline:
options: PATHLINE traces ONE individual PARTICLE's history through time; STREAKLINE joins at an instant all particles that have PASSED a given fixed point
explanation: Particle history vs instantaneous locus through a marker-point — coincide in steady flow.

stem: Curves of constant stream function coincides with streamlines, and the difference of Psi between two lines equals discharge per unit depth between them.
explanation: True — both properties define the stream function in 2-D flow.

stem: The VELOCITY POTENTIAL function ϕ exists only when the flow is:
options: IRROTATIONAL — then velocity components are gradients of ϕ: \(u=\partial\phi/\partial x\) (Cauchy-Riemann links ϕ, Ψ in 2-D if ideal)
explanation: τω = 0 (irrotational) is the existence condition for the potential function.

topic: One-, two- and three-dimensional continuity equations in Cartesian coordinates
stem:
Assertion (A): For steady one-dimensional incompressible flow, A1V1 = A2V2.
Reason (R): Mass conservation across any two streamtube sections requires constant discharge when density is uniform.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Constant discharge per mass balance (R) is exactly the continuity statement (A).

topic: One-, two- and three-dimensional continuity equations in Cartesian coordinates
stem: The 3-D continuity equation for INCOMPRESSIBLE flow in Cartesian coordinates is:
options: \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial w}{\partial z}=0\)
explanation: Mass conservation for incompressible flow: the velocity DIVERGENCE vanishes.

stem: Classes of forces acting on fluid elements:
options: SURFACE forces (pressure, viscosity/shear) acting on the element faces + BODY forces (gravity, centrifugal) distributed through volume
explanation: Pressure/shear on the surface, gravity through the body — summed in the motion equation.

stem: EULER'S EQUATION of motion is an equation for:
options: acceleration of an IDEAL (non-viscous) fluid under pressure and gravity — force balance per unit mass along the streamline
explanation: Ideal-fluid momentum balance — the seed from which Bernoulli's equation is integrated.

stem: BERNOULLI'S EQUATION along a streamline for steady incompressible inviscid flow is:
options: \(\frac{p}{\rho g}+\frac{V^2}{2g}+z=\text{constant}\) — sum of pressure head + velocity head + elevation head
explanation: Euler's equation integrated along a streamline — head form of the statement.

topic: Branching of pipes, three reservoir problem
stem: The THREE-RESERVOIR problem of interconnected pipes is solved by:
options: assuming a JUNCTION LEVEL and iterating flows so that Q_in = Q_out balances (continuity at junction within the loop)
explanation: Guessing junction piezometric head, iterating to continuity balance — the classic branch-node method.

stem: The ENERGY/EULER-Bernoulli principle in real pipe flow says that between two sections:
options: the upstream total head equals the downstream total head PLUS the HEAD LOSSES (h_f + minor) suffered along between
explanation: H1 = H2 + h_L — observed mechanical-energy balance with friction/dissipation toll.

topic: Practical applications of Bernoulli's equation: venturimeter, orifice meter and pitot tube
stem: Which statements on venturimeters hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: Bernoulli + continuity produce the discharge formula
Throat pressure RISES with converging speed
A differential U-tube manometer reads the pressure drop
explanation: Throat pressure falls, not rises; the other three statements are correct.

topic: Flow through laterals, flows in dead end pipes, siphon
stem: A SIPHON lifts water over a summit between reservoirs when:
options: the highest-point PRESSURE must remain ABOVE the vapour pressure and priming established — atmospheric pressure drives the flow
explanation: Summit pressure exceeding vapour pressure is the siphon's operating condition.

stem: The MOMENTUM principle applied to a control volume with steady flow states:
options: Σ Forces on the CV = RATE of change of momentum flux: \(\sum F = \dot m (V_2 - V_1)\)
explanation: Force balances momentum-flux change — the working tool for jet/bend/nozzle forces.

topic: Forces exerted by fluid flow on pipe bend
stem: At a horizontal pipe BEND, the anchoring force must resist:
options: the VECTOR change of momentum flux through the deflected flow plus pressure contributions — resolved into x and y components
explanation: Deflecting the stream changes its momentum vector; the bend/thrust-block must supply that force.

stem: Which statements distinguish vortex flows? (Select all that apply.)
options: Forced vortex needs external energy input
Free vortex also needs external torque
explanation: Free vortex is torque-free (conserved energy); the first three statements characterize both.

stem: BUCKINGHAM'S Π-THEOREM states that a relation of n variables with m fundamental dimensions can be written in:
options: n - m independent DIMENSIONLESS pi-groups — the counting rule of dimensional analysis
explanation: Counting fundamental dimensions (M, L, T) reduces variables to n−m dimensionless groups.

stem: DIMENSIONAL HOMOGENEITY of a correct physical equation demands that:
options: all ADDED terms carry the SAME dimensions (velocity + head is ill-formed; head + head is well-formed)
explanation: Only same-dimension terms may add — a built-in check on every derived formula.

topic: Similitude, Model studies, Types of models
stem: Complete SIMILITUDE between model and prototype requires:
options: GEOMETRIC (shapes scaled), KINEMATIC ( velocities ratios ) and DYNAMIC similitude (force/number ratios equal)
explanation: Geometric + kinematic + dynamic similarity jointly make model results transferable.

topic: Dynamic Similitude: Definitions of Reynolds Number, Froude Number, Mach Number, Weber Number and Euler Number
stem: Match dimensionless numbers to their governing comparisons:
options: Re = inertia/VISCOSITY; Froude = inertia/GRAVITY; Mach = inertia/COMPRESSIBILITY; Weber = inertia/SURFACE-TENSION; Euler = pressure/inertia
explanation: The five force-ratio numbers underpinning different similitude regimes.

topic: Laminar flow through: circular pipes, annulus and parallel plates
stem: HAGEN-POISEUILLE's law for laminar pipe flow gives discharge:
options: \(Q=\frac{\pi\, i\, d^4}{128\mu}\) with \(\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\) — discharge ∝ d⁴ and ∝ (−dp/dx)/μ
explanation: Laminar circular-tube flow is exquisitely diameter-sensitive — d⁴ dependence.

stem: Stoke's law states the settling drag as 6 pi mu V R — linear in velocity, valid only at very low Reynolds number.
explanation: True — linear low-Re drag that underpins falling-sphere viscometry.

stem: VISCOSITY is measured in the lab classically by:
options: CAPILLARY-TUBE, rotating-cylinder/cup, and falling-sphere VISCOMETERS (plus Saybolt etc. industrial efflux-time types)
explanation: Capillary, rotational and viscometer families quantify µ for oils/mixtures.

topic: Flow through Pipes: Loss of head through pipes, Darcy-Wiesbatch equation, minor losses, total energy equation, hydraulic gradient line
stem: The DARCY-WEISBACH formula for friction head loss in a pipe is:
options: hf = f L V^2/(2 g D) — friction head loss over length L in a pipe of diameter D with friction factor f
explanation: The workhorse pipe-friction relation — f from Re and roughness (Moody).

topic: Flow through Pipes: Loss of head through pipes, Darcy-Wiesbatch equation, minor losses, total energy equation, hydraulic gradient line
stem: The HYDRAULIC GRADIENT LINE and ENERGY LINE differ by:
options: the VELOCITY HEAD V^2/2g — the EGL lies the velocity head above the HGL (pressure + elevation heads)
explanation: HGL = p/γ + z; EGL adds V²/2g — separated by the velocity head.

topic: Pipes in series, equivalent pipes, pipes in parallel
stem:
Assertion (A): Pipes in parallel share the same head loss while discharges add.
Reason (R): Branches join the SAME two junctions, so each branch experiences the same head difference between them.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Common junction heads (R) force the equal-head division of flows (A).

topic: Analysis of pipe networks: Hardy Cross method
stem: The HARDY CROSS method analyses pipe networks iteratively by:
options: BALANCING each loop's head losses: assume discharges, then CORRECT flows per loop from the residual head imbalance until convergence
explanation: Successive-correction loop-balancing — the classical network solver before computers.

topic: Water hammer in pipes and control measures
stem: WATER HAMMER in a closed conduit describes:
options: the PRESSURE SURGE produced when flow is arrested suddenly (valve closure) — wave speed c ≈ 1400 m/s transmitting damaging transients
explanation: Abrupt flow stoppage converts kinetic energy into a destructive pressure wave in the pipe.

stem: The falling-sphere viscometer determines a liquid's viscosity by:
options: timing the steady TERMINAL settling velocity of a known ball and applying Stokes' law
explanation: Stokes' drag at terminal velocity gives mu from descent time.

stem: Saybolt and Redwood viscometers report viscosity as:
options: seconds of EFFLUX TIME for a standard volume through a standard orifice, converted to kinematic viscosity by formula
explanation: Empirical efflux-time instruments; seconds convert to nu via instrument constants.

stem: In a capillary viscometer, Q = pi.p.r^4/(8.mu.l), so the computed viscosity is most sensitive to errors in:
options: tube radius - it enters with the FOURTH power
explanation: The r^4 term dominates the uncertainty budget of capillary viscometry.

stem: Falling-sphere viscometry is valid only in the Stokes regime, hence the setup needs:
options: transparent liquid and sufficient depth so a TRUE low-Re terminal velocity is measured
explanation: Only low-Re terminal settling yields the linear Stokes drag relation used.

stem: Which parameters affect a falling-sphere viscosity reading? (Select all that apply.)
options: attainment of steady terminal velocity before timing
explanation: Colours are irrelevant; geometry, temperature and terminal state govern the result.

stem: A piezometer tube is suitable for measuring:
options: moderate POSITIVE gauge pressures of liquids in pipes
explanation: Simple liquid-column device, limited to modest positive liquid pressures.

stem: A differential U-tube manometer joins two pipe points carrying fluid of sp. gr. S1 with gauge liquid S2; the pressure-head difference in terms of the flowing fluid equals:
options: x(S2/S1 - 1), x being the manometric deflection
explanation: Balancing limb pressures yields h = x(S2/S1 - 1).

stem: A Bourdon-tube pressure gauge senses pressure through:
options: elastic deformation of a curved, flattened tube that tends to straighten as internal pressure rises
explanation: Tube straightening drives a linkage and pointer on the dial.

stem: An inverted U-tube carrying light oil is chosen to measure SMALL pressure differences because:
options: the light separating liquid AMPLIFIES the deflection for a given head difference
explanation: Small Sg of the gauge liquid magnifies the readable leg difference.

stem: Modern pressure transducers convert fluid pressure into an electrical signal using strain-gauge or piezoelectric elements, enabling continuous recording.
explanation: True - electromechanical conversion permits data logging and transients capture.

stem: In the metacentric-height experiment, a small mass w is shifted transversely by x and the vessel of weight W heels by angle theta; GM is computed as:
explanation: Equating applied and righting moments gives the standard GM formula.

stem: A floating vessel is stable in heel when its metacentre M lies:
options: ABOVE the centre of gravity G (GM > 0)
explanation: Positive metacentric height supplies a restoring (righting) moment.

stem: For small heels, the METACENTRE is the intersection of the new buoyant-force line of action with:
options: the vertical axis through the upright centre of buoyancy
explanation: Definition of M used in the stability experiment.

stem:
Assertion (A): Raising the centre of gravity can render the vessel unstable even if GM was positive before.
Reason (R): GM = BM - BG, so increasing BG directly shrinks the righting lever.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: R accounts for the loss of stability in A.

topic: Hydrostatics Force on Flat Surfaces/Curved Surfaces
stem: In the quadrant-balance hydrostatics experiment, the fluid force on the end surface is found by balancing its moment against:
options: a known WEIGHT on the opposite arm, then comparing observed and theoretical centre of pressure
explanation: Moment equilibrium of the torqued quadrant locates resultant and CP.

topic: Hydrostatics Force on Flat Surfaces/Curved Surfaces
stem: For a fully submerged plane surface in a static liquid, the centre of pressure lies:
options: BELOW the centroid - approaching it as depth increases
explanation: Pressure grows with depth, pushing the resultant below the centroid.

topic: Hydrostatics Force on Flat Surfaces/Curved Surfaces
stem: Which statements about the quadrant-balance hydrostatics experiment hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: partial immersion: measured moment matches hydrostatic theory for the end face
fully submerged: readings verify the computed centre-of-pressure depth
the resultant acts NORMAL to the surface
explanation: Buoyancy is not the whole story; the other three statements are correct.

stem: In the Bernoulli apparatus, the piezometer risers at each section read the:
options: STATIC head (pressure + datum) at that section
explanation: Side tappings sense static pressure; velocity head is added separately.

stem: Plotting total head H = (piezometric head) + V^2/2g along the tapered duct in the rig typically shows:
options: an almost constant H with a SLIGHT DECLINE from wall friction in the real fluid
explanation: Ideal Bernoulli demands constant H; real friction nibbles at it.

stem: In the DIVERGING portion of the Bernoulli duct, as area increases:
options: velocity head falls and pressure head RECOVERS - energy merely changes form
explanation: Continuity lowers V; Bernoulli converts that drop into pressure rise.

stem:
Assertion (A): The measured total head falls slightly along the test duct though ideal Bernoulli theory expects constancy.
Reason (R): Real-fluid friction continuously converts mechanical energy into heat along the flow.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Friction loss (R) explains the observed head decline (A).

stem: In a venturimeter experiment, the coefficient of discharge Cd is obtained from:
options: ACTUAL discharge (tank/weighing) divided by the THEORETICAL Bernoulli discharge
explanation: Cd = Q_actual / Q_theoretical - the standard calibration number.

stem: The DIVERGING cone of a venturi is made longer (5-7 deg half-angle) than the converging cone because:
options: a GRADUAL expansion prevents boundary-layer separation and and recovers most of the pressure head
explanation: Separation recovery, not cost, dictates the long diffuser.

stem: A typical coefficient of discharge for a venturimeter lies around:
explanation: Streamlined passage gives very high Cd.

stem: In a horizontal venturimeter, the static pressure at the throat is lower than the inlet pressure.
explanation: True - continuity speeds the flow at throat, Bernoulli drops its pressure.

stem: The vena contracta of an orifice installation is the section where the jet:
options: has MINIMUM area and maximum velocity, slightly downstream of the plate
explanation: Streamtube keeps contracting past the sharp edge before recovering.

stem: The orifice meter Cd (about 0.6) is far below the venturimeter's (about 0.98) because:
options: the sharp edge forces sudden contraction plus jet separation and strong eddy losses
explanation: Geometric contraction coefficient times losses depresses Cd to about 0.6.

stem: On identical duty, the ORIFICE METER wastes much more permanent head than a venturimeter chiefly due to:
options: sudden expansion of the jet downstream of the plate, dissipating energy in eddies
explanation: Little pressure recovery downstream of the plate = big permanent loss.

stem: Which statements about orifice meters are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: cheaper and more compact than a venturi
accuracy degrades as the edge wears
explanation: Loss is NOT negligible; the other three statements hold.

stem: The impact-of-jets rig loads the vane with known weights to demonstrate that the measured force equals:
options: the MOMENTUM-FLUX change of the jet, F = rho.Q.(V1 - V2x)
explanation: Comparison of reaction force with momentum change verifies the momentum equation.

stem: A jet striking a HEMISPHERICAL vane that reverses it through 180 degrees exerts (stationary vane) a force close to:
explanation: Full reversal doubles the momentum flux of the normal flat plate.

stem: For a jet hitting a vane MOVING at velocity u in the jet direction, the impact force becomes:
explanation: Relative velocity squared scales the absolute deflection force.

stem:
Assertion (A): Doubling jet velocity quadruples the impact force on a fixed normal plate.
Reason (R): The momentum equation gives F = rho.a.V^2 - force grows with velocity squared.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: R states the quadratic law used in A.

stem: A Hele-Shaw (flow visualisation) table can demonstrate ideal-flow patterns around shapes because:
options: slow viscous motion between closely spaced plates obeys equations analogous to 2-D potential flow
explanation: Creeping Hele-Shaw flow shares the 2-D potential streamline solution.

stem: In ideal-flow visualisation around a circular cylinder, the STAGNATION points observed at front and rear imply:
options: ZERO velocity there, with maximum velocity at the cylinder sides
explanation: Potential-flow solution: stagnation at poles, top speed at shoulders.

stem: The flow net drawn from dye streams shows streamlines meeting equipotential lines at:
explanation: Stream and potential functions are conjugate; the net is orthogonal.

stem: The entrance (establishment) length of pipe flow is the upstream stretch where:
options: wall boundary layers grow and MERGE at the axis - beyond it the fully developed profile exists
explanation: Development continues until the profile becomes invariant downstream.

stem: For LAMINAR flow in a circular tube, the entrance length is approximately:
explanation: Standard correlation Le/D = 0.05 Re for laminar developing flow.

stem: A pitot traverse across a pipe in LAMINAR flow reveals a velocity profile that is:
options: PARABOLIC with centre velocity = 2 x mean velocity
explanation: Hagen-Poiseuille profile: u_max = 2 u_mean.

stem: Reynolds' dye experiment classifies pipe flow as laminar for Re below about:
options: 2100-2300 - the dye thread stays a straight, unbroken filament
explanation: Critical Re roughly 2300 marks the transition observed with the dye.

stem: Ordinary Portland cement's principal clinker compounds are:
explanation: Bogue compounds: tri/di-calcium silicates, aluminate and ferrite drive strength and heat.

stem: The cement compound contributing the GREATEST EARLY-STRENGTH gain is:
explanation: Alite (C3S) hydrates fast, giving 7-day strength.

stem: Per IS 4031, the INITIAL setting time of cement should not be less than:
explanation: 30 minimum minutes allow mixing and placing before stiffening.

stem:
Assertion (A): The 43 and 53 grades of Portland cement denote its 28-day characteristic compressive strength in MPa.
Reason (R): Standard cement mortar cubes are tested at 28 days to certify the strength grade.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: R states the very test that backs the grade definition in A.

stem: Pozzolana Portland Cement (fly-ash based) gains later strength because fly ash silica:
options: reacts with liberated Ca(OH)2 forming MORE C-S-H over time
explanation: Secondary pozzolanic reaction densifies paste beyond 28 days.

stem:
Assertion (A): Excess gypsum beyond its retarder dose retards setting indefinitely.
Reason (R): Gypsum regulates C3A hydration as a retarder but only within its proper 2-4% dosage.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: beyond dosage, effects reverse with expansion risk; R itself is true.

stem: M-Sand (manufactured sand) is produced by:
options: crushing hard granite/basalt rock in vertical-shaft impactors and grading to zone sizes
explanation: Crushed rock fines replace increasingly scarce river sand.

stem: A key ADVANTAGE of M-Sand over river sand in concrete:
options: consistent gradation and cubical particles with no silt/clay impurities
explanation: Control of gradation and cleanliness gives reliable strength and workability.

stem: Excessive micro-fines beyond code limits in M-Sand primarily cause:
options: higher water demand and loss of workability/strength
explanation: Code caps fines (IS 383 limits) to protect mix water and strength.

topic: Concrete (plain, reinforced and steel fibre/ glass fibre-reinforced, light-weight concrete, High Performance Concrete, Polymer Concrete)
stem: The essential difference between PLAIN and REINFORCED cement concrete:
options: RCC embeds steel bars that take tensile stresses that plain concrete cannot
explanation: Concrete is strong in compression, weak in tension; steel supplies tensile capacity.

topic: Concrete (plain, reinforced and steel fibre/ glass fibre-reinforced, light-weight concrete, High Performance Concrete, Polymer Concrete)
stem: STEEL-FIBRE reinforced concrete is used mainly to improve:
options: post-crack toughness, impact resistance and crack control
explanation: Fibres bridge cracks, adding ductility after matrix cracking.

topic: Concrete (plain, reinforced and steel fibre/ glass fibre-reinforced, light-weight concrete, High Performance Concrete, Polymer Concrete)
stem: LIGHTWEIGHT concrete is made with aggregates like expanded clay/pumice primarily to:
options: reduce self-weight in long spans, precast and insulated slabs
explanation: Low density cuts dead load, offset by lower strength - useful in high rises.

topic: Concrete (plain, reinforced and steel fibre/ glass fibre-reinforced, light-weight concrete, High Performance Concrete, Polymer Concrete)
stem: HIGH PERFORMANCE CONCRETE (HPC) is distinguished from ordinary concrete chiefly by:
options: very low w/b ratio with mineral and chemical admixtures for high strength AND durability
explanation: HPC specs target permeability and durability beyond mere cube strength.

topic: Concrete (plain, reinforced and steel fibre/ glass fibre-reinforced, light-weight concrete, High Performance Concrete, Polymer Concrete)
stem: POLYMER concrete replaces cement binder with:
options: polymeric resin binders (epoxy/polyester) giving fast cure and chemical resistance
explanation: Resin-bonded aggregates cure in hours, used in overlays and repairs.

topic: Concrete (plain, reinforced and steel fibre/ glass fibre-reinforced, light-weight concrete, High Performance Concrete, Polymer Concrete)
stem: Glass fibre-reinforced concrete uses ALKALI-RESISTANT glass fibres because:
options: ordinary E-glass fibres degrade in the alkaline pore solution of cement
explanation: High pH attacks common fibres; AR-glass retains strength in the matrix.

stem: Most construction ceramics (bricks, tiles, sanitaryware) are manufactured by:
options: shaping clay minerals and then FIRING to sinter the body
explanation: Ceramics consolidate by high-temperature firing, not chemical setting.

stem: REFRACTORY materials used in furnace linings must primarily resist:
options: high temperatures and their corrosive slag environments
explanation: Refractoriness and chemical inertness at temperature define refractories.

stem: Silica-based ACIDIC refractories should NOT be used with:
options: basic slags like lime-rich melts that react with and dissolve silica
explanation: Acid-base reaction at high temperature degrades the lining.

stem: High-alumina bricks (mullite/corundum) are selected over fireclay bricks when the furnace:
options: operates at still higher temperatures and needs better load-bearing at heat
explanation: Higher alumina content raises refractoriness and hot strength.

stem: Bitumen used in flexible pavements behaves as:
options: a thermo-viscoelastic binder - soft with heat, stiff/brittle when cold
explanation: Temperature-susceptible binder gluing aggregates in asphalt mixes.

stem: Under the IS 73 VG system, a VG-30 bitumen's figure refers to:
options: the absolute viscosity range at 60 deg C
explanation: Viscosity grading replaced penetration grades for rational selection.

stem: The ring-and-ball softening point is the temperature at which the bitumen softens enough for a standard ball to sink through it.
explanation: True - the sink-through temperature defines softening point.

stem: High ductility of bitumen is desirable because it lets the binder stretch under thermal and traffic strains without cracking.
explanation: True - ductile binder resists reflection cracking.

stem: Cutback and emulsion bitumens are preferred for COLD applications because:
options: solvent or water carriers lower working viscosity without heating the binder
explanation: Fluid carriers evaporate/break, leaving the binder after placement.

stem: Seasoned timber is preferred for structural use chiefly because drying:
options: reduces shrinkage, decay risk and improves strength-to-weight behaviour
explanation: Moisture below fibre saturation stabilizes dimensions and fights fungi.

stem: Teak and sal are favoured structural timbers in India because of their:
options: natural oils and durability with good strength
explanation: Dense, oil-rich heartwood resists termites and rot.

stem: KNOTS in a timber member weaken it primarily by:
options: distorting grain continuity, concentrating stress and lowering tensile capacity
explanation: Local grain deviation and stress concentration cut design strength.

stem: Chemical preservative treatment of timber works by:
options: impregnating fungicides/toxics that resist decay and insect attack
explanation: Pressure impregnation extends service life in exposed conditions.

stem: Ordinary window GLASS is chemically a:
explanation: Noncrystalline random lattice - the structural secret and fragility of glass.

stem: Toughened (tempered) glass gains strength from:
options: surface COMPRESSIVE pre-stress introduced by rapid cooling after heating
explanation: Cracks must overcome surface compression before propagating.

stem: THERMOSET plastics differ from thermoplastics in that thermosets:
options: crosslink irreversibly on curing and cannot be remoulded by heating
explanation: Bakelite/epoxy networks set permanently; PE/PVC reclamp on reheating.

stem: Typical civil uses of PLASTICS (uPVC, HDPE) include:
options: pipes, water tanks, damp-proof membranes and conduits
explanation: Corrosion-proof, light polymer sections serve service lines heavily.

stem: Fe 415 / Fe 500 HYSD bar grade numbers denote the:
options: characteristic yield stress of the steel in MPa
explanation: fy values used directly in limit-state design of RCC.

stem: Structural steel's chief advantage over RCC in tension members:
options: high tensile strength with confirmed elastic modulus 2x10^5 MPa
explanation: Steel uses elastic design strength with E = 200 GPa.

stem: CAST IRON differs from wrought iron/steel chiefly by its:
options: high carbon content (2-4%) making it hard, brittle, good in compression
explanation: Carbon-rich, castable, brittle metal - poor ductile behaviour.

stem: GALVANIZING protects structural steel by:
options: a ZINC coating acting as barrier AND sacrificial anode
explanation: Zinc corrodes preferentially, shielding the base steel.

stem:
Assertion (A): Mild steel shows a well-defined yield plateau in its stress-strain curve, unlike HYSD bars.
Reason (R): Low-carbon steels exhibit upper and lower yield points due to dislocation locking, while HYSD marks its 0.2% proof stress.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: R explains the plateau distinction in A.

stem: Which statements about corrosion protection of steel hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: painting isolates steel from moisture and oxygen
cathodic protection forces the steel to be cathode in the cell
de-scaling and coating are needed near coasts
explanation: Corrosion weakens sections; passive, coating and cathodic methods protect steel.

stem: Which statements comparing M-Sand and river sand hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: M-Sand conserves river ecology by replacing dredged sand
angular M-Sand demands slight mix adjustment for workability
river sand has superior angular interlock always
M-Sand gradation can be engineered to IS 383 zones
explanation: Rounded river grains give no superior interlock; the other statements are correct.

stem: Which properties make aluminium attractive in some civil applications? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Cost is higher than steel; the other three justify its structural/facade use.

stem: A paint film comprises essentially:
explanation: Four components; binder forms the film, pigment gives colour/opacity.

stem: The PIGMENT in paint provides:
options: colour, opacity and protective hiding power
explanation: Pigments hide the substrate and boost durability.

stem: DRIERS (e.g., cobalt/manganese naphthenates) in paint shorten:
options: oxidation/polymerization time of the oil binder
explanation: Catalyze film curing of oil-based binders.

stem: VARNISH differs from paint principally because it:
options: lacks pigment - a clear resin/oil film allowing the base texture to show
explanation: Clear transparent finish over wood and over painted coats.

stem: A good exterior paint must have:
options: weathering resistance - UV stability and impermeability to moisture
explanation: Exterior durability hinges on UV and moisture resistance.

stem: Peeling/flaking failure of a paint film is most often traced to:
options: moisture behind the film or painting over dirty/damp surfaces
explanation: Adhesion fails on damp or unprepared substrates - correct surface prep first.

stem: ACOUSTICAL materials in halls work chiefly by:
options: absorbing sound energy (porous or resonant) to control reverberation
explanation: Absorption reduces reverberation time to the design value.

stem: Sabin's formula for reverberation time T = 0.161 V/A links it to:
options: hall volume V and total absorption A
explanation: Classic room-acoustics relation used in hall design.

stem: GEOTEXTILES placed between subgrade and granular fill perform the function of:
options: separation plus filtration and reinforcement of the soil system
explanation: They stop fines pumping while letting water pass, and add tensile capacity.

stem: A main difference between woven and nonwoven geotextiles:
options: nonwovens (needle-punched) give better drainage/filtration; wovens give higher tensile reinforcement
explanation: Structure decides the design function each fabric serves.

stem: Geotextile PERMEABILITY requirements exist so that:
options: seepage water can drain through while soil particles are retained
explanation: The filter criterion: retain soil yet pass water without clogging.

stem: Fibrous acoustic boards (wood-wool/soft fibre) absorb MOSTLY in:
options: high-frequency sound by viscous friction in their pores
explanation: Open pores damp airflow-born sound energy, stronger at high frequency.

stem: Which properties make geotextiles useful in roadworks? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Geotextiles persist; the first three are their documented functions in pavements.

stem: Natural RUBBER is vulcanized with sulphur mainly to:
options: crosslink chains into an elastic, durable, thermally stable network
explanation: Sulphur crosslinks prevent flow and restore resilience after stretch.

stem: Rubber BEARINGS and pads in bridges operate by:
options: absorbing vibration and allowing limited rotation/horizontal movement
explanation: Elastomeric bearings accommodate deck movements and isolate vibration.

stem: Rubber's waterproof sheet membranes serve civil works as:
options: lining of water bodies, damp-proof courses and expansion-joint fillers
explanation: Impermeable elastomer sheets seal water and absorb joint motion.

stem: Chrysotile ASBESTOS fibres were prized in construction for their:
options: heat resistance, non-combustibility and tensile reinforcement in cement
explanation: Asbestos-cement sheets/pipes exploited incombustibility and reinforcement.

stem: Asbestos use in buildings is now BANNED/restricted because airborne fibres cause:
options: asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma on inhalation
explanation: Serious carcinogenic hazard drove global phase-out.

stem: Neoprene (synthetic rubber) is selected over natural rubber for bridge pads because it:
options: resists ozone, oils, sunlight and weathering far better
explanation: Chloroprene withstands the outdoor chemical/aging environment.

stem: Crumb-rubber-modified bitumen in roads gains:
options: better elasticity, fatigue and rutting resistance from rubber's elastic network
explanation: Elastomer modifies binder rheology against permanent deformation.

stem: LAMINATES (plywood, laminboards) gain their strength by:
options: bonding crossed veneers so shrinkage and strength even out in both directions
explanation: Cross-grain construction balances anisotropy and resists warping.

stem: A structural ADHESIVE's lap-joint strength depends MOST on:
options: thorough surface preparation and correct binder/curing
explanation: Clean, abraded, degreased surfaces let adhesive wet and anchor the substrates.

stem: Epoxy adhesives bond concrete-to-concrete in repairs because they:
options: achieve chemical anchorage and negligible shrinkage on cure
explanation: Two-part resins polymerize with strong polar bonds onto hydrated surfaces.

stem: Common civil uses of decorative laminates (HPL sheets) are:
options: surfacing of furniture, panels, doors and lab worktops
explanation: Kraft-paper/resin pressed sheets serve interior wear surfaces.

stem:
Assertion (A): Polymer latex is dosed into repair mortars.
Reason (R): The polymer film interlocks the cement matrix, cutting permeability and raising bond and flexural strength.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Interlocking film (R) explains why latex-modified mortars repair better (A).

stem: GRAPHENE is best defined as:
options: a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon atoms in a hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice
explanation: Single-layer sp2 carbon - the thinnest, strongest known 2-D material.

stem: Graphene's exceptional properties include:
options: strength about 200 times that of steel with outstanding conductivity
explanation: Record stiffness/strength with electron mobility make it a research focus.

stem: Graphene added to cement composites is reported to:
options: accelerate hydration, densify the matrix and raise strength at small dosage
explanation: High-aspect sheets seed C-S-H and refine pores.

stem: A practical BARRIER to mass graphene use in construction today is:
options: high production cost and dispersion difficulties at scale
explanation: Cost-effective bulk production and uniform mixing remain unsolved.

stem: Graphene oxide, unlike pristine graphene, disperses in water because its sheets:
options: carry OXYGEN-bearing functional groups that make them hydrophilic
explanation: Functionalization enables aqueous processing into cement mixes.

topic: Carbon composites and other engineering materials including properties and uses of these
stem: CARBON FIBRE reinforced polymer (CFRP) wraps are applied to RCC columns to:
options: confine concrete and restore/raise axial and shear capacity
explanation: External confinement jacket - a standard retrofit/strengthening technique.

topic: Carbon composites and other engineering materials including properties and uses of these
stem: CFRP rebars are chosen over steel in aggressive zones because carbon fibre:
options: does not corrode and keeps high tensile strength at low weight
explanation: Corrosion immunity suits marine and chemically harsh exposure.

topic: Carbon composites and other engineering materials including properties and uses of these
stem: A drawback of FRP reinforcement versus steel inside concrete is its:
options: brittle failure without yield plateau and lower handling tolerance at bends
explanation: Linear-elastic to failure - design codes limit strains accordingly.

topic: Carbon composites and other engineering materials including properties and uses of these
stem: In a carbon composite, the POLYMER MATRIX functions to:
options: transfer load between fibres and protect them from abrasion/chemicals
explanation: Matrix supports, aligns and loads the reinforcing fibres.

topic: Carbon composites and other engineering materials including properties and uses of these
stem: Which advanced composite materials appear in civil works? (Select all that apply.)
options: CFRP sheets for flexural strengthening of beams
explanation: Asbestos is banned; carbon/glass/aramid FRPs are in active use.

stem:
Assertion (A): Graphene cement additives can cut permeability of the hardened paste.
Reason (R): Nano-layers fill pores and densify the interfacial zone around aggregates.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Seeding and pore-filling (R) explains lower permeability (A).

stem:
Assertion (A): Primer coat is applied before the final paint on new plaster.
Reason (R): Primer seals the porous alkaline surface and keys adhesion of subsequent coats.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Sealing/keying function (R) justifies priming (A).

stem: Vulcanized rubber regains its shape after large strains because sulphur crosslinks pin the molecular network.
explanation: True - crosslinks store elastic recovery in the network.

stem: Geotextiles can simultaneously act as filters and separators in a pavement section.
explanation: True - one fabric layer commonly serves both functions.

topic: Carbon composites and other engineering materials including properties and uses of these
stem: Which statements about carbon composites hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: very high specific strength and stiffness
explanation: Cost remains high; the first three are defining advantages.

stem: Materials engineering as a discipline connects a material's:
options: processing - structure - properties - performance in real service
explanation: The classic tetrahedron linking processing and microstructure to service performance.

stem: STIFFNESS of a material in the elastic range is measured by its:
options: modulus of elasticity (slope of the stress-strain line)
explanation: E = stress/strain in the elastic zone - unit deformation resistance.

stem: DUCTILITY of a material denotes its ability to:
options: undergo large plastic (permanent) deformation before fracture
explanation: Percent elongation/reduction in area quantify ductility.

stem: TOUGHNESS, distinct from strength, means the material's capacity to:
options: absorb energy in BOTH elastic and plastic range up to fracture
explanation: Area under the full stress-strain curve - energy absorbed before fracture.

stem: Hooke's law of linear elasticity states:
options: stress is proportional to strain within the proportional limit
explanation: sigma = E.epsilon characterizes the elastic regime.

stem: Poisson's ratio of most structural metals lies close to:
explanation: Lateral-to-axial strain ratio is about 0.3 for steels.

stem: Modulus of RIGIDITY (shear modulus) G relates to E through:
explanation: Isotropic elastic constants interrelate through Poisson ratio nu.

stem: PLASTIC deformation of metals proceeds mainly by:
options: dislocation slip along close-packed crystallographic planes
explanation: Slip of dislocations on slip systems produces permanent strain.

stem: The YIELD POINT of a metal marks the stress at which:
options: appreciable plastic deformation starts without load increase
explanation: Onset of plasticity; for non-yield metals the 0.2% proof stress substitutes.

topic: Tensile test: standards for different material (brittle, quasi-brittle, elastic and so on)
stem: A standard tensile test on a steel specimen determines:
options: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, percentage elongation and E
explanation: Complete engineering stress-strain data comes from the UTM pull.

topic: Tensile test: standards for different material (brittle, quasi-brittle, elastic and so on)
stem: UTS (ultimate tensile strength) of a metal is:
options: the maximum stress reached on the ENGINEERING stress-strain curve
explanation: Peak of engineering curve - necking starts right after it.

topic: Tensile test: standards for different material (brittle, quasi-brittle, elastic and so on)
stem: Standard gauge length in tensile tests of rubbers/wires/steels varies because:
options: elongation percentages differ so much that codes fix comparison gauge lengths per material class
explanation: IS/ASTM prescribe material-specific gauge lengths and speeds.

topic: Tensile test: standards for different material (brittle, quasi-brittle, elastic and so on)
stem: A QUASI-BRITTLE material like concrete tested in tension is usually characterized using:
options: split-cylinder and flexural indirect tests rather than direct pulling
explanation: Indirect tensile indices avoid gripping problems in brittle samples.

topic: True stress: strain interpretation of tensile test
stem: TRUE stress in a tensile test uses:
options: the INSTANTANEOUS (actual reduced) cross-sectional area, unlike engineering stress
explanation: True stress rises up to fracture instead of dropping as the engineering plot does.

topic: True stress: strain interpretation of tensile test
stem: TRUE strain is computed as:
options: ln(l/l0) - the integral of dl/l over the deformation
explanation: Logarithmic strain is additive for successive deformation stages.

stem: HARDNESS tests measure a material's resistance to:
options: localized plastic deformation - indentation or scratching
explanation: Indentation resistance correlates with strength and wear resistance.

stem: The BRINELL test uses a hardened steel/tungsten-carbide BALL indented under load; the BHN derives from:
options: load divided by the CURVED AREA of the spherical indentation
explanation: BHN = P / surface area of indentation.

stem: Vickers microhardness suits THIN sections and coatings because:
options: its tiny diamond-pyramid indent can be placed locally and measured optically
explanation: Small loads allow mapping hardness gradients across welds/case depths.

stem: TORSION test chiefly determines a shaft/specimen's:
options: shear modulus and shear strength of the section
explanation: Angle of twist under torque gives G; breaking torque gives shear strength.

stem: In pure torsion, maximum shear stress on a round shaft occurs at the:
explanation: tau = T.r/J - linearly from zero at centre to maximum at the surface.

stem: Which statements on bend/torsion testing hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: pure bending has zero shear within the central span
torsion on thin tubes approximates uniform shear
modulus of rupture exceeds direct tensile strength
explanation: Four-point loading renders pure bending; dense-flow clauses give rupture above direct tensile strength.

stem: A ceramic's strength is NOT a single value because results scatter widely; this scatter is handled using:
options: Weibull statistics - defect (flaw) population governs strength
explanation: Largest-flaw fracture statistics give characteristic strength values.

stem: INTERNAL FRICTION in oscillated solids reveals:
options: damping from atomic/defect mobility, measured via logarithmic decrement
explanation: Damping spectra locate defect relaxation processes in the material.

stem: CREEP of materials means:
options: time-dependent permanent deformation under CONSTANT sustained stress
explanation: Long-duration loadings produce viscous progressive strain.

stem: Creep in metals accelerates dramatically when service temperature exceeds about:
explanation: Homologous-temperature threshold where diffusion-controlled creep switches on.

stem: For CONCRETE, creep causes particular concern as:
options: increased long-term deflections and prestress loss in members
explanation: Sustained-loaded deflections can double over years; prestress bleeds away.

topic: Brittle fracture of steel: temperature transition approach
stem: Ships and bridges built of steel fail in brittle cleavage mainly:
options: below the DUCTILE-TO-BRITTLE transition temperature in cold service
explanation: BCC steels lose notch toughness sharply past DBTT.

topic: Brittle fracture of steel: temperature transition approach
stem: The ductile-to-brittle TRANSITION temperature of steel is normally determined by:
options: Charpy/Izod impact energy plotted against test temperature
explanation: Absorbed-energy curve vs temperature locates DBTT.

stem: Fracture mechanics differs from conventional strength design by explicitly considering:
options: CRACK-like defects with stress intensity acting at their tips
explanation: Defect-tolerant design methodology replacing pure allowable-stress criteria.

stem: Crack growth under sustained service reaches instability when K equals the material's:
explanation: K >= K_IC causes rapid unstable fracture.

topic: Discussion of fracture toughness testing: different materials
stem: FRACTURE TOUGHNESS testing (CT or SENB specimens) measures K_IC by:
options: loading a notched, pre-cracked specimen and reading the load at instability
explanation: Standard tests per ASTM E399 use fatigue-precracked compact/bend specimens.

stem: FATIGUE failure of materials occurs under:
options: repeated/cyclic stresses below the static ultimate strength
explanation: Progressive crack nucleation and growth under cycling ends in sudden failure.

stem: The ENDURANCE LIMIT of certain steels denotes a stress amplitude:
options: below which fatigue life is effectively infinite
explanation: Horizontal knee of the S-N curve for ferrous alloys.

topic: Structural integrity assessment procedure and fracture mechanics
stem: Which steps belong to a structural-integrity assessment? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Coating cannot substitute integrity analysis; NDT + FM criteria decide fitness.

stem: Which measures improve fatigue life in steel connections? (Select all that apply.)
options: removing stress concentrations and sharp notches
explanation: Spatters seed cracks; the other three delay crack initiation.

stem:
Assertion (A): Two steels of equal tensile strength can behave very differently in impact.
Reason (R): Toughness depends on absorbed energy, governed by composition and microstructure beyond mere strength.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Energy absorption (R) explains the impact difference in A.

stem:
Assertion (A): Prestressed concrete cables gradually lose some of their prestress.
Reason (R): Creep and shrinkage of concrete continuously shorten the member, relaxing the tendon.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Time-dependent shortening (R) drives prestress loss (A).

stem:
Assertion (A): Most fatigue cracks nucleate at the surface of a component.
Reason (R): Surface stress concentrations, scratches and finishes control fatigue crack initiation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Initiation mechanics (R) explains surface nucleation (A).

stem: A material that is HARD is not necessarily TOUGH; the two qualities are distinct mechanical properties.
explanation: True - hardness resists indentation, toughness absorbs fracture energy.

stem: In brittle materials the breaking stress equals nearly the maximum (ultimate) stress.
explanation: True - no yielding plateau separates them in brittle behaviour.

stem: The UNIVERSAL TESTING MACHINE (UTM) in a materials laboratory can perform:
options: tension, compression, bending and shear tests on specimens by one frame
explanation: Versatile loading frame with interchangeable grips and fixtures.

stem: An EXTENSOMETER fitted on a tensile specimen measures:
options: actual small elongation over the gauge length for computing E accurately
explanation: Precise local strain measurement needed for modulus determination.

stem: Load cells in modern UTMs convert force into a reading through:
options: strain-gauge bridges bonded to an elastic element deforming under load
explanation: Proportional electrical signal gives accurate load trace.

stem: A materials-testing LABORATORY layout must primarily ensure:
options: safe access, vibrating-machine isolation and standard-specimen storage/traceability
explanation: Safe functional workspace with calibration records meets code practice.

stem: CALIBRATION of a testing machine's load reading is periodically verified against:
options: proving rings or dynamometers traceable to national standards
explanation: Tie to national force standards keeps test results certifiable.

stem: Machine loads in a lab should be applied quasistatically, without impact, to stay within calibration validity.
explanation: True - shock application invalidates both machine and material response.

stem: The four BASIC mechanical loadings a specimen can experience are:
explanation: Fundamental stress states underlying all structural ade loading.

stem: A COMPRESSION test on concrete cubes uses the cube face area to compute:
options: crushing strength equal to maximum load over loaded cube area
explanation: f_ck = P/A - the classical acceptance-test number for concrete.

stem: SHEAR testing of rivets/pins is usually performed in:
options: single or double shear fixtures depending on the connection form
explanation: Fixtures reproduce the service number of shear planes.

stem: Mechanical testing of WOOD/steel/concrete requires DIFFERENT speeds and methods because:
options: rate-sensitive and structural behaviour differ so codes specify distinct procedure classes
explanation: Standards tailor loading rates, gauge lengths and sample geometry per material.

stem: The purpose of repeating a test on MULTIPLE specimens is to:
options: average over scatter and establish reliable characteristic/design values
explanation: Min 3 cube results are averaged; outliers rejected per IS.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: In the AISI/SAE system, 1020 steel means:
options: plain carbon steel containing about 0.20% carbon
explanation: First two digits class the steel; last two give 100x carbon percent.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: AISI 41xx steel grade signals presence of which alloying pair:
explanation: The 4 denotes the Cr-Mo family whose last two digits still give carbon.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: Indian designation IS 2062 E250 for structural steel uses the number to indicate:
options: minimum YIELD strength 250 MPa at quality grade E
explanation: Fe/E-classes name minimum yield strength in MPa per IS 2062.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: Grey cast iron FG 200 under IS 210 is coded by its:
options: minimum tensile strength 200 MPa of grey flake iron
explanation: FG + strength number denotes class of flake-graphite cast iron.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: Nonferrous aluminium alloy designation 6061 identifies:
options: a heat-treatable Mg-Si series alloy of the 6xxx family
explanation: First digit gives major alloying group of wrought aluminium.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: Copper alloys are named per their principal solute - bronze denotes Cu-Sn while brass denotes:
explanation: Classic division: tin for bronze, zinc for brass.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: Which naming-number facts hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: AISI last two digits give carbon x100
IS 1786 grades use yield strength numbers
explanation: 1045 has 0.45% carbon, not 45%; other statements correct.

topic: Naming systems for various irons, steels and nonferrous metals
stem: Steel specification codes fix testing rules and acceptance limits so that materials supplied under the same designation are interchangeable in quality.
explanation: True - designation acceptance rests on standard-specified tests.

stem: ELASTIC deformation is, by definition, the strain that:
options: fully recovers when the load is removed
explanation: Recoverable strain characterizes elasticity.

stem: ANELASTICITY means elastic strain that:
options: takes TIME to recover fully after unloading, seen as delayed elasticity
explanation: Time-dependent elastic response found in polymers and concrete.

stem: Elastic strain in metallic crystals is fundamentally the:
options: small reversible stretching of interatomic bonds about equilibrium positions
explanation: Bond stretching underlies the high elastic moduli of metals.

stem: The ELASTIC AFTER-EFFECT observed after prolonged loading appears as:
options: delayed additional strain even at constant stress in viscoelastic bodies
explanation: Slow equilibration of the structure parallels anelastic recovery.

stem: Microstrain precision in elastic deformation studies is typically resolved using:
explanation: Sub-millistrain resolution is needed for modulus and elastic-limit studies.

stem:
Assertion (A): A specimen that snaps back wholly on unloading has remained in the elastic regime throughout the loading.
Reason (R): Elastic deformation by definition is completely recoverable upon removal of load.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Recoverability (R) directly defines the elastic claim (A).

stem: PLASTIC deformation in metals occurs mostly by SLIP, which involves:
options: dislocations gliding on preferred planes producing permanent shape change
explanation: Line-defect motion - the operative plastic-flow mechanism in metals.

stem: TWINNING differs from slip because mechanical twins:
options: reorient the crystal lattice by shear creating mirror-image regions
explanation: Important in HCP metals (zinc, tin) where slip systems are limited.

stem: The HALL-PETCH relation states yield strength increases as:
options: grain size DECREASES - sigma = sigma_i + k.d^(-1/2)
explanation: Grain boundaries block dislocation slip - fine grains strengthen metals.

stem: CRITICAL RESOLVED SHEAR STRESS for slip activation measures:
options: the shear stress on the slip plane along slip direction required to start glide
explanation: Schmid factor links applied stress to the local slip driving force.

stem: Ductile-to-brittle differences between FCC and BCC plasticity stem chiefly from:
options: number and activity of slip systems at a given test temperature
explanation: Slip-system availability explains temperature-sensitive clay ductility.

stem:
Assertion (A): Cold-worked metals carry higher hardness and lower ductility than annealed ones.
Reason (R): Dislocation density rises during plastic work and their mutual hindering raises flow stress.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Work-hardening mechanism (R) explains the cold-work response (A).

stem: Which mechanisms permanently deform metals? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Vibration is thermal, not plastic; the first three give permanent deformation.

stem: The CHARPY impact test measures:
options: energy absorbed in breaking a notched specimen by a swinging pendulum
explanation: Pendulum height loss gives absorbed impact energy in joules.

stem: Charpy versus IZOD specimens differ in that:
options: Charpy lies horizontal as a simple beam struck opposite the notch; Izod stands as a cantilever
explanation: Support geometry differs - the classic Charpy-Izod distinction.

stem: The V-NOTCH in impact specimens serves to:
options: concentrate stress, converting the test into a measure of notch toughness
explanation: Triaxiality at the notch reveals brittle-response tendency.

stem: Plotting Charpy energy versus temperature for BCC steel reveals:
options: a transition from low-energy cleavage grabs lower shelf to ductile upper shelf
explanation: Lower/upper shelf energies mark temperature-dependent toughness.

stem: The 50% FATT APPEARANCE criterion defines ductile-to-brittle transition temperature by:
options: halved shear (fibrous) area fraction on the fracture surface
explanation: Fracture-Appearance Transition Temperature is one accepted DBTT definition.

stem: Low-temperature embrittlement of structural steel matters in civil works when members serve in:
options: cold regions, cryogenic plants or winter bridge exposures
explanation: Selection by transition temperature guards against brittle service failures.

stem:
Assertion (A): Absorbed Charpy energy of a structural steel rises as test temperature passes above its DBTT.
Reason (R): Above DBTT the microscopic fracture mechanism changes from cleavage to ductile microvoid coalescence.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Mechanism change (R) explains rising absorbed energy (A).

stem: Which statements about impact testing hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: absorbed energy is read from scale or pointer on the pendulum
tests are run at several temperatures for transition curves
cold testing makes steels tougher always
explanation: Cooling lowers toughness of BCC steel; the other statements are correct.

stem: Griffith's classical concept states fracture occurs when released strain energy at a crack covers:
options: surface energy needed to FORM TWO NEW FACES of the crack
explanation: Energy-balance criterion - the birth of fracture mechanics for brittle solids.

stem: The THREE MODES of crack-surface displacement in fracture mechanics are:
explanation: Mode I opening usually limits engineering fracture resistance.

stem: The stress singularity at an ideal sharp crack tip in an elastic body has order:
options: 1/sqrt(r) - stress tending infinite at the tip
explanation: The 1/sqrt(r) singularity motivates K-field description.

stem: Crack-tip plasticity in metals is admitted by fracture mechanics through:
options: plastic-zone corrections and J-integral / CTOD concepts beyond LEFM
explanation: Elastic-plastic fracture parameters extend Griffith/Irwin to ductile metals.

stem: A STRUCTURAL CRACK grows stably when:
options: K increases with crack length under the current load channel and stays below K_IC
explanation: Stable-tearing regime precedes instability in resistance-curve behaviour.

stem: FRACTURE MECHANICS parameters needed for design assessments include K_IC, fracture energy and the:
explanation: Materials data feed remaining-life and integrity calculations.

stem: Non-destructive testing (NDT) links to fracture mechanics by supplying:
options: flaw LOCATION and SIZE data to evaluate against critical crack dimensions
explanation: Detected defects are rated against a_crit = (K_IC/(Y.sigma))^2/pi.

stem: Mode I (opening) loading is the most dangerous crack mode and controls the majority of structural fractures.
explanation: True - opening tex tension normal to crack plane gives minimum toughness demand.

stem: Which entities follow from fracture mechanics? (Select all that apply.)
options: allowable defect size for a structure
explanation: Paint shade is irrelevant; the others are genuine design by-products of FM.

stem: K_IC values rise in general order from ceramics through:
options: ceramics lowest, then high-strength steels, then ductile metals
explanation: Toughness trends mirror available crack-tip plasticity.

stem: PLAIN STRAIN condition required for valid K_IC testing is met when the specimen is:
options: thick enough (B >= 2.5(K_IC/sigma_y)^2) that tip triaxiality fully develops
explanation: Thickness criterion assures the lowest, size-independent toughness.

stem: A valid fracture-toughness TEST records K_Q at instability and requires the fatigue pre-crack and thickness criteria before it qualifies as K_IC. A valid test certifies K_IC because:
options: P_max/P_Q ratio and crack geometry satisfy ASTM E399 validity checks
explanation: Only validity-checked values carry the K_IC designation.

stem: METALS show the highest typical fracture toughness values because crack tips:
options: blunt by plastic flow, demanding extra energy for further extension
explanation: Plastic dissipation is the toughness foundation in ductile metals.

stem: CONCRETE's fracture toughness is enhanced in practice by adding:
options: steel or polymer fibres bridging the cracks
explanation: Fibre bridging resists widening and dissipates energy - a toughness lever.

stem: Glass has extremely low apparent fracture toughness in service mainly because:
options: surface flaws amplify stress greatly - lacking any crack-tip slip relief
explanation: Sharp flaws lack blunting - the classic Griffith material.

stem: Raising the STRENGTH level of a structural steel generally does what to its fracture toughness K_IC?
options: LOWERS K_IC because the crack-tip plastic zone shrinks
explanation: Stronger steel means smaller tip plasticity and lower measured toughness - a classic trade-off.

stem:
Assertion (A): A stronger steel is not automatically safer against fracture in welded bridges.
Reason (R): High strength low-alloy grades may carry lower K_IC, allowing small flaws to become critical.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Strength-toughness balance (R) explains the assertion (A).

stem: Which statements on fracture toughness hold? (Select all that apply.)
options: K_IC is thickness-dependent until plane strain sets in
toughness can fall with temperature in BCC steel
fatigue pre-cracking simulates a sharp natural crack
thicker specimens always give HIGHER K_IC values
explanation: Thicker sections lower reported K toward the K_IC minimum; other statements correct.

stem: Fatigue crack growth per cycle under constant-amplitude loading is described by the PARIS law:
explanation: Empirical power law bridging the stress-intensity range and crack extension.

stem: The fatigue THRESHOLD delta K_th means:
options: the stress-intensity range below which existing cracks do NOT propagate
explanation: Sub-threshold cracks are treated as non-growing in life calculations.

stem: Beach marks / striation bands on a fatigue fracture surface record:
options: successive crack-front positions through progressive cyclic growth
explanation: Morphology signatures diagnostic of fatigue failures.

stem: Fatigue STRENGTH of welded details is much reduced because:
options: weld toe notches and residual tensile stresses act as crack starters
explanation: Codes assign detail categories with specific S-N classes for welds.

stem: MEAN STRESS influence on fatigue life is represented through:
options: Goodman / Gerber diagrams relating alternate stress capacity to mean stress
explanation: Tensile mean stress shortens life - corrected in the diagrams.

stem: CORROSION FATIGUE shortens fatigue life compared with air because:
options: aggressive environment assists crack initiation and increases growth rates
explanation: S-N curves may lose any endurance-limit knee in corrosive ambience.

stem: Shot PEENING improves fatigue life by introducing:
options: surface COMPRESSIVE residual stresses that delay crack nucleation
explanation: Compressive layers fight the tension that drives surface cracking.

stem: The S-N curve of a material is used in design to predict:
options: fatigue LIFE expected at a chosen cyclic stress amplitude
explanation: Stress amplitude vs cycles to failure - read life at service stress off the curve.

stem:
Assertion (A): Rotating axles of vehicles fail in classic fatigue even at stresses below yield.
Reason (R): Alternating bending produces millions of stress reversals that progressively nucleate cracks at surface defects.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Reversal-driven crack initiation (R) explains the axle failures (A).

stem: Which measures extend fatigue life? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Arc strikes seed cracks; the other three extend life.

stem: For metals the CREEP RATE during the steady (secondary) stage is described by Arrhenius form:
explanation: Temperature and stress sensitivity combine in the creep-law constants.

stem: CREEP RUPTURE (stress rupture) tests record:
options: time to failure under constant load at temperature
explanation: Larson-Miller style parameters summarize long-time rupture data.

stem: Creep mechanisms at very high homologous temperature are dominated by:
options: dislocation climb AND diffusion-controlled grain-boundary processes
explanation: Nabarro-Herring / Coble and climb govern high-T creep regimes.

stem: In CONCRETE, creep strain under sustained stress may reach:
options: several times the initial elastic strain over years
explanation: Specific creep and ultimate creep coefficients guide long-term design.

stem: Creep deformation in concrete is popularly attributed to:
options: moisture movement plus sliding/adjustment within the C-S-H gel structure under load
explanation: Gel microstructure response under sustained stress explains concrete creep.

stem: Reducing creep of structural concrete is aided by:
options: higher strength, steam curing, adequate humidity curing and lower water-cement ratio
explanation: Denser, mature paste creeps less - practical mitigation steps.

stem: POLYMER materials creep at ambient temperature because:
options: their glass transition lies near room temperature making chains mobile at service conditions
explanation: Service T near Tg makes polymers time-dependent load carriers.

stem:
Assertion (A): Timber props under floors sag gradually over years of sustained load.
Reason (R): Wood creeps - sustained stress plus moisture cycles produce time-dependent deflection.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Time-dependent strain (R) explains the observed sag (A).

stem: Stress-relaxation and creep are two facets of viscoelastic response: at constant deflection the load/stress decays with time.
explanation: True - fixed strain gives relaxation, fixed stress gives creep.

stem: Transformation TOUGHENED zirconia ceramics raise their K_IC chiefly via:
options: stress-induced martensitic phase change at crack tips that closes the crack
explanation: Volume-expanding transformation near the tip squeezes the crack shut - ceramic toughening route.

stem: The LARSON-MILLER parameter P = T(C + log t) lets engineers:
options: merge long-duration creep-rupture data into one master curve for extrapolation
explanation: Time-temperature equivalence projects long-life behaviour from short tests.

stem: CTOD (crack-tip opening displacement) is preferred to K when assessing fracture in:
options: elastic-plastic materials where the tip plastic zone invalidates pure LEFM
explanation: CTOD parameterizes crack driving force beyond linear-elastic validity.

topic: Gradation of coarse and fine aggregates
stem: SIEVE ANALYSIS (gradation) of aggregates plots percentage passing against:
options: sieve aperture size on a semilog scale
explanation: Gradation curve (IS 2386) shows size distribution of the aggregate sample.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Gradation of coarse and fine aggregates
stem: FINENESS MODULUS of an aggregate is the:
options: sum of cumulative percentages retained on standard sieves divided by 100
explanation: FM sums cumulative retained fractions - higher FM means coarser material.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Gradation of coarse and fine aggregates
stem: For good concrete, fine aggregate should fall in grading:
options: one of Zones I-IV of IS 383 with uniform band, avoiding too fine or too coarse
explanation: IS 383 zoning controls workability and water demand of the mix.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Gradation of coarse and fine aggregates
stem: Which aggregate tests enter design/quality-control routines? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Grading and index values govern mix design and QC; smell and taste are no tests.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Different corresponding tests and need/application of these tests in design and quality control
stem: The AGGREGATE IMPACT VALUE test appraises aggregate:
options: resistance to sudden impact loading relevant to road surfacing
explanation: AIV limit values qualify aggregates for pavement layers.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Different corresponding tests and need/application of these tests in design and quality control
stem: LOS ANGELES abrasion test measures aggregate:
options: percent wear under steel-ball abrasion - hardness against traffic attrition
explanation: Abrasion loss predicts degradation in service of road aggregates.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Different corresponding tests and need/application of these tests in design and quality control
stem: The FLAKINESS INDEX expresses the percentage of particles whose:
options: least thickness is less than 0.6 times the mean sieve size
explanation: Thickness gauge passes flaky particles - restricted for good interlock and strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Tensile Strength of materials & concrete composites
stem: In a SPLIT-TENSILE (Brazilian) test on a cylinder, tensile strength equals:
options: 2P/(pi.d.L) with P the failure load along the diametral plane
explanation: Indirect tension formula for concrete cylinders diametrically loaded.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

topic: Tensile Strength of materials & concrete composites
stem: DIRECT tension tests on brittle concrete specimens are avoided in practice mainly because:
options: grips induce local stresses and misalignment that spoil pure tensile failure
explanation: Stress non-uniformity invalidates direct pulls for brittle matrices.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

stem: AGGREGATE CRUSHING VALUE limits (30% surfacing, 45% other) judge aggregate:
options: resistance to gradual crushing under sustained compressive load
explanation: Crushing under the 40-tonne load for 10 minutes classifies aggregate strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Materials Testing & Evaluation Lab

stem: The TEN PERCENT FINES VALUE of aggregate is obtained from the crushing apparatus by:
options: computing the load that produces 10% material passing the finer sieve
